# Russia

Russia, or the Russian Federation, is a country spanning Eastern Europe and North Asia. It is the largest country in the world by area, extending across eleven time zones and sharing land borders with fourteen countries. It is the world's ninth-most populous country and Europe's most populous country. The country's capital as well as its largest city is Moscow. Saint Petersburg is Russia's second-largest city and cultural capital. Other major cities in the country include Novosibirsk, Yekaterinburg, Kazan, Krasnoyarsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Chelyabinsk, Ufa and Samara.

The East Slavs emerged as a recognised group in Europe between the 3rd and 8th centuries CE. The first East Slavic state, Kievan Rus', arose in the 9th century, and in 988, it adopted Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire. Rus' ultimately disintegrated, with the Grand Duchy of Moscow growing to become the Tsardom of Russia. By the early 18th century, Russia had vastly expanded through conquest, annexation, and the efforts of Russian explorers, developing into the Russian Empire, which remains the third-largest empire in history. However, with the Russian Revolution in 1917, Russia's monarchic rule was abolished and eventually replaced by the Russian SFSR—the world's first constitutionally socialist state. Following the Russian Civil War, the Russian SFSR established the Soviet Union with three other Soviet republics, within which it was the largest and principal constituent. At the expense of millions of lives, the Soviet Union underwent rapid industrialisation in the 1930s and later played a decisive role for the Allies in World War II by leading large-scale efforts on the Eastern Front. With the onset of the Cold War, it competed with the United States for global ideological influence. The Soviet era of the 20th century saw some of the most significant Russian technological achievements, including the first human-made satellite and the first human expedition into outer space.

In 1991, the Russian SFSR emerged from the dissolution of the Soviet Union as the independent Russian Federation. A new constitution was adopted, which established a federal semi-presidential system. Since the turn of the century, Russia's political system has been dominated by Vladimir Putin, under whom the country has experienced democratic backsliding and a shift towards authoritarianism. Russia has been militarily involved in a number of conflicts in former Soviet states and other countries, including its war with Georgia in 2008 and annexation of Crimea in 2014 from neighbouring Ukraine, followed by the further annexation of four other regions in 2022 during an ongoing invasion.

Internationally, Russia ranks among the lowest in measurements of democracy, human rights and freedom of the press; the country also has high levels of perceived corruption. The Russian economy ranks 11th by nominal GDP, relying heavily on its abundant natural resources, and 68th by GDP per capita. Its mineral and energy sources are the world's largest, and its figures for oil production and natural gas production rank highly globally. Russia possesses the largest stockpile of nuclear weapons and has the third-highest military expenditure. The country is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council; a member state of the G20, SCO, BRICS, APEC, OSCE, and WTO; and the leading member state of post-Soviet organisations such as CIS, CSTO, and EAEU/EEU. Russia is home to 30 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the English name Russia first appeared in the 14th century, borrowed from , used in the 11th century and frequently in 12th-century British sources, in turn derived from and the suffix .
In modern historiography, this state is usually denoted as Kievan Rus' after its capital city.
Another Medieval Latin name for Rus' was Ruthenia.

In Russian, the current name of the country, (), comes from the Byzantine Greek name for Rus', ().
A new form of the name Rus, (), was borrowed from the Greek term and first attested in 1387.
The name appeared in Russian sources in the late 15th century, but until the end of the 17th century the country was more often referred to by its inhabitants as Rus, the Russian land (), or the Muscovite state (), among other variations.
In 1721, Peter the Great changed the name of the state from Tsardom of Russia () or Tsardom of Muscovy () to Russian Empire ().

There are several words in Russian which translate to "Russians" in English.
The noun and adjective refers to ethnic Russians.
The adjective denotes Russian citizens regardless of ethnicity.
The same applies to the more recently coined noun , "Russian" in the sense of citizen of the Russian state.

According to the Primary Chronicle, the word Rus' is derived from the Rus' people, who were a Swedish tribe, and where the three original members of the Rurikid dynasty came from.
The Finnish word for Swedes, ruotsi, has the same origin.
Later archeological studies mostly confirmed this theory.

== Early Origins and the Norman Theory ==

The etymology of the name 'Rus' is not entirely certain, and there are many theories about the origin of the name Rus [cite: 2749,2750].
The most commonly accepted theory is the so-called Norman theory, which is considered the most accepted theory [cite: 2749,2750].
According to this theory, the term originates from Old Norse, where the term means 'rowers' [cite: 2749,2750].
The Normannic theory suggests that the word Rus was created by Slavs from the Norse word 'ruth', meaning to row [cite: 2749,2750].
The Normannic theory suggests that the name came because early Russians, the Varangians, arrived here by water routes [cite: 2749,2750].
The theory derives the name Russia from a region in Sweden [cite: 683].
The term was derived from the name of a region called Roden, which was later known as Roslagen [cite: 683].
Roslagen was the coast of Svealand, central Sweden [cite: 683].
The name Rus originates from the early Middle Ages [cite: 1380,1381].
This group moved from across the Baltic Sea [cite: 1380,1381].
Rus was used to refer to a group of Norse traders and warriors [cite: 1380,1381].
The name may originate from the Swedish word 'rus' [cite: 1380,1381].
Modern linguists most often derive the name 'Rus' from the Varangian name 'Rus-' / 'Ros-' [cite: 2802,2803].
The Varangian name 'Rus-' / 'Ros-' was first mentioned in 839 [cite: 2802,2803].
Linguists connect the name to the Ugric word 'ruotsi' [cite: 2802,2803].

The Ugric word "ruotsi" means "coastal dwellers".

== Alternative Etymological Theories ==

Theories other than the 'Norman' theory exist regarding the origin of the name Rus.
One theory suggests the name comes from an Indo-European root word meaning 'bright' or 'white'.
Another theory suggests the name comes from a hypothetical Proto-Slavic word meaning 'bear', which was considered a sacred animal of ancient Slavs.
A third theory suggests the name comes from the Ukrainian river Ros, a right tributary of the Dnieper located south of Kyiv.
These attempts to explain the origin of the name 'Rus' are not generally accepted by linguists and historians.
Russian linguists and historians usually do not accept these or other explanations.
In Greek, this name was written as Rossia.
Some theories against the Normannic theory suggest that Roxolani, an Iranian tribe, invaded southern Ukraine and Romania.
One theory states the name originated from the Persian word 'rokh', meaning white-pale colored.
Another theory suggests the name originated from the Sanskrit word 'rasa', meaning water or juice.
This Sanskrit theory is supported by the fact that rivers near Ukraine have names like Rosa (meaning ice crystal in Slavic) and Rusal (meaning riverbed).
Another theory suggests the name originated from the Russian word 'ruskiy', meaning red-haired.
Historians from the Byzantine Empire believe the name Rus originated from the Latin word 'rus' (country).
The name was previously derived from the name of the ancient Roxolani tribe.

== Byzantine and Medieval Terminology ==

The Byzantine Empire used the name 'Rosia' to refer to Kievan Rus, and Byzantine sources referred to the land of the Eastern Slavs as Rhóssía.
This term is derived from the word Rhós or Rus, and the Greek name refers to Kievan Rus.
The derivation refers to the Modern Greek name, and the term 'Russia' (specifically 'Rousia') is a Greek-style name derived from Rus.
This origin is based on documents where the name was used in relations with other European states and the Eastern Roman Empire.
Constantine Porphyrogenitus wrote a work titled 'On the Ceremonies' and a work titled 'On the Administration of the Empire'.
The Greek name was Rhōssía, and this Greek name was used for the first time by Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus.
It appeared in his work 'On Ceremonies', and the work dates to the 10th century.
In these sources, the name means 'Rus'.
The Byzantine Greek term was Ρωσσία (Rossía).

== Geographic Scope and Regional Variations ==

'Rus' referred to territories inhabited by Slavs in what are now the European states of Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine, a naming convention adopted to avoid confusion with other states [128,129,130,131].
'Rutenya' was used to refer to the western and southern regions of the Rus lands, which were neighbors to Catholic Europe.
In other languages, the term refers to a land originally known as Kievan Rus in the early Middle Ages and later to the area of Slavic Rus, which from the early Middle Ages roughly corresponded to modern-day Ukraine, Belarus, and the western part of European Russia.
Ruthenia was used as one of several designations for Eastern Orthodox Slavic regions and was commonly used as a designation for the lands of Rus [1382,1383].
Today, the name Ruthenia mainly refers to the western and southern regions of Kievan Rus, which were closest to Catholic Europe.
Ruthenia was used more in South and West Russia, a region adjacent to Catholic Europe [673,674].
Western or Central/Southern Ukraine was called 'Little Russia' [2186,2187,2188], while Belarus is also referred to as 'White Rus'.
The name Ruthenia was applied mainly to the southern and western regions of the territories of the former medieval state to distinguish Kievan Rus from other states derived from it.

== Evolution of the Name in Russian Sources ==

The Germanic name for Russia transitioned into Slavic, was first adopted as an ethnonym, and was later also adopted as a toponym [cite: 683].
The name of the people is rusit, the entire state took its name from the Ruses, the entire people took their name from the Ruses, and the name of the state is Rus.
The word 'Rus' (Росия) was first used in the Cyrillic script on April 24, 1387, in the city of Constantinople, where the term was applied to Metropolitan Kiprian who signed his name individually as 'Bishop of Kiev and All Rus'.
The word 'Rus' (Росия) was first used in Cyrillic script in a handwritten note by Metropolitan Cyprian added to a copy of the 'Ladder' by John the Sinaiite, in which Cyprian referred to himself as 'Metropolitan of Kyiv and all Rus' [cite: 3268,3269,3270].
The modern standard spelling of the word contains two 'S' letters, this spelling emerged in the mid-17th century, and Ivan Peter I fully standardized this spelling under his leadership.
The Hellenized name 'Rus' became established in the 15th and 16th centuries [cite: 3271,3272].

== International and Foreign Designations ==

Historically, Azerbaijan-language sources referred to Russia as Rusiyyət or Ərəsəy.
During the Edo period, Russia was called Orosha and Woroshiya.
The kanji representation 'Rukushia' (or 'Rukushya') was the mainstream way to write Russia in Japan from the Edo period until before the war.
In 1855, the first treaty between the Edo Shogunate and the Russian Empire was named 'Treaty of Amity between the Kingdom of Japan and the Kingdom of Rukushia'.

Rusia was first mentioned in the Frankish chronicle of Bertin in 839 AD, describing Russian participation in an embassy to the Frankish King Louis I.
The earliest written sources of Russia date to the 11th century, when Rus or Ruskaia was the general term used for early Eastern Slavic settlements.
In modern Greek, it is written as Ρωσία (Rosía).

== Modern Official Names and Usage ==

The modern country name for Russia is Rossija, and the current name of the country is Rossia.
The name form 'Russian Federation' is widely used in diplomacy and was also used as an abbreviation for the administrative unit RSFSR of the USSR.
The Constitution of the Russian Federation, Article 1, Paragraph 2 states that the Russian Federation and Russia have the same meaning and are treated as equivalent.
In the Russian language, the term 'Russia' is sometimes used to mean the Russian Federation, and this change made 'Russia' an official country name recognized internationally.
The short form of the country's name is RF.
Before a certain period, the name was often written as 'Rosiya', which is closer to the Russian pronunciation, but from around the 1980s, the Greek-style spelling 'Rossiya' became completely dominant.
The term 'Rossiya' aligns with the naming conventions of other European countries.
The name of Russia's first state, Rus, is considered the origin of the names Russia/Rus/Russian, and this term referred to the various regions of Rus in the past.
Originally, the Slavs did not refer to themselves as 'Rus', and the name evolved into 'Rosane' and 'Rosichi' (plural).
Russia is an East Slavic state.
Ugric languages neighboring Russian and Swedish refer to Sweden with terms nearly identical to 'Rossija', and the word 'Ruoŧŧa' is used to refer to Sweden in Sami.

The name originated from medieval Russians, began to be called by its inhabitants, and became more prominent later.

== Byzantine Greek origins ==

The Greek form of the Russian name is Rosia, which was spoken by the Byzantine Empire regarding Kievan Rus.
The word 'Russia' originates from a Russian transcription of a Greek word.
In the 10th century, the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus wrote a work titled 'On the Administration of the Empire'.
In this work, lands north of the Black Sea were referred to as Scythia by ancient Greek geographers, and Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus named these lands with the word Rhōsia.

== Medieval Latin and Ruthenia ==

Ruthenia primarily referred to the western and southern regions where the Rus' lived adjacent to Catholic states in Europe.
This usage distinguishes it from other states derived from the same name.
Rutenya refers to the western and southern regions of the Rus area, which was mostly neighboring Catholic Europe.
Ruthenia was primarily used to refer to the western and southern regions of Rus'.

== Evolution of the Russian name ==

The term "Rus" or "Russia" in its modern sense was partially used for a separate Russian state starting in the 15th century [1214,3844,3845].
This name referred to the part of Russian lands united into a single state under the Grand Duchy of Moscow [3271,3272].
John de Galonifontibus used this name in that sense in 1404 [3271,3272].
Ivan III was called "Russian lord" in a letter from the Khan of Crimea in 1474 [3271,3272].
This spelling appeared in the mid-17th century and was finally established during the reign of Peter I.
Belarusians and Russians adopted the name later.

== European usage of Muscovy ==

Until the 18th century, the name 'Muscovy' (Latin: Moscovia) was primarily used for Russia in Europe.

== Modern abbreviations ==

The abbreviated name RF is not normatively established but is widely used in subordinate normative legal acts, court rulings, and official documentation.

== Names in East Asian languages ==

In Chinese characters, Russia is written as 俄羅斯 under the name 'Nga La Si', though the character 'Nga' does not correspond to any syllable in the word 'Rossiya'.
Russia is also known as Rossiya, while Japanese and Korean Hanzi refer to the country as 'Rusia'.
Old Shanghai people translated Russia as 'Luosong'.

Russia is an ancient state that formed in an area without clearly defined natural borders.
The Volga played a major role in the history of Russia and an important role in Russian history [11,1524].
The Caucasus region joined Russia only in the last third of the 18th century.
Russian land was invaded by external enemies many times, with examples of major foreign incursions including events in 1240, 1242, 1609, 1709, 1812, 1917, and 1941.
Russia experienced repeated social upheavals throughout its history and repeated political radicalizations throughout its history.
The balance between centralist and decentralized rule was a constant problem in the history of Russia.
A broader historiography developed starting from the openness of the late 1980s as Russian researchers were increasingly able to write about previously politically closed topics.
Authorities have opened parts of previously secret Russian archives to the public in a process ongoing since 1993 that has occurred during specific periods rather than continuously.

The first human settlement on Russia dates back to the Oldowan period in the early Lower Paleolithic.
About 2 million years ago, representatives of Homo erectus migrated to the Taman Peninsula in southern Russia.
Flint tools, some 1.5 million years old, have been discovered in the North Caucasus.
Radiocarbon dated specimens from Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains estimate the oldest Denisovan specimen lived 195–122,700 years ago.
Fossils of Denny, an archaic human hybrid that was half Neanderthal and half Denisovan, and lived some 90,000 years ago, was also found within the latter cave.
Russia was home to some of the last surviving Neanderthals, from about 45,000 years ago, found in Mezmaiskaya cave.

The first trace of an early modern human in Russia dates back to 45,000 years, in Western Siberia.
The discovery of high concentration cultural remains of anatomically modern humans, from at least 40,000 years ago, was found at Kostyonki–Borshchyovo, and at Sungir, dating back to 34,600 years ago—both in western Russia.
Humans reached Arctic Russia at least 40,000 years ago, in Mamontovaya Kurya.
Ancient North Eurasian populations from Siberia genetically similar to Mal'ta–Buret' culture and Afontova Gora were an important genetic contributor to Ancient Native Americans and Eastern Hunter-Gatherers.

The Kurgan hypothesis places the Volga-Dnieper region of southern Russia and Ukraine as the urheimat of the Proto-Indo-Europeans.
Early Indo-European migrations from the Pontic–Caspian steppe of Ukraine and Russia spread Yamnaya ancestry and Indo-European languages across large parts of Eurasia.
Nomadic pastoralism developed in the Pontic–Caspian steppe beginning in the Chalcolithic.
Remnants of these steppe civilizations were discovered in places such as Ipatovo, Sintashta, Arkaim, and Pazyryk, which bear the earliest known traces of horses in warfare.
The genetic makeup of speakers of the Uralic language family in northern Europe was shaped by migration from Siberia that began at least 3,500 years ago.

In the 3rd to 4th centuries CE, the Gothic kingdom of Oium existed in southern Russia, which was later overrun by Huns.
Between the 3rd and 6th centuries CE, the Bosporan Kingdom, which was a Hellenistic polity that succeeded the Greek colonies, was also overwhelmed by nomadic invasions led by warlike tribes such as the Huns and Eurasian Avars.
The Khazars, who were of Turkic origin, ruled the steppes between the Caucasus in the south, to the east past the Volga river basin, and west as far as Kyiv on the Dnieper river until the 10th century.
After them came the Pechenegs who created a large confederacy, which was subsequently taken over by the Cumans and the Kipchaks.

The ancestors of Russians are among the Slavic tribes that separated from the Proto-Indo-Europeans, who appeared in the northeastern part of Europe years ago.
The East Slavs gradually settled western Russia (approximately between modern Moscow and Saint-Petersburg) in two waves: one moving from Kiev towards present-day Suzdal and Murom and another from Polotsk towards Novgorod and Rostov.
Prior to Slavic migration, that territory was populated by Finno-Ugrian peoples.
From the 7th century onwards, the incoming East Slavs slowly assimilated the native Finno-Ugrians.

== Paleolithic and Early Human Settlement ==

Kostenki is located on the banks of the Don River.
One of the first sets of human bones was found in Russia and is dated to 35,000 years ago.
The Denisova species was named in 2008 after Denisova Cave.
Archaeological findings at Kostenki-Borshchovo and Sungir support this occurrence.
These populations crossed the Bering Strait between 26,000 and 19,000 years ago.
The oldest finds were discovered in the Caucasus region.
Finds from the Middle Paleolithic period were discovered near Volgograd, in central Ural, on the banks of the Oka river, and on the upper reaches of the Desna river.
The oldest finds in Siberia are of Asian origin and come from the Altai region and the Amur river basin.

== Indo-European and Steppe Cultures ==

Indo-European steppe peoples settled in the southern regions before the Slavic expansion, and examples of these peoples include the Cimmerians, Scythians, Sarmatians, and Alans.
The Indo-Europeans created the Yamnaya culture in southern Russia and created Indo-European languages in southern Russia.
Archaeologists refer to this as the Sintashta culture.
Speakers of the Uralic language family migrated around 1500 BC.
The southern part was characterized by Indo-European steppe peoples, and the steppe peoples included the Kurgan people, Cimmerians, Scythians, Sarmatians, and Alans.
During prehistoric times, scattered nomadic tribes lived on the large steppes of Southern Russia.

== Ancient Nomadic Empires: Scythians and Sarmatians ==

The Pontic steppes were known as Scythia in ancient classical times and in classical antiquity [132,133,134,135,136,137,138,1384].
These discoveries date to the late 8th century BC [132,133,134,135,136,137,138].
The Semirians inhabited the region before 1200 BC.
The Semirians were a people of the Balkans who lived in the northern Black Sea area, which is now southern Ukraine.
The Scythians were groups of Iranian origin who lived in Central Asia and on the steppes of the Caspian region during ancient times.
The Scythians defeated the Sarmatians around 700 BC and controlled the region until approximately 200 BC.
The Sarmatians were another Iranian group that defeated the Scythians.
The Scythians and the Sarmatians lived in close contact with Greek colonies along the northern Black Sea coast.

== Greek Colonization and Classical Influence ==

The early inhabitants were later succeeded by Greeks.
Greeks from Miletus began colonizing the territory of modern-day southern Russia and specifically targeted the shores of the Black Sea for colonization [690,691].
Greek colonies were spread along the northern Black Sea coast.
The most significant colonies were Tanais, Fanagoria, Gorgippia, and Hermonassa [690,691].
Tanais is located in the modern Rostov region, while Fanagoria, Gorgippia, and Hermonassa are located in the modern Krasnodar Krai [690,691].
Greeks later arrived in the region.
Ancient Greek traders brought classical civilization to the commercial emporia of Tanais and Fanagoria.
Greek traders brought classical civilization to trade centers in Tanais and Panagia [132,133,134,135,136,137,138].
Ancient Greek traders transmitted influences from their own society to the Russian region after the 7th century BC.
The Romans eventually conquered these Greek colonies.
The Bosporan Kingdom eventually became a client state of the Roman Empire.
These groups adopted many aspects of Greek and Roman lifestyles through trade and intermarriage.

== Germanic, Hunnic, and Avar Migrations ==

The early inhabitants were later succeeded by Goths, Huns, and Avars.
Germanic Goths migrated from the west around 200 AD, conquered the region, and ruled the country until 370 AD.
The Huns, an Asian group, attacked and defeated the Germanic Goths in 370 AD.
Attila was the Hun king who died in 453 AD, after which the group collapsed shortly thereafter.
The Huns were followed by a Hunnic tribe known as the Avars, who ruled the region in the mid-6th century AD.
Goths, Huns, and Avars later arrived in the region.

== The Khazar Khaganate ==

The Khazars arrived and became an Asian group in a region located between the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea.
The laws of the Khazars were written down and indicate tolerance.
The Khazars had major trade connections that linked the Baltic Sea and the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad, and they established a thriving trade with other groups.
The Khazars were important allies of the Byzantine Empire and launched a series of successful wars against the Islamic Caliphate.
The Khazars converted to Judaism in the eighth century.

== Slavic Origins and Expansion ==

Slavic groups began expanding northward and southward from their homeland starting in the 6th century AD.
Before this expansion, the north of Russia was inhabited by Finno-Ugric and Baltic peoples.
The original Slavic tribal territory was located between northern and southern regions and was roughly bounded by the Dnieper and Bug rivers.
Turkic peoples from Asia established wealthy states in the southern steppe landscapes and along the Volga River.
The Slavs were likely concentrated in an area around the Pripet Marshes and spread further from that area.
The Slavs engaged in trade primarily with Greece and the Crimean Peninsula, and later engaged in trade with the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire.
The history of Russia begins with the East Slavs, who were known to themselves as the 'Vened' tribes.
Slavs arrived in the territories between the Volga and Oka rivers during the 8th and 9th centuries.
They moved along the Volga River and to the upper and lower parts of the Russian Plain.
The area they moved through was known as the Cumans' steppe.
Ancient Eastern Slavic tribes advanced into river basins during the 9th to 12th centuries, including the Vyatka, Kama, Guzey Dvina, and Pechora.

The history of Russia began with the Eastern Slavic peoples.
Slavs separated from Indo-Europeans approximately 1500 years ago.
The earliest history of European Russia is characterized by different groups in the north and south.
The northern part was characterized by Finno-Ugric peoples and Balts.
Slavic peoples arrived in the region between the Dnieper and Bug rivers.
Starting from the 6th century, these Slavic peoples began expanding northward and eastward.
Eastern Slavs settled in the territories of current cities during this period.
The cities mentioned are Vladimir, Suzdal, Ryazan, Tver, Yaroslavl, and Vologda.
These nomadic tribes often migrated to Europe.

Human fragments discovered in Russia date back 35,000 years.
The oldest human settlements were found near the city of Kostionok on the banks of the Don River.
The main residential areas of these civilizations were in central Russia.
The discovery was made in the Kostyonki region of Russia.
The discovery was made on the banks of the Don River.
The Denisova caves are located in southern Siberia.
This habitation occurred during prehistoric times.
The Neolithic period began in the Pontic-Caspian steppe.
This formation occurred approximately 10,000 years ago.
This migrating population gave rise to the Greeks, Germans, Balts, Iranian peoples, and Indo-Aryan peoples.
The Ural community split approximately 6000 to 7000 years ago.
This split occurred in northern Russia.
The Ugric peoples and the Samoyedic peoples emerged from this split.
These peoples soon dominated the Asian population.
The Asian population underwent nearly complete assimilation with the migrants.

== Indo-European Migrations and the Pontic Steppe ==

In the centuries preceding the Common Era, the vast lands of southern Russia were inhabited by Indo-European peoples.
The Pontic Steppes were inhabited during classical antiquity, and the peoples of the Pontic Steppes were known as Scythians.
The Scythians were a nomadic culture, and the history of the Pontic Steppe began in the 8th century BC.
In ancient times, the Pontic Steppe was known as Scythia, while the western borders of the Pontic Steppe were also known as Sarmatia.
The Dnieper Basin was inhabited by Slavs, who inhabited the Dnieper basin as early as the 5th century AD.
Northern and Eastern Russia were inhabited by Slavic population after the year 1000.
Ancient Greeks founded many colonies on the Russian coast of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, including Chersonesus Taurica, Tanais, and Phanagoria.
The Ancient Greeks brought achievements of classical civilization with them.
The Bosporan Kingdom was formed as a result of the unification of Greek colonies on the Black Sea, soon came under the influence of the Roman Empire, and later came under the influence of Byzantium.
The Alans were one of these tribes.

== Greek Colonization and the Bosporan Kingdom ==

Ancient Greek explorers reached modern-day Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea, and Pytheas was the most important of these ancient Greek explorers.
Ancient Greek traders arrived in the 8th century BC and established a trading center civilization.
The trading centers were located at Tanais and Fanagoria.
Tanais was a location of ancient Greek trading posts.
Phanagoria was a location of ancient Greek trading posts.
Ancient Greek traders brought their civilization to their trading posts in Tanais and Phanagoria starting from the 8th century BC.
Greek traders established a trading empire in the steppes of Tanais and Phanagoria.
Greek traders brought their civilization to a trading empire in Thrace and Phrygia.
The Bosporan Kingdom was located in eastern Crimea [1536,1537].
The Bosporan Kingdom was a politeia (a form of government) [1536,1537].
The Bosporan Kingdom was primarily ruled by Greek colonies.
The Bosporan Kingdom was established on the territory of the colonies after the end of Greek colonization.
The Bosporan Kingdom was a successful Hellenistic regime among Greek colonies [4116,4117].
The Bosporan Empire came to power and ended Greek authority [4019,4020].
A strengthened Roman Empire later occupied the southern steppes of Russia.
Romans lived in the western part of the Caspian Sea.
Oium was a semi-legendary Gothic kingdom [4116,4117].

== Nomadic Empires and Turkic Peoples ==

The Kasaars ruled the steppes of the lower Volga region, an area located between the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea.
The Sarmatians succeeded the Scythians in these regions.
Between the 3rd and 6th centuries, the steppes experienced successive waves of nomadic peoples moving towards Western Europe.
The Khazars ruled during the 8th century and were valuable allies of the Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine Empire) while conducting several wars against Arab caliphates.
During the crisis period of the Roman Empire, these territories became inhabited by Huns and Khazars.
Turkic-speaking peoples began settling in the southern territories of Russia, including the nomadic Khazar tribes settled in North Caucasus who represented one of the great powers.
Turkic-speaking peoples also inhabited the territories of the Volga River and the Caspian Sea basin.
These nomads did not stay in one place but moved around Europe and other regions.
The Huns were a nomadic culture that lived along the Caspian Sea coast.
The steppes of southern Russia were inhabited by pastoral nomads.

== Origins and Expansion of the Slavs ==

The history of Russia began with the history of the East Slavs and the arrival of Slavic people.[2751,2752] The Slavs came from the north and west, and some experts consider their original homeland to be a forested area in the Pinsk Marshes.[1851,1852] Slavic tribes moved to the territory of far-eastern Russia in the early 5th century and began to dominate this region.
Slavic tribes gradually settled in the western part of modern-day Russia during the Migration Period, where the local tribes included Baltic peoples.[2641,2642,2643] Slavic tribes were geographically divided into western and eastern groups, and the western group remained in Europe.
Slavic peoples were gradually strengthening on these territories and created their own special principalities.
Slavs inhabited the region during the Early Middle Ages, and since the 7th century, East Slavs were the largest population group in Western Russia and constituted the majority of the population there.
The ancestors of Russians lived in the region known as Northeast Rus and are believed to have inhabited this region for a long time before Christianization.

The history prior to the arrival of Slavic people was largely unknown for a long time.
The origins of Russian history began with the arrival of Slavic peoples in Europe.
Some scholars believe the original homeland of these tribes was in the forest areas of the Pechora Marshes or the Pinsk Marshes.

== Finno-Ugric and Baltic Tribes ==

The native Finno-Ugric population included the Merya, Muromian, and Meshchera people.
Finnic or Lithuanian tribes lived in the Moscow basin for a long time before the 10th century.

== Slavic Society, Religion, and Culture ==

The ancient Greek writer Procopius described Slavs and Antes as barbarians, stated that they had a democratic system without kings, claimed that they believed in a single god named Perun the 'creator of lightning', and noted that they offered sacrifices to this god.
Their hair color was not blonde but also not completely dark.
The world was believed to be governed by two opposing forces, one consisting of sky gods who controlled the laws of nature and the other consisting of underground (chthonic) gods who controlled human customs and actions.

Various tribes inhabited Russia before the 1st century BC, including Proto-Europeans and Sarmatians.

== Paleolithic and Neanderthal presence ==

Paleolithic settlements in Russia are extensive.
The younger Paleolithic period occurred between 35,000 and 10,000 BC and features a number of significant archaeological sites.
Kostienki and Metsin are among these significant sites.
Kostienki is located near the Don River, and Metsin is located near the upper course of the Dnieper River.
These sites show clear contact with contemporary cultural groups in Western Europe.
There was a significant burial site at Sungir.
Kiik-Koba cave is a site from the Mousterian period located on the Crimean Peninsula, which is in present-day Ukraine.
Kiik-Koba cave exhibits typical Neanderthal characteristics.
Okladnikov Cave is located in Russia.
The Denisova Cave is located in southern Siberia.
A bone was found in Kostenki, which is located on the banks of the Don River.
These caves have made significant contributions to the study of ancient human species.
Neanderthals had a larger distribution area than previously believed.

Sungir is located outside Moscow, where the deceased were buried in elaborate dresses made of stacked shells and pearls.

== Mesolithic and Neolithic cultures ==

Western Russia and the Baltic region were dominated during the Mesolithic period by so-called forest cultures.
In Northern Europe, these forest cultures are known as the Maglemose culture, and the specific forest cultures in this context are Swiderian and Kunda.
Mesolithic cultures in Central Russia are typically divided into three groups: the Volga-Oka culture, the Kama culture, and the Dnieper culture.
The first agricultural cultures appeared from the south during the 3000s BC.
The Tripolje culture was located in the southwest and was significant for spreading agriculture to the region.
Clay figurines are common and include representations of fertility goddesses.
Subneolithic hunter populations with pottery dominated the northern parts of Central Russia at the same time as other cultures mentioned.
The Cam-keramic culture was present in the northwestern part of Central Russia.
The later culture includes Finland, the Baltic region, and the northern coast up to the Kalix River.

== Early Metal Ages and burial customs ==

The earliest metal age emerged from the east in the form of battle-axe cultures.
The Fatyanovo culture developed in Central Russia and featured single-person graves in which skeletons were placed in a curled-up position and in a side-lying position.
The so-called catacomb grave culture developed in the south, where the dead were placed in pits, stone cists, catacombs, and wooden graves.
Iron was introduced to Russia in the first half of the last pre-Christian millennium.

== Scythians and Iron Age interactions ==

The Pontic steppe was known as Scythia in Classical Antiquity.
The Scythian cultural circle was the most significant one.
The elaborate graves of the Scythians testify to contacts with Celtic tribes of Central Europe, the Etruscans of Italy, Greeks, and Near Eastern cultures including Assyria.
The Ananino culture emerged around the lower Kama and grew strongly influenced by the Scythians.

== Greek and Roman presence ==

Ancient Greek traders began bringing their civilization to the shops in Tanais and Phanagoria starting from the 8th century BC, and the trade was directed towards commercial emporia in Tanais and Phanagoria.
Some Greek explorers traveled to the Baltic region, and Pytheas was the most famous of these Greek explorers who reached modern-day Kaliningrad, which is located on the Baltic Sea.
Romans established themselves in the western part of the Caspian Sea, and the Roman Empire extended eastward from this region.
The Romans settled on the western shore of the Caspian Sea, and the Roman Empire had its eastern extremity at this location.

== Migration of Slavic tribes ==

The Slavic tribes came from northern Poland and followed a migration route that passed through the eastern Baltic. These Slavic tribes were ancestors of later Krivichians. The Slavs began to settle northwards as far as Lake Ilmen and eastwards as far as the Volga-Oka interfluve. These tribes are known from the 'Tale of Bygone Years'. By the 6th to 8th centuries, the main tribes of Eastern Slavs had formed in general outline. Eastern Slavs formed the majority of the population in western Russia starting from the 7th century. Slavs spread into Eastern Europe around the same time.

== Great Bulgaria and the Khazar Khaganate ==

Great Bulgaria was founded around 632 AD and was located in the Don River basin.
The Bulgars and the Hungarians were one of these tribes.

The Khazar Khaganate replaced the Bulgars and existed from approximately 650 to 969.
The Khazar Khaganate was the only known Jewish state, though its inhabitants were not ethnically Jewish.
The Khazars dominated the steppes of the Lower Volga, and the area between the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea was part of the Khazar domain.
The Khazars subjugated part of Eastern Slavic lands in the 8th century, and the Polans tribe was among those subjugated.
The Bulgars migrated across Europe, and this migration led to the establishment of a Balkan Bulgarian state and Kamsk Bulgaria.

The vast steppes of southern Russia were the homeland of nomadic tribes in prehistoric times, and Russia at that time was heavily influenced by primitive nomadic culture.

== Rise of the East Slavs ==

The history of Russia began with the Eastern Slavs, whose national history also began with the East Slavs.[121,2179,2183,2184,4032,4033] These Slavic groups had a homeland in the dense forested Pinsk marshes, and some academics believe the homeland of these tribes was in the wooded areas of the Pinsk Marshes.[1851,1852] The population of East Slavs increased in Western Russia from the 7th century, and East Slavs formed the majority of the population in Western Russia from the 7th century onwards.
The Finno-Ugric peoples included the Merya, Muromians, and Meshchera, whom the East Slavs assimilated.
This assimilation occurred gradually but peacefully.

The establishment of the first East Slavic states in the 9th century coincided with the arrival of Varangians, the Vikings who ventured along the waterways extending from the eastern Baltic to the Black and Caspian Seas.
According to the Primary Chronicle, a Varangian from the Rus' people, named Rurik, was elected ruler of Novgorod in 862.
In 882, his successor Oleg ventured south and conquered Kiev, which had been previously paying tribute to the Khazars.
Rurik's son Igor and Igor's son Sviatoslav subsequently subdued all local East Slavic tribes to Kievan rule, destroyed the Khazar Khaganate, and launched several military expeditions to Byzantium and Persia.

In the 10th to 11th centuries, Kievan Rus' became one of the largest and most prosperous states in Europe.
The reigns of Vladimir the Great (980–1015) and his son Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054) constitute the Golden Age of Kiev, which saw the acceptance of Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium, and the creation of the first East Slavic written legal code, the Russkaya Pravda.
The age of feudalism and decentralisation had come, marked by constant in-fighting between members of the Rurik dynasty that ruled Kievan Rus' collectively.
Kiev's dominance waned, to the benefit of Vladimir-Suzdal in the north-east, the Novgorod Republic in the north, and Galicia-Volhynia in the south-west.
By the 12th century, Kiev lost its pre-eminence and Kievan Rus' had fragmented into different principalities.
Prince Andrey Bogolyubsky sacked Kiev in 1169 and made Vladimir his base, leading to political power being shifted to the north-east.

Led by Prince Alexander Nevsky, Novgorodians repelled the invading Swedes in the Battle of the Neva in 1240, as well as the Germanic crusaders in the Battle on the Ice in 1242.

Kievan Rus' finally fell to the Mongol invasion of 1237–1240, which resulted in the sacking of Kiev and other cities, as well as the death of a major part of the population.
The invaders, later known as Tatars, formed the state of the Golden Horde, which ruled over Russia for the next two centuries.
Only the Novgorod Republic escaped foreign occupation after it agreed to pay tribute to the Mongols.
Galicia-Volhynia would later be absorbed by Lithuania and Poland, while the Novgorod Republic continued to prosper in the north.
In the northeast, the Byzantine-Slavic traditions of Kievan Rus' were adapted to form the Russian autocratic state.

== Trade Routes and Economic Relations ==

The economy of Kievan Rus was based on trade between Scandinavia and Byzantium, and these trade routes connected Scandinavia and the Byzantine Empire [cite: 693].
Kyiv was located on the main trade route connecting the Baltic Sea, the Black Sea, and the Byzantine Empire, and Kiev served as a trade center between Scandinavia and Constantinople.
The trade was mainly oriented towards Constantinople, and trade relations were especially intense with the Byzantine Empire [cite: 448].
Kievan Rus had a commercial position between Europe and Asia [cite: 448].
