Ivan III completely stopped paying tribute and repelled retaliatory Tatar attacks in 1472 and 1480.

== Legal and Cultural Unification ==

Legal unification occurred in Rus during this period.
The new Sudebnik of Ivan III in 1497 was based on several legal documents, including the Ruska Pravda from the 11th century, the Dvinskaya and Belozerskaya Ustavny Gramota from 1397 and 1488, and the Pskov and Novgorod Sudnaya Gramota from 1467 and 1471.
The marriage of Ivan III to Sophia Palaiologina in 1472 was intended to emphasize this status.
Ivan III adopted the Byzantine court ceremonial.
Moscow formulated aspirations for the Muscovite principality.
These aspirations were expressed in the thesis of Moscow as the 'Third Rome'.

== Final Annexations under Vasili III ==

Vasili III annexed Pskov in 1510, Smolensk in 1514, and Ryazan in 1521.
The Grand Duchy of Moscow became the only independent Russian state.

== Incorporation of Russian Republics ==

The Novgorod Republic existed from 1136 to 1478.
The Republic of Pskov existed from 1348 to 1510 and was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
The Republic of Vyatka existed from 1452 to 1489 and was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

== Demographics, Environment, and Assimilation ==

The lands of the principality were divided into several small feudal states, and Ruthenia eventually disintegrated into several small states [cite: 3110].
Muscovy was the successor state of Kiev and the Grand Duchy of Moscow was the most powerful successor state to Kievan Rus, also known as Muscovy in Western chronicles.
Muscovy fought for independence against the Mongol Golden Horde and came to dominate the cultural and political legacy of Kievan Rus.
The Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal and the Republic of Novgorod laid the foundations for the modern Russian nation, and Moscow princes' unification efforts gained significance.
Novgorod and Pskov were largely spared from the atrocities that affected the rest of the country [cite: 2993].
The assimilation of native Finno-Ugric peoples occurred peacefully and included the Merya people and the Muromians [cite: 2987].
Agriculture was difficult since the beginning of the Little Ice Age [cite: 2425,2994].
Plagues affected Russia and hit some regions once every five or six years between 1350 and 1490 [cite: 2425,2994].
The death toll from plagues was not as severe in Russia as it was in Western Europe [cite: 2425,2994].
The practice of banya (steam baths) was widespread in Russia [cite: 2425,2994].

The Russian principalities period began in the mid-12th century and ended in the early 16th century, and before 1480 this period was known as the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
The rulers of the Vladimir-Suzdal principality fought for Kiev and Novgorod but always preferred to stay in Vladimir, a preference that led to the rise of Vladimir as a new all-Russian center.
Vladimir-Suzdal and the Republic of Novgorod laid the foundations for modern Russian statehood.
Slavic colonization of Northeast Rus continued until the 14th century.
Most Russian lands were subjected to a destructive invasion by Batu.[3327,3328] The invading Mongol elite formed the Tatar people together with Turkic peoples conquered by them.
The Tatars continued to raid Russian principalities from the Golden Horde, and the Mongols maintained this dominance for over two centuries.
Novgorod and Pskov were largely spared from the atrocities that affected the rest of the country and maintained a certain degree of autonomy during Mongol domination.
These victories interrupted attempts to colonize Northern Rus'.
Moscow began asserting its influence in the center of the Ruthenian region in the 14th century.
In Romanian chronicles, the Grand Duchy of Moscow is referred to as 'Țara Muscălească'.
The territorial expansion of Russia was largely realized in the 16th century under the Cossack Yermak Timofeyevich.

The cities of Vladimir, Ryazan, Kiev, Chernigov, Pereyaslavl, and Galich were destroyed, and southern and south-eastern regions lost a significant portion of their settled population.
Russian principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde, and princes in these principalities received power over their lands with the sanction of the Khans of the Golden Horde, a period known in history as the Mongol-Tatar yoke.
Novgorodian lands entered a series of military conflicts in the 13th century to establish dominance in Eastern Baltic, during which Prince Alexander Nevsky was summoned by the Novgorod Veche.
New political centers began to form among Russian lands from the late 13th century, including the Moscow Principality and the Tver Principality.
Moscow princes won the struggle for the Grand Prince of Vladimir title, which the Golden Horde khans issued, and the Grand Prince of Vladimir acted as a tax collector, served as the supreme ruler, and held authority over North-Eastern Rus and Novgorod.
Prince Dmitry Donskoy began his reign before 1363, and starting in 1363, the charter for the Grand Principality of Vladimir was awarded only to princes of the Moscow house.

Russia won a series of military victories under Ivan III.
The end of Russian tribute payments marked the conclusion of the Mongol yoke.
The Grand Prince of Moscow was named 'Gosudar' (Ruler), and this change in title was a recognition of his sovereignty.
The Sudebnik was a compilation of general Russian laws, and the Moscow Kremlin was built during this period.
The Golden Horde disintegrated in the mid-15th century as military defeats and internal strife led to its weakening.
The Golden Horde split into several khanates, including the Crimean Khanate, the Astrakhan Khanate, the Kazan Khanate, and the Siberian Khanate.
Vasily III fought wars against the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Khanate of Kazan.
Stone construction in Moscow and other cities intensified during Vasily III's reign.
The physical expansion of Russia took place under Yermak Timofeyevich.
The Novgorodians repelled German crusaders in the Battle on Lake Chud.
Russia lagged behind European social development.
Moscow's grand princes laid the foundations of a centralized state.

The church, cities, and a new nobility helped Moscow's grand princes establish this state.
Vladimir was a capital city during the first centuries, and Moscow is mentioned in chronicles for the first time in the year 1147.
The Russian region was obligated to pay tribute to the Mongols for 250 years, and the Mongol capital was the Golden Horde.
The Mongols attacked Russian cities at regular intervals, and the Russian princes technically held power according to law.
The final battle against the Mongols took place in 1480 at the Ugra River.
Polish forces attempted to install puppet tsars, and a period of ten years of struggle and power struggles occurred.
Mongols captured many of these small states and established these captured territories as their vassal states.[121,4011]
The Grand Duchy of Moscow emerged as a leading power in the cultural and political traditions of Kievan Rus.[2183,2184,4012]
The migration was caused by continuous attacks from Turkish groups such as the Kipchaks and Pechenegs.
The Tatars plundered Russian principalities.
A guberniya was one of the higher administrative units in Imperial Russia, and an uyezd was a constituent part of a guberniya.

Vladimir-Suzdal and Novgorod were located near the borders of Kiev and formed the foundation of modern Russia.
Novgorod and Smolensk had a small degree of self-governing authority during the Mongol invasion, and these regions escaped the atrocities that occurred in other parts of the country.
These victories stopped attempts to occupy northern Russia.
Moscow was a very powerful state and is referred to as 'Moskovi' in Western references.
The region suffered from continuous Mongol invasions, the onset of winter, and damage to agriculture.
The plague also affected Russia, similar to other parts of Europe, and Russian regions were affected by the plague every five or six years between 1350 and 1490.
Russia had a lower population density compared to Western Europe and had better hygiene practices, including widespread steam baths.
Due to low population density and good hygiene practices, losses from the plague in Russia were not as severe as those seen in Western Europe.
Russia's population in 1500 was higher than before the plague.
The Russian army received assistance from the Russian Orthodox Church.
Ivan III the Great brought all of Central and Northern Russia under Moscow's rule.
The reason for joining was social and religious oppression under Polish rule.
The war lasted from 1654 to 1667.

The Grand Duchy of Moscow came to dominate the cultural and political legacy of Kievan Rus, while most of Rus was conquered by Mongol invasions and became a vassal state of the nomadic Golden Horde.[121,2179,2183,2184,4032,4033] Historical records first mention Moscow in 1147, when Prince Yuri Dolgorukiy, the crown prince of Kyiv, ordered the construction of a wooden fortress or 'Kremlin' on Borovitsky Hill by the Moskva River.
In the early 13th century, a Mongol army led by Batu Khan invaded Russia, after which Russia was cut off from the outside world and required to pay taxes to the Mongols.
Kings and clergy moved the center of power northward, and Ivan I was crowned king in 1328 with the nickname Ivan the Moneybag.
Ivan I collected taxes and tributes to send to the Mongols, and during this era, the king moved his residence to Moscow.
The Mongols began to lose power during the reign of Ivan II (1353-1359), and Prince Dmitry, son of Ivan II, successfully drove out the Mongols at the Battle of Kulikovo on the Don River.
In 1380, Dmitry was crowned Dmitry Donskoy (Dmitry of the Don), united the cities of Vladimir and Suzdal, which were important to the Muscovite realm, and rebuilt the Kremlin with white stone walls instead of oak wood.
Moscow was also known as the White Stone Wall City during that time, but soon after, the Tatars returned and destroyed the Kremlin completely.

== Mongol Invasion and the Golden Horde ==

The state of Kievan Rus disintegrated quickly, and most of its small states were conquered during the Mongol invasion.
The Mongols conquered these principalities one by one, and most of Kievan Rus became part of the Golden Horde in the 13th century.
This surrender occurred in the 1230s, and most of these small states became vassals of the Golden Horde.
The land became branches of the Golden Horde State, which was a Turkic-Mongol state that ruled over southern and central Russia for two centuries.
The Mongol invasion caused the population of the Kievan Rus' to lose half its members, and Mongol-Tatar raids occurred frequently.
The Golden Horde State weakened significantly.

== Rise of Moscow and Political Consolidation ==

The reunification resulted in the establishment of the Moscow Principality.
The Principality of Moscow was the strongest successor to the Principality of Kiev and became a vassal of the Horde until 1480.
This expansion of power occurred after the Tver Uprising, which Ivan Kalita organized under the pretext of collecting taxes without additional Mongol burdens.
Local leaders fought to inherit the cultural and political legacy of Kievan Rus', including some from Novgorod and some from Pskov.
The political fragmentation of Kievan Rus separated the Russians in the north from the Belarusians and Ukrainians in the west, and Russia became the cultural and political successor of Kievan Rus.

== The Novgorod Republic and Regional Autonomy ==

Galicia-Volhynia and Vladimir-Suzdal were two regions surrounding Kiev that formed the basis for the modern Russian nation, while Galicia-Volhynia was assimilated by the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Novgorod and Pskov were protected to a certain degree of autonomy, and Novgorod remained autonomous for a period under Mongol domination while being spared from the cruelties that largely affected the rest of the country.
The Novgorodians blocked the Teutonic Knights' attempt to colonize Northern Russia in the Battle on Lake Peipus in 1242.

== Demographics, Plague, and Society ==

Agriculture was devastated at the beginning of the Little Ice Age.
Plague outbreaks occurred between 1350 and 1490, happening every five or six years during this period in a pattern similar to the rest of Europe.
Population loss was not as severe in the region as it was in Western Europe, where the population density was lower and better hygiene conditions contributed to the less severe loss.
The Rus banyosu (Russian steam bath) was commonly used, and the Russian Orthodox Church provided assistance.

== Decline of the Golden Horde and Independence ==

Russia became a vassal state of the Tatars again in 1382.
The old Golden Horde State was fragmented, and 1480 marked the beginning of the fragmentation of the Golden Horde into khanates.
Three Tatar khanates were established in place of the Golden Horde.
The Russian volunteer army was led by two national heroes.
The formation of the Muscovite state was completed at the end of the 15th century and at the beginning of the 16th century.

== Reign of Ivan III and State Formation ==

Ivan III, also known as Ivan the Great, reigned from 1462 to 1505.
In 1472, Ivan III married a granddaughter of the previous Byzantine Emperor.
In 1480, Ivan III drove the Tatar forces out of Russia completely, and the expulsion of the Tatars ended two centuries of Mongol rule.
Ivan III renovated the Kremlin with high towers and beautiful churches inside it.
Ivan III's reign is considered an era of prosperity for Russia.
Moscow became a cultural center, a process that began after the 13th century.
Russia was the only active Orthodox country on the eastern European border after 1453.
Russian principalities declared their independence.

In development of the Third Rome ideas, the grand duke Ivan IV ("the Terrible") was officially crowned the first tsar of Russia in 1547.
The tsar promulgated a new code of laws (Sudebnik of 1550), established the first Russian feudal representative body (the Zemsky Sobor), revamped the military, curbed the influence of the clergy, and reorganised local government.
During his long reign, Ivan nearly doubled the already large Russian territory by annexing the three Tatar khanates: Kazan and Astrakhan along the Volga, and the Khanate of Sibir in southwestern Siberia.
Ultimately, by the end of the 16th century, Russia expanded east of the Ural Mountains.
However, the Tsardom was weakened by the long and unsuccessful Livonian War against the coalition of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania (later the united Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth), the Kingdom of Sweden, and Denmark–Norway for access to the Baltic coast and sea trade.
In 1572, an invading army of Crimean Tatars were thoroughly defeated in the crucial Battle of Molodi.

The death of Ivan's sons marked the end of the ancient Rurik dynasty in 1598, and in combination with the disastrous famine of 1601–1603, led to a civil war, the rule of pretenders, and foreign intervention during the Time of Troubles in the early 17th century.
The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, taking advantage, occupied parts of Russia, extending into the capital Moscow.
In 1612, the Poles were forced to retreat by the Russian volunteer corps, led by merchant Kuzma Minin and prince Dmitry Pozharsky.
The Romanov dynasty acceded to the throne in 1613 by the decision of the Zemsky Sobor, and the country started its gradual recovery from the crisis.

Russia continued its territorial growth through the 17th century, which was the age of the Cossacks.
In 1654, the Ukrainian leader, Bohdan Khmelnytsky, offered to place Ukraine under the protection of the Russian tsar, Alexis; whose acceptance of this offer led to another Russo-Polish War.
Ultimately, Ukraine was split along the Dnieper, leaving the eastern part, (Left-bank Ukraine and Kiev) under Russian rule.
In the east, the rapid Russian exploration and colonisation of vast Siberia continued, hunting for valuable furs and ivory.
Russian explorers pushed eastward primarily along the Siberian River Routes, and by the mid-17th century, there were Russian settlements in eastern Siberia, on the Chukchi Peninsula, along the Amur River, and on the coast of the Pacific Ocean.
In 1648, Semyon Dezhnyov became the first European to navigate through the Bering Strait.

== Ideology and Early Reforms ==

Constantinople was also known as the second Rome, and Moscow became the third Rome because it is the last center of the Orthodox Church.
Ivan III derived his title from Roman and Byzantine emperors.
Ivan the Terrible ruled from 1533 to 1584 and initially devoted himself to peaceful reforms and renewals.
Ivan sought new trade opportunities and opened the port of Arkhangelsk on the White Sea for English traders.
Ivan IV succeeded in making the power of the Tsar absolute over all of Russia and established autocracy.

== Territorial Expansion and Settlement ==

In the early 16th century, territories inhabited by Volga peoples were added to the Russian state, where fortress-cities such as Simbirsk, Samara, Saratov, Kamysheva, and Sarytsyn (now Volgograd) were built.
Russian movement into the forest-steppe region of Eastern Europe intensified in the 16th century, leading to the construction of fortress-cities such as Tambov and Voronezh, while Cossack settlements were established along the lower reaches of the Don River.
By the late 16th century, Russians had settled in the West Siberian Plain, where the city of Tobolsk was founded and served as the capital of Siberia for a long time.
Russian fortresses were built on the banks of the Yenisey River and the Lena River in the 17th century.
By the end of the 16th century, Russia became a multinational and multi-religious state.
Russia annexed Eastern Siberia.

== Military Conflicts and External Threats ==

He became involved in the so-called Livonian War, which lasted for 22 years and ruined the Russian economy and army.
The Crimean Khanate, the only remaining successor of the Golden Horde State, launched raids into Southern Russia.
Crimea and the Ottomans were allies, an alliance motivated by efforts to regain control of the Khanates of the Volga.
The Crimean Tatars, the only remaining representatives of the Golden Horde, continued raids into southern Russia, took many people into Ottoman slavery, and prevented greater settlement of the territory.
The Crimean Tatars devastated Ryazan in 1570, where they encountered only weak resistance.
In 1571, Tatars from the Crimean Khanate, supported by their Ottoman allies, invaded central Russia with a force consisting of 80,000 Tatars, 33,000 Turks, and 7,000 Janissaries.
In 1571, the Crimean-Ottoman alliance occupied, looted, and set fire to villages surrounding Moscow.
The threat of Ottoman-Crimea expansion into Russia was eliminated forever.

The invaders crossed the Ugra River and crushed a wing of the Russian army that had 6,000 fighters.
The Russian army lacked the strength to stop the invasion.

== Social Legislation and Serfdom ==

The law restricted the freedom of movement of peasants, which was an important step toward later serfdom.
The recipients were landowners who served him in the army or government, and these laws defined the number of soldiers and horses landowners had to provide.
Later, land was managed by the emperor.

== The Oprichnina and Reign of Terror ==

His later reign was characterized by a period of terror.
An era of terror began under Ivan IV's rule.
Ivan IV formed a special police force.
A police force was created in 1564.
The police force was called the Opritsjniki.
The Opritsjniki became a murderous terror band.
The Opritsjniki killed people among both the nobility and the common people.
Ivan sometimes suffered from madness.
Ivan IV ordered the arrest of hundreds of aristocrats.
Ivan IV ordered the execution of these arrested aristocrats.
Ivan burned many villages and cities.
Ivan killed some church leaders who opposed him.

== Personal Tragedy and Decline ==

Ivan's wife, Anastasia Romanovna, died, and Ivan believed that the boyars murdered her.
He could not recover from this blow, his health began to decline, he deteriorated mentally, he became paranoid, and he became violent.
Ivan hit his eldest son in 1581 during a fit of rage, and Ivan's eldest son died as a result of the attack.
Ivan killed his eldest son in a fit of rage.

== Succession Crisis and the Time of Troubles ==

Ivan died and was succeeded by his son Fyodor, who was mentally disabled.
Dmitri Ivanovich was the second oldest surviving son and was only two years old at the time.
Dmitri Ivanovich was murdered shortly thereafter, and Dmitry was found dead in 1591.
Boris Godunov, who was Fyodor's brother-in-law and guardian, held the real power during Fyodor's reign [cite: 76].
The Tsar's authority collapsed after Ivan's death, and the era of troubles began due to the decline of the tsar's authority.
Theodore I was Ivan's second son and was a weak tsar.
Boris Godunov became the actual ruler of Russia.
A chaotic period began after Fyodor's death [cite: 76].
Russia was ruled by False Dmitry I during this period [cite: 76].
Russia was ruled by False Dmitry II during this period [cite: 76].
The last mentioned person was assassinated on December 11, 1610 while he was half-drunk.

Theodor died in 1598 and left no heir to the throne, while his younger brother was named Dmitry.
Fyodor I was Ivan the Terrible's son and became Ivan the Terrible's successor.
A period of civil wars occurred during Fyodor I's reign and foreign intervention occurred during Fyodor I's reign.
The summers of 1601 to 1603 were extremely cold.
These cold summers caused a major famine between 1601 and 1603 and led to an increase in social disorganization.
Boris Godunov ruled Russia, implemented significant reforms in Russia, and his reign was followed by large uprisings and revolts.
Boris Godunov was succeeded by his son Fyodor II, who reigned for only a few months and was killed by opponents of his father.
The occupation lasted from 1610 to 1612 and Moscow was largely burned down.
The Poles were expelled from Moscow in February 1613.
The National Assembly consisted of representatives from fifty cities.

The National Assembly included representatives from some villages.
Boris Godunov, the Tsar's brother-in-law, became regent for Fedor I after Ivan IV's death.
Fedor I died in 1598, after which Boris Godunov crowned himself Tsar.
The country's economy was ruined, and Boris Godunov's rule failed to restore it.
Crisis phenomena intensified after his death, and the period known as the Time of Troubles began.
The country was often invaded by foreign armies, and Polish forces occupied Moscow until 1612.
Rulers changed quickly on the throne.
In 1610, Polish forces under Władysław IV Vasa occupied Moscow.
The struggle for power ended in 1613.

== The Pretenders and Political Instability ==

The Zemsky Sobor was a parliament with limited powers and elected Boris as Tsar of the country.
There was a man believed to be named Gregory Otrepyev who was a former priest and claimed to be Dmitry.
The pretender Dmitry claimed that Dmitry did not die and that he fled to Lithuania to escape arrest.
False Dmitry invaded Russia in 1604 and was accompanied by some Polish soldiers.

== Religious Schism and Late 17th Century Politics ==

The Romanov dynasty lasted for three hundred years.
The Russian Orthodox Church made changes to religious rituals in the 17th century, which caused opposition among some Russians, while some Russians remained loyal to the Old Belief tradition.
A struggle for power broke out in 1682, leading to the coronation of Peter I (later known as Peter the Great) alongside his half-brother Ivan V, though actual power was held by Peter's half-sister Sophia as regent until supporters of Peter forced her to abdicate in 1689.
Peter entered Moscow with his supporters in 1689, and Sophia surrendered power to Peter in 1689.

== Ivan IV and the Rise of the Tsardom ==

Ivan IV was the grandson of Ivan the Great and continued his grandfather's policy with determination [cite: 2009].
Ivan the Terrible reigned from 1533 to 1584, while Ivan IV ruled for 37 years [cite: 74,1543].
Ivan IV's reign lasted from 1547 to 1584, and Ivan IV the Terrible ruled from 1547 to 1584 [cite: 74,1543].
Ivan IV was known as 'the Terrible' in the West, a reputation due to his drastic methods.
Ivan IV conquered Kazan in 1552, and Yermak Timofeyevich served during the reign of Ivan IV Vasilyevich [cite: 1907].
The title of Tsar means Eastern Roman Emperor [cite: 448].
The word 'Tsar' derives from the Latin word 'Caesar' [cite: 448].
'Caesar' was a cognomen of Gaius Julius Caesar [cite: 448].
Michael Romanov was chosen as Tsar in 1613.

== The Third Rome Ideology ==

Moscow is considered the Third Rome, a concept according to which Moscow alone preserves the true Christian faith.
The monk Filofei of Pskow called Moscow the Third Rome, a naming that implied a claim by the Tsardom to inherit Constantinople and asserted a special status for Russia.
Ivan III compared Moscow to a Third Rome, and after the fall of Constantinople, the Grand Duchy of Moscow remained the only Christian state on the eastern frontier of Europe.
Thomas Palaiologos, the brother of Constantine XI and Despot of Morea, claimed the throne of Constantinople.
Sophia Paleologa, the daughter of Thomas Palaiologos, was also known by her original Greek and Orthodox name, Zoe.
The marriage led to the transfer of the remaining court of Constantinople to Moscow, including its ceremonial and entire apparatus and the double-headed eagle.
Ivan III invited a large number of artists to Moscow, began the construction of the Kremlin, and maintained regular correspondence with Emperor Maximilian I of the Holy Roman Empire, who often referred to Ivan III as 'brother'.
Ivan III and his wife decided that their capital should succeed Constantinople.

== Territorial Expansion and Conquests ==

This conquest started after the capture of the Tatar capital Kazan.
Tsar Ivan IV completed the consolidation of Russian territories that were primarily inhabited by East Slavs.
Ivan IV expanded Russia into a multi-ethnic state and the Russian state under Ivan IV included a significant number of Muslims [74,1543].
Ivan the Terrible completed these conquests by seizing the main Mongol khanates.
Ivan the Terrible did not possess the city of Kiev, which was held by the Lithuanian Jagiellonian dynasty.
Ivan IV unified the fragmented regions.
Russia acquired most of its territorial expansion in the late 16th century.
Yermak formed an army and defeated Khan Kuchum, the leader of that territory.
At the beginning of the 16th century, the Grand Duchy of Moscow annexed all territories of Kievan Rus that had been targets of Tatar invasions.

== Cossacks and Eastern Colonization ==

The colonizers were Russian peasants, while Cossacks were peasants and fugitives who settled on the margins.
Cossacks organized themselves into an army and played the role of pioneers and border guards.
The Cossacks assisted these sovereigns in expanding the empire, led most of this expansion, and reached the Pacific Ocean in 1640.
The Cossacks gradually occupied Siberia during this period, which occurred under Yermak Timofeyevich [cite: 1907].
Irkutsk was founded in 1632 and is located on the shore of Lake Baikal.
These Cossacks hunted valuable furs and ivory.
Fedot Popov was a Russian explorer who, along with Semyon Dezhnyov, were the first Europeans to sail through the Bering Strait.
They sailed from the Bering Strait to North America.

== Wars in the West and South ==

Moscow-based centralized Russia fought frequent wars in the west between the 15th and 17th centuries against the Catholic Kingdom of Poland, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and the Commonwealth (Rzeczpospolita), a union of Lithuania, Ruthenia, and Samogitia that included former territories of the Grand Duchy of Kiev along with Orthodox subjects.
These wars took place during the fragmentation of the Golden Horde and occurred in the Black Sea region, where Russia fought against Islamic khanates formed in the area, specifically Astrakhan, Crimea, and Kazan.
The Grand Duchy of Moscow protected its southern border regions, which were attacked by the Crimean Tatars and other Turkic populations.

== Crimean Tatar Raids and the 1571 Invasion ==

The Crimean Tatars succeeded in burning Moscow in 1571 [cite: 1544,1545].
Devlet Giraj was supported by the Ottoman Empire [cite: 701].
The Russian army retreated to Moscow.
The rural population fled to the capital city.
The Crimean Tatar army devastated cities and villages around Moscow.
The Crimean Tatar army burned most of the capital city.
It is estimated that 80,000 people died during the Tatar invasion [cite: 701].
150,000 Russians were taken captive during the invasion [cite: 701].
The following year, Crimean Khan Devlet Giraj planned to fully conquer Russia [cite: 701].
This defeat eliminated the threat of Crimean-Ottoman expansion into Russia [cite: 701].
Tatar raids were conducted for the purpose of capturing slaves [cite: 701].
These raids continued until the end of the 17th century [cite: 701].
Russians were continuously taken into slavery in large numbers [cite: 701].

== Centralization and State Administration ==

State administration was centralized during the reigns of Ivan III and Ivan IV the Terrible, and Prikazy (administrative departments) were established during this period.
Ivan IV granted local self-government to rural areas [74,1543].
Landowners were required to serve their sovereign, and nobles were granted landholdings by the sovereigns.
Nobles were obligated to serve in the army, and the system of land grants became one of the foundations of the noble cavalry army.

== Serfdom and the 1649 Code ==

A code was enacted in 1649.
The 1649 code bound peasants and their descendants to the land and to their general owner.
The 1649 code generalized serfdom.
The 1649 code contradicted the evolution of peasant status in Western Europe.

== Religious Schism and Reform ==

This tension was clearly demonstrated in the church schism of 1666/1667.
Patriarch Nikon reformed the Russian Orthodox dogma, which caused the schism of the Old Believers.
The Old Believers were severely repressed.

== The Time of Troubles and Romanov Succession ==

The state fell into a struggle for Ivan the Terrible's inheritance after his death, and Ivan the Terrible considered himself the sole heir of Vladimir.
Epidemics weakened the state.
The construction of new fortifications throughout southern Russia was narrowing the space accessible to Crimean Tatar raids.
Russia became a multi-denominational state, and these changes occurred by the end of the 16th century.
Michael I Romanov was elected head of state.
The Romanov dynasty ruled for 304 years, and the Romanov dynasty's rule ended in 1917.
Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich began the modernization of Russia in the mid-17th century.
Russian colonization of the Volga and Ural basin began to flourish.
The Russian Empire developed after the return of the Tsars.
The title of Tsar symbolized his great power.
The rule of Tsars followed, during which the Russian Empire became powerful towards Europe and the East.
Tsar Nicholas I emphasized Orthodoxy, autocracy, and nationality.

== Ivan IV and the Rise of Autocracy ==

The policy aimed to strengthen absolute monarchy and sought to the detriment of the high nobility of the boyars [cite: 2009].
Elizabeth I Tudor in Great Britain used similar means and methods, and Henry IV in France used similar means and methods [cite: 2009].
The Sudebnik of 1550 introduced local self-government in rural areas [cite: 2010,2011].
By the end of the 16th century, Russia had consolidated and cemented the nature of its state, which was consistently described as 'Roman' in nature [cite: 448].
The use of this name began in the 16th century during the reign of Ivan IV (the Terrible), and initially, the name was used only as a self-designation by the Tsardom of Russia.
Moscow devised a theory to explain the legitimacy of its power [cite: 2190].
The Grand Duchy of Moscow claimed to be the successor to the power of 'Great Rus' and considered itself a member of European nations [cite: 2191].
Consequently, the Grand Duchy of Moscow officially adopted the Greek-style name 'Russia' as its state name [cite: 2191].
The Middle Ages in Russia came to an end, and the kingdom was particularly strengthened during Ivan's reign.
The theory of the Third Rome was developed later, and from this period onwards, Russian monarchs held the title of Tsar [cite: 2395].
The theory of the Third Rome was developed during the reign of Ivan IV, the first Tsar of Russia [cite: 2395].
After the fall of the Byzantine Empire, Russia claimed primacy over the Orthodox world [cite: 2395].
Moscow, known as the 'Third Rome', declared itself the protector of all Orthodox Christians [cite: 2395].

The hopes of these Orthodox Christians were partly linked to Moscow.
The Russian state gradually became stronger.
Ivan the Terrible started the Livonian War in 1558 due to this desire.
Ivan the Terrible died in 1584.

== Territorial Expansion and Eastern Frontiers ==

Russia's borders had already crossed the Volga River, which allowed Russia to advance towards the Siberian Khanate.
A battle against the Siberian Khanate was initiated by Ataman Ermak, leader of a Cossack detachment along the Volga, and the battle continued even after Ermak's death.
The conflict ended with the incorporation of the Siberian Khanate into the kingdom.
Fedot Popov and Semën Dežnëv crossed the Bering Strait in 1648, a crossing that may have been the first time the strait was traversed, though news of this crossing did not reach Europe.

== The Crimean Threat and Southern Defenses ==

The Crimean Khanate was the only remaining successor of the Golden Horde.
The Crimean Tatars continued to raid southern Russia, invaded central Russia, and attempted to restore the Volga khanates.
The Ottoman Empire was an ally of the Crimeans, and together they burned parts of Moscow in 1571.

== Political factions and ideologies ==

Industrialists and nobles were liberals who implemented peaceful social reforms, advocated for a constitutional monarchy, and formed the Constitutional Democratic Party.
Russian liberals formed the Constitutional Union of Zemstvos in 1903 and the Union of Liberation in 1904, and these unions called for the establishment of a constitutional monarchy.
Russian socialists were organized into two main groups: the Socialist Revolutionary Party and the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.
Social revolutionaries combined Narodnik traditions, called for the distribution of land among actual workers specifically peasants, and the party called for completing the social, economic, and political revolution.
Another extreme group was the Social Democratic Party, which advocated for Marxism in Russia.
The Russian Social Democratic Labour Party split in 1903 in London and divided into two factions: the Mensheviks and the Bolsheviks.
The Mensheviks were the moderate faction and the Bolsheviks were the radical faction.

The Mensheviks believed that Russian socialism would grow gradually and peacefully, that the Tsarist system should transform into a republic, and that in this envisioned republic socialists would cooperate with liberal bourgeois parties.
The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, called for the formation of a small elite of professional revolutionaries who were to be subject to strong party discipline, intended to serve as the vanguard of the working class, and whose goal was to seize power by force.
The Socialist Revolutionary Party played a significant role in Russian history and was founded in 1902.

== Causes and outbreak of the Russo-Japanese War ==

The war lasted from 1904 to 1905.

== Major battles and the war's conclusion ==

The Japanese began besieging Port Arthur in early August 1904, and the fortress garrison was forced to surrender on January 2, 1905.

The war ended with the signing of a peace treaty in Port Smith on August 23, 1905 [cite: 245].
Under the terms of the peace, Russia renounced its rights to the southern part of Sakhalin Island, its right to lease the Liaodong Peninsula, and its right to the railway in southern Manchuria [cite: 245].

An alternative socialist establishment co-existed, the Petrograd Soviet, wielding power through the democratically elected councils of workers and peasants, called soviets.
The rule of the new authorities only aggravated the crisis in the country instead of resolving it, and eventually, the October Revolution, led by Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin, overthrew the Provisional Government and gave full governing power to the soviets, leading to the creation of the world's first socialist state.

The Allied powers launched an unsuccessful military intervention in support of anti-communist forces.
In the meantime, both the Bolsheviks and White movement carried out campaigns of deportations and executions against each other, known respectively as the Red Terror and White Terror.
By the end of the violent civil war, Russia's economy and infrastructure were heavily damaged, and as many as 10 million perished during the war, mostly civilians.
Millions became White émigrés, and the Russian famine of 1921–1922 claimed up to five million victims.

== Overview and Duration ==

The history of Russia from 1922 to 1991 is the history of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and the history of the Soviet Union.

== Political Structure and Ideology ==

The Soviet Union was ruled by a one-party dictatorship under the Communist Party and continued imperial policies.
They based their views on the writings of German philosopher Karl Marx, and Marxism-Leninism served as the ideology inspiring and founding the Communist Party.
Communist ideology imposed a change in values, and the Soviet Union was a state entirely based on ideology.
The approach to building socialism varied at different points in Soviet history.
State atheism in the Soviet Union was based on Marxist-Leninist ideology, which has always supported controlling, suppressing, and removing religion from social life.

== Nationalities and Imperial Character ==

The Soviet Union was an empire of united nationalities, and nationality served as a political instrument to consolidate Soviet power.
The connection between communal and authoritarian elements was pronounced until the end of the Soviet Union.
These conceptions were continued in the Soviet Union, and Marxists and socialists built upon these conceptions of the collective.
The USSR included neighboring territories previously conquered under the Empire.
There was a politically motivated desire to create an exclusively 'Soviet' people.
Russia dominated the remaining fourteen republics for all sixty-nine years of its history.
During this time, it was known as the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR).

The Soviet Union was often referred to as 'Russia'.
The people of the Soviet Union were referred to as 'Russians'.

== Cultural Policy and Arts ==

The Soviet Union's policy regarding culture was controversial, and this desire was expressed through the concept of Soviet culture and exemplified by Socialist Realism.
Folkloric cultural practices were officially supported, recurring campaigns were held to preserve national cultures, and each ethnicity had its own 'native great writers'.
Socialist realism was the only cultural form recognized in the USSR, and the Soviet Union also had a long-standing tradition in science, culture, and art.

== Demographics and Economy ==

The population recovered to its pre-war level by 1955 and increased by nearly 35% after 1955.
The former Soviet Union was the largest country in terms of area, had the largest population, and had the largest industrial production.
The Soviet Union was the world's second-largest industrial superpower.
The Soviet military budget typically accounted for 10% to 20% of the Soviet GDP.

== Religious Persecution ==

This factor contributed to the Bolsheviks' attitude towards religion.
The government implemented an anti-religious policy during the Soviet era and attempted to spread atheism.
The state publicly defamed religions and their followers and attempted to propagate atheism in schools.
The state seized all property of churches within one year after the October Revolution and even seized the churches themselves.
Between 1922 and 1926, 28 Russian Orthodox bishops were killed and more than 1,200 priests were killed.
Studies indicate that religious persecution by the government was widespread during the Soviet period.

== Heritage Conservation ==

The tradition of conservation was interrupted due to this change in values, and independent heritage conservation societies were abolished by the end of the 1920s.
Some of these societies defended only secular monuments, and OIRU in Moscow was an example of such a society.

The Soviet Union was formed by four constituent republics that inherited most of the former Russian Empire's territory [cite: 2203].

== Social Reforms and Rights ==

The Bolsheviks established free education, the right to housing, and the right to work.

Council democracy was introduced in the early Soviet period during the dictatorship of the proletariat.
Under this system, the bourgeoisie and the clergy lost voting rights.
The Bolsheviks initiated ambiguous social reforms that severely restricted the rights of surviving non-Bolshevik social groups from the Civil War, including the nobility, clergy, merchants, wealthy peasants, and members of the old political, military, and scientific elites.
These reforms reduced the level of social inequality and abolished exclusive access to quality education, medicine, housing, and high government posts for privileged classes.

== Urbanization and Industrial Planning ==

Urban development was centrally planned during the Soviet era, the Socialist city model prevailed, and massive urbanization policies were implemented during the Soviet era.
As a result of these policies, 73% of the population now lives in urban settlements.
The Soviets were declared owners of land and owners of means of production.
All means of industrial production were placed under state control, and in the planned economy, all means of production were controlled by the State.
Regarding the Soviet Union's economy, a planned economy was implemented after the October Revolution.

== Religious Persecution and Ideological Control ==

The imprisonment of Jehovah's Witnesses occurred from the outbreak of World War II until 1965, and many were deported to Siberia in the Soviet Union in an operation known as Operation North.
All activities related to religion were condemned and religion was banned.
The Communist Party gained control over all aspects of social life and used its massive security apparatus to achieve this control.
Communist ideology and atheism were imposed on the population.

== Foreign Relations and Military Conflicts ==

Starting in 1924, a number of Western countries began to recognize the USSR, with the exception of the USA, while the Soviet Union was not admitted to the League of Nations.
Lenin attempted to export the revolution to the West, an attempt that triggered a war against Poland which ended in a crushing failure for Russia.
The Russian army was nearly twice as large as the Polish army but was defeated at the gates of Warsaw in August 1920.
The Battle of Warsaw is known as the 'Miracle on the Vistula' and was the eighteenth decisive battle in world history, a victory led by Marshal Joseph Pilsudski's strategic genius.
The new government adopted an isolationist policy that was implemented for twenty years after the end of the Civil War.
Russia continued its imperial policy as the Russian SFSR conducted aggressive wars and recovered certain territories lost after World War I.

== Administrative Divisions and Capital Relocation ==

The Russian Soviet Republic was proclaimed in 1921, and the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic evolved into the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.
After the establishment of the single-party system of the VK(b)P, the state became the RSFSR, which existed from 1918 to 1937.
In 1937, the RSFSR was renamed the Russian SFSR, which is also known as the Russian Republic [cite: 2203].
The capital of the Soviet Union and the Russian Republic was moved from St.
Petersburg to Moscow [cite: 2203], a relocation that occurred for the first time in approximately 200 years [cite: 2203].
St.
Petersburg was renamed Leningrad at the same time [cite: 2203].
Autonomous republics, autonomous oblasts, and national districts were established for ethnic minorities residing within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.
The establishment of these administrative regions was based on factors such as population size, and these regions operated under a governance system that was effectively different from that of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.
Moscow served as the capital of the USSR between 1922 and 1991.

The Povolzhye famine of 1921 occurred and resulted in up to 5 million deaths.

== State Control and Party Power ==

A state-controlled economic policy was announced, and the Soviet state promoted research and development in these areas very generously while the state promoted this development very intensively, with one of these areas being the arms industry.
Personal ownership was almost non-existent during the communist era.
The USSR was a one-party dictatorship led by the Communist Party, and the previous party held unlimited and immense power before the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The tricolor flag of Russia lost its status as a national symbol, and the intention was to include non-Russian nationalities.

== Political Structure and Governance ==

The 1924 constitution established the beginning of a federal system of government based on the soviet structure.
Soviets were established in villages, factories, and cities across major parts of the country, forming a Soviet pyramid structure in the USSR where a Union Congress of Soviets stood at the top in each republic.
Moscow was the capital of the Soviet Union and controlled the Political Bureau of the Central Committee of the CPSU.
The Bolsheviks established a dictatorial, single-party totalitarian system in Russia that was controlled by the Communist Party.
Delegates' Councils were elected at the local and central levels, while the Congress of Soviets served as the parliament and, according to the constitution, held legislative and executive power.
The Congress of Soviets elected an Executive Committee from its own members, and every soviet elected an Executive Committee from its own members.
The Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic was proclaimed by a decree of the II All-Russian Congress of Soviets.
This entity was called the Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic between 1918 and 1936 and existed from 1922 to 1991 as a union republic within the USSR.

The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formed as a result of the Bolshevik victory, and its establishment was formalized by the Treaty on the Creation of the Soviet Union.
The Soviet government was based on a one-party foundation from its early years, which consisted of Communists who referred to themselves as Bolsheviks.

== Economic Nationalization and Policy ==

The period from the consolidation of the 1917 revolution to 1921 is known as War Communism.

The Soviet Union had a division of labor in production.

The Soviet regime significantly contributed to the advancement of medical services and improved healthcare infrastructure and access.

The number of doctors increased, life expectancy increased, and infant mortality decreased.

The Soviet Union had a state doctrine of state atheism, and the government promoted atheism and materialism, which undermined the foundations of Marxist theory.
Communists implemented a state program for forced conversion, and the communist regime attacked religions based on state interests.
Most organized religions were not banned, but believers were harassed and religious properties were confiscated.
Atheism was promoted through schools.

Writers enjoyed broad tolerance during the 1920s, and Ilf and Petrov are among the most famous leading writers of this era.

== Industrialization and Economic Policy ==

The promise was to rapidly develop the Russian industrial sector and to promote economic progress in underdeveloped rural areas.

== Industrialization and economic planning ==

The Soviet era ensured state modernization after the October Revolution.
The country implemented continuous five-year economic development plans starting in 1928 [cite: 2591], and the five-year plan for the development of the national economy began in 1929 [cite: 2397].
These plans led to the country developing into an industrial power second only to the United States [cite: 2591], and the Soviet Union became the world's second industrial power.
Stalin's orientation was towards heavy industry, and the Soviet Union focused heavily on developing heavy industry under Stalin.
Heavy industry played a major role in the USSR's economy [cite: 2788,2789,2790], and this heavy industry was military-industrial in nature [cite: 2788,2789,2790].
This transition was achieved through extensive mobilization of internal resources, hyper-centralization of economic life, and the formation of an integrated administrative-command system in the USSR.
The industrial development reached levels comparable to the United States, and the Soviet Union caught up with leading countries of that time in military technology [cite: 2397].
This transformation occurred in a very short period of less than 20 years.
Before 1937, the Soviet Union's industrial output surpassed that of Germany and the United Kingdom.
By 1937, the Soviet Union was the leading industrial power in Europe and the second-largest industrial power in the world.

== Collectivization and agricultural transformation ==

Collectivization was carried out mainly by force, and many people were turned into kulaks as a result of collectivization.
Massive collectivization began in 1929.
Russia was behind in agricultural development.
Agriculture was primarily conducted in collective farms and state-owned farms.
Before the dissolution of the Soviet Union, there were approximately 26,000 collective farms and approximately 23,000 state farms across the entire Soviet Union.
The decline in agricultural production was mainly due to reduced output from collective farms and reduced output from state-owned farms.
Land aristocrats opposed collectivization and were sent to labor camps because they opposed collectivization.
This opposition was particularly strong in Ukraine, where the land aristocrats engaged in sabotage and rebellion activities that caused a decline in agricultural production.
The number of Ukrainians changed significantly after the dekulakization in the 1930s.

== Social conditions and living standards ==

Living standards in cities and villages were extremely low, and citizens had to live frugally for a long time.
Construction of light industry was lagging, and chronic famine was difficult to remedy.

== Cultural and religious repression ==

Publishing new literary works became difficult in the 1930s due to Stalin's policies and regime, during which a large number of writers were imprisoned and persecuted.
A new anti-religious campaign was launched in 1929 and coincided with the collectivization of peasants.
The destruction of churches in cities reached its peak around 1932, and the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour in Moscow was demolished.

== Regional development and infrastructure projects ==

The Soviet government implemented various land development plans, including the greening of deserts and semi-deserts that cover about one-sixth of the country's territory, the construction of the Volga-Don Canal connecting the Volga River and the Don River, and the development of the Siberian Arctic region, which holds nearly inexhaustible resources.
The development of the Siberian Far East was officially launched by the 7th Seven-Year Plan.
A comprehensive plan was launched after 1966.
Development projects include abundant hydropower resources from rivers such as the Angara and Yenisei.
Development projects include oil, natural gas, coal, and various metals.
Development projects include timber from vast forest areas.

== Totalitarian nature and ideological shifts ==

Soviet democracy and the dictatorship of the proletariat disappeared in practice during Stalinism, a period when Stalin's rule had a totalitarian character and was characterized by a widespread personality cult.
Stalin abolished Lenin's market economy policies.

== Persecution of intellectuals and scientists ==

Many leading researchers were deported under Stalin and sent to special settlements within the Gulag system known as sharashkas, where they were separated from the rest of society.

== Historical context and legacy ==

Lev Trotsky led a faction within the Communist Party.
One such topic was Joseph Stalin's war and purges.
This collapse was caused by severe laws.

The Soviet Union entered World War II on 17 September 1939 with its invasion of Poland, in accordance with a secret protocol within the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact with Nazi Germany.
The Soviet Union later invaded Finland, and occupied and annexed the Baltic states, as well as parts of Romania.
On 22 June 1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union, opening the Eastern Front, the largest theater of World War II.

Eventually, some 5 million Red Army troops were captured by the Nazis; the latter deliberately starved to death or otherwise killed 3.3 million Soviet POWs, and a vast number of civilians, as the "Hunger Plan" sought to fulfil Generalplan Ost.
Although the Wehrmacht had considerable early success, their attack was halted in the Battle of Moscow.
Subsequently, the Germans were dealt major defeats first at the Battle of Stalingrad in the winter of 1942–1943, and then in the Battle of Kursk in the summer of 1943.
Another German failure was the Siege of Leningrad, in which the city was fully blockaded on land between 1941 and 1944 by German and Finnish forces, and suffered starvation and more than a million deaths, but never surrendered.
Soviet forces steamrolled through Eastern and Central Europe in 1944–1945 and captured Berlin in May 1945.
In August 1945, the Red Army invaded Manchuria and ousted the Japanese from Northeast Asia, contributing to the Allied victory over Japan.

The 1941–1945 period of World War II is known in Russia as the Great Patriotic War.
The Soviet Union, along with the United States, the United Kingdom and China were considered the Big Four of Allied powers in World War II, and later became the Four Policemen, which was the foundation of the United Nations Security Council.
During the war, Soviet civilian and military death were about 26–27 million, accounting for about half of all World War II casualties.
The Soviet economy and infrastructure suffered massive devastation, which caused the Soviet famine of 1946–1947.
However, at the expense of a large sacrifice, the Soviet Union emerged as a global superpower.

== Pre-war diplomacy and the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact ==

Britain and France pursued a policy of appeasement towards Adolf Hitler that involved allowing the annexation of the Rhineland, Austria, and Czechoslovakia.
Hitler's expansion of Nazi Germany significantly strained relations between Germany and the Soviet Union, making war between the two countries imminent.
Around the same time, Nazi Germany formed an alliance with Imperial Japan, a rival of the Soviet Union in the Far East with which Russia had historical conflicts dating back to 1938 and 1939.
Several armed conflicts between the Soviet Union and Japan took place between 1937 and 1939 on the border of Manchuria, which was occupied by Japan at the time.
The Soviet government agreed to sign the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact with Germany in August 1939 after the failure of final Soviet attempts to form an anti-Nazi alliance with both Britain and France [cite: 269].
The pact included a commitment between the two countries not to attack each other and a division of spheres of influence in Eastern Europe [cite: 269].
A secret protocol outlined an agreed-upon division of Eastern Europe.
Hitler planned an attack war against Poland in early September 1939, which was coordinated with a Soviet attack on eastern Poland in mid-September.
The attacks led to the division of Poland between Nazi Germany and the USSR.
A non-aggression pact was negotiated in April 1941.

In August 1939, the Soviet government decided to improve relations with Germany following the failure of attempts to form an anti-Nazi alliance with the United Kingdom and France.
The Soviet government sought a non-aggression pact between the two countries and aimed to divide spheres of influence in Eastern Europe.
The agreement reached was the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, which was signed based on this decision.
The German-Soviet Pact was a non-aggression pact that guaranteed that no war would occur between the two countries.
The pact ensured the division of spheres of influence in Eastern Europe and included an agreement to divide Eastern Europe.
The non-aggression pact included a clause for the partition of Poland and the Baltic states.
The secret protocols established terms for dividing Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania.
The division was to be shared between the Reich and the Soviet Union.
This arrangement did not trigger a notable reaction from France or Great Britain.
The pact remained valid until the end stages of World War II.

== Operation Barbarossa and the Eastern Front ==

Hitler focused on a single front during the early stages of World War II, which was not the Soviet Union, allowing the Soviet Union to build up its military strength while Germany focused elsewhere.
On June 22, 1941, Germany criticized the non-aggression pact and invaded the Soviet Union without declaring war.
This invasion, known as Operation Barbarossa, was carried out by Germany with its allies and constituted the largest invasion forces in world history.
The invasion led to the German-Soviet War, after which the Soviet Union joined the Anti-Hitler Coalition.
Nazi forces controlled most of the European part of the Soviet Union as the German army advanced deep into Russia, reaching near Moscow and conquering Belarus and Ukraine.
The Red Army, which was under-equipped and disorganized by Stalin's purges, retreated.
Germany began to face defeats as winter arrived, with these defeats occurring on the outskirts of Moscow.

The German forces were pushed westward after being blocked at Stalingrad.

== Major battles and the turning of the tide ==

Under Stalin and leaders such as Georgy Zhukov and Konstantin Rokossovsky, Soviet forces advanced towards Eastern Europe between 1944 and 1945.
The conflict included many of the deadliest battles in human history.
Hitler's army was halted by the Russian winter during World War II.
The Battle of Kursk took place on a massive salient located in southwestern Russia near the border with Ukraine, with Orel located to the north and Belgorod to the south.
This push westward occurred notably following the Battle of Kursk, which was one of the battles that determined the outcome of World War II in Europe.
Soviet generals gradually regained the initiative as the Red Army was reinforced by Allied weapon deliveries.
After these battles, the tide of the war turned in favor of the USSR and its Western allies.

== Casualties and the Generalplan Ost ==

Soviet military losses reached 10.6 million and Soviet civilian losses reached 15.9 million.

== Operation Barbarossa and the German advance ==

Nazi Germany posed a serious threat to the Soviet Union.

== Major battles and the turning point ==

The Soviet Union successfully defended Moscow in early 1942, and after the Battle of Moscow in December, the fascists retreated.
Nazi German forces reached the suburbs of St.
Petersburg and the suburbs of Moscow.
The Allied powers, including Britain and the United States, assisted the Soviet Union.

== Economic reforms and privatization ==

An economic reform program was announced in October 1991, and its implementation began in early 1992.
The reform program included removing internal and external trade from state monopoly.
Russia claimed ownership of all property within its territory, a claim that included remaining gold reserves.
A program for privatizing state property was approved in the summer of 1992, resulting in the privatization of 40,000 enterprises.

== Economic collapse and production decline ==

Industrial production decreased between 1990 and the end of 1995.
The GDP decreased by 50% between 1990 and 1995, and industrial production decreased by 50% between 1990 and 1995.
The Russian economy was less developed in the early 1990s, production decreased in this environment, and prices increased in this environment.
Industrial production decreased by 16.2% in 1992, and agricultural production decreased by 4% in 1992.
National income decreased by 57% in 1993 compared to 1990, industrial production decreased by 63% in 1993 compared to 1990, and capital investment decreased by 43% in 1993 compared to 1990.
Russia's share of the world's GDP decreased between 1990 and 1997, falling from 3.7% to 1.7% during this period.
Russia's share of industrial production decreased between 1990 and 1997, falling from 4.6% to 1.8% during this period.
Russia's share of global GDP fell from 8th-9th place to 14th-15th place during the reform period, and Russia's per capita GDP fell from 43rd place to 58th place during the reform period.
Highly specialized production processes broke down, specialized distribution processes broke down, and many cities were suddenly cut off from previous networks.

Gross domestic product and the economy declined by 50% between 1990 and 1995.[78,81,2438] Russia's GDP declined from 1990 to the end of 1995 and declined by approximately 40 percent during this period.[78,81] The volume of industrial production declined by more than 50 percent.[78,81] Russia's GDP before the 1998 crisis was half of what it was at the beginning of the 1990s.
The surge in money supply caused inflation.
Russia issued Eurobonds in November 1996 and the amount of the first issuance was $1 billion.
The poverty rate increased from 1.5% during the Soviet era to 39-49% by mid-1993.[80,1571,2439,2440,2441] Approximately 40% of Russians lived below the national poverty line in 1998.[48,2497] Unemployment in Russia was 12.4% in 1999.[2676,2677,2678] The living standards of the fixed-salary class deteriorated rapidly.
Russia's population decreased by 5 million after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
An increase of approximately 25% was observed in the economic sector over 4 years.
The Russian Federation is close to the level of economic activity from 1989.

Yeltsin was in conflict with the Supreme Soviet, which was a stronghold of conservatives, and he began to face strong opposition from the People's Congress, which was also a stronghold of conservatives.

The Russian Federation has a transitional economy, and changes were introduced to the sectoral structure of the economy and to the financing system.

== Shock therapy and initial reforms ==

A rapid economic transformation known as 'shock therapy' was recommended by the United States and the International Monetary Fund.[81,1569] The reforms began in January 1992.
The Yeltsin-Gaidar government implemented retail price liberalization, foreign trade liberalization, and reorganized the tax system.
These reforms radically changed the economic situation in the country and resulted in a transition to a market economy.
State price regulation was abolished on January 2, 1992, and freedom of trade was declared on January 2, 1992.[3405,3406,3407,3408] Inflation reached approximately 2,520% for the entire year of 1992.
The ruble became freely convertible into foreign currencies starting in July 1992 and could be exchanged for US dollars.
There was an intention to keep the exchange rate reasonably stable, but this intention was soon abandoned.
The exchange rate of the ruble fell dramatically between July 1992 and October 1995.
In July 1992, the exchange rate was 144 rubles for one US dollar, and by October 1995, the exchange rate had fallen to approximately 5,000 rubles for one US dollar.

Deep changes were implemented following the 'shock therapy' approach recommended by the United States and the International Monetary Fund.

== Privatization and the rise of oligarchs ==

All companies were owned by the government, and the goal of the program was to reduce the role of the government and to encourage private initiative [cite: 2775].
Privatization was carried out through voucher privatization and also through pledge auctions [cite: 2775].
On October 1, 1993, every citizen received a voucher worth 10,000 rubles that could be exchanged for shares in companies [cite: 2775].
In June 1994, approximately 70% of medium-sized and large companies were in private hands, and approximately 90% of small businesses were in private hands [cite: 2775].
A large number of enterprises were privatized in the first half of the 1990s.
The privatization process had multiple phases, and in the second phase of the privatization round, the government decided to sell its interests in companies.
The privatization process was plagued by many corruption scandals, the population lost trust, and the transfer occurred for very low prices [cite: 2775].
Some recipients were members of the Russian mafia [cite: 2775].
The period was characterized by 'wild' capitalism, involved the initial accumulation of capital, and was linked to a rejection of a centralized planned economy [cite: 3405,3406,3407,3408].

== The 1993 Constitutional Crisis ==

Yeltsin dissolved the Congress of People's Deputies and the Supreme Soviet of Russia via a decree (ukaz) because the bodies had opposed his efforts to implement economic reforms and the results of a referendum held on April 25, 1993.

Yeltsin ordered a violent storming of the parliament building, which is known as the White House, and sent the army to take control of it, which was the Russian parliament [cite: 1574].

A further uprising against him was violently suppressed on October 3 and 4, during which there were 190 deaths in Moscow.
Large protests occurred against Yeltsin, and this crisis was Moscow's most severe internal struggle since the October Revolution [cite: 1555].

A coup d'état took place in October 1993.

== Adoption of the 1993 Constitution ==

The current Constitution of the Russian Federation was adopted on December 12, 1993, in a referendum that took place after the constitutional crisis in Russia.
This new constitution established a presidential administration and was modeled after the French De Gaulle constitution.
The adoption replaced the previous constitution, which was adopted on April 12, 1978.
In the referendum, 58,187,755 people participated, with 32,937,30 voting in favor, representing more than 58 percent of voters.
This grant of power aligns with the historical tradition of political power concentration in the country and is proportional to that tradition.

== Economic Growth Drivers (1999–2008) ==

Russia experienced significant economic growth from 1999, which was interrupted only by the global economic crisis in 2009.
The evolution of raw material prices significantly favored the economic recovery, and the improvement in debt repayment was due to rising oil prices and rising natural gas prices.
The Russian state was able to repay loans taken out during the peak of the financial crisis in advance, and Russia reduced its public debt to 8% by the end of 2007.
Russia built the world's third-largest foreign exchange reserves, an achievement due to a current account surplus of 10% of GDP during that period.
The state budget was regularly in surplus, and financial resources included more effective tax revenues.
These factors allowed for the creation of a stabilization fund in 2004.
Capital investments increased significantly.
The Russian economy grew in 2006, which was the eighth consecutive year of growth for the Russian economy since the 1998 crisis.
A weak exchange rate followed high oil prices, and rising domestic demand, rising consumption, and rising investment helped the economy grow.
The economy grew for 9 consecutive years.

Russia's GDP grew by an average of 6.8% per year.
The economic growth was primarily driven by oil extraction and exports, the extraction of other valuable minerals and exports, and factors other than commercial services and goods in the domestic market.

== Consolidation of the Power Vertical ==

The power vertical is seen as incompatible with changing parliamentary majorities and with free competition among political parties.

== Political Parties and the Party Cartel ==

Russian political parties rarely possessed a stable identity.
The Russian government has supported a new, independent power base since the 1995 parliamentary election.
The 'Parties of Power' are administrative entities that were established from the top down, are loose ad-hoc coalitions, rely on bureaucrats for support, and are supported by bureaucrats loyal to the President.
These parties were able to mobilize specific voter groups.
Since the turn of the millennium, only a few parties functioned as social networks.
From 2008 to 2011, there were only seven political parties in Russia.
This limited number of parties was the result of legal regulations that required a high minimum number of members for parties and required parties to have offices in two-thirds of the regions.
A new party law was passed in December 2011 that allowed the admission of new parties with a minimum membership of 500 people, whereas the previous minimum membership requirement was 40,000 people.
The European Court of Human Rights made a ruling in favor of the Party of Freedom, which was an opposition party.

== Centralization of regional power ==

A federalism with regional centers emerged during the first years of the Russian Federation under Boris Yeltsin, during which the regions built up a political counterweight [cite: 1013][cite: 1028].
Under Vladimir Putin, a centralizing process occurred that involved the successive disempowerment of federal institutions in favor of the presidential administration and the personalization of political power [cite: 1028].
This variant curtailed the political rights of the regions [cite: 1013].
Under Putin, there was a return to centralization and control [cite: 985].
The goal of the reform was to strengthen the vertical distribution of power and to tighten control over regional leaders [cite: 1051].
Under Putin, governors were more closely tied to the central level through an appointment system that began in 2002, under which regional parliaments were replaced by governors in the appointment of representatives for the Federation Council and local representatives such as mayors [cite: 1014][cite: 1016].
Under Putin, governors were eliminated as actors with their own base and were weakened as independent power factors [cite: 1016].
Between 2005 and 2012, governors and republic heads of state were appointed by the president and were no longer elected by the population [cite: 1017].

This practice continued until May 2012, during which regional parliaments could only confirm the nominees.

A mixed electoral procedure was installed under which candidates have been nominated by the regional parliament since 2012.
Candidate nomination requires a specific percentage of members from regional parliaments and involves consultation with the president.

== The Yukos Case and Corporate Governance ==

Mikhail Khodorkovsky was arrested, prosecuted for tax evasion and other crimes, and resigned as CEO of Yukos in 2003, while the merger with Sibneft was cancelled.

Rosneft was the government's side in the case, and a compensation order was issued on June 26, 2010.
In July 2014, the Russian government was ordered to pay 1.9 billion euros in compensation related to the Yukos collapse case, and in December of that year, the European Court of Human Rights rejected the government's appeal.

== The 2008–2009 financial crisis and recovery ==

The global financial crisis hit in autumn 2008.

Stock prices on the Moscow Exchange fell sharply by the end of the year, the value of the ruble depreciated by approximately 20 percent in total, and foreign exchange reserves shrank significantly.
The central bank was forced to devalue the ruble in 2009, which was a second devaluation of the ruble by the central bank, and the ruble reached its lowest level against the US dollar in nearly six years.
Gross domestic product (GDP) decreased in 2009 by nearly 8 percent, falling from 1,661 billion US dollars to 1,223 billion US dollars, and unemployment increased.
Russia recovered relatively quickly and showed a growth rate of 4 percent in 2010 and 2011.

== State events and commemorations ==

A military parade took place at Red Square in 2010.

In early 2014, following a revolution in Ukraine, Russia occupied and annexed Crimea from neighbouring Ukraine following a disputed referendum, then used Russian mercenaries and military forces, supported by local separatist militias, to start a war in the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine where most of the inhabitants wanted to stay in Ukraine.
In a major escalation of the conflict, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022.
The invasion marked the largest conventional war in Europe since World War II, and was met with international condemnation, as well as expanded sanctions against Russia.
As a result, Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe in March, and was suspended from the United Nations Human Rights Council in April.
In September, following successful Ukrainian counteroffensives, Putin announced a "partial mobilisation", Russia's first mobilisation since World War II.
By the end of September, Putin proclaimed the annexation of four Ukrainian regions, the largest annexation in Europe since World War II.
Putin and Russian-installed leaders signed treaties of accession, internationally unrecognized and widely denounced as illegal, despite the fact that Russian forces have been unable to fully occupy any of the four regions.
A number of supranational and national parliaments passed resolutions declaring Russia to be a state sponsor of terrorism.
In addition, Russia was declared a terrorist state by Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
Hundreds of thousands are estimated to have been killed as a result of the invasion.
The war in Ukraine has further exacerbated Russia's demographic crisis.

In June 2023, the Wagner Group, a private military contractor fighting for Russia in Ukraine, declared an open rebellion against the Russian Ministry of Defense, capturing Rostov-on-Don, before beginning a march on Moscow.
However, after negotiations between Wagner and the Belarusian government, the rebellion was called off.

== Internal Dissent, Emigration, and Public Opinion ==

More than 200,000 people left Russia, a departure estimated to be motivated by fear of consequences caused by economic sanctions and police repression.
The Russian population did not rise up in resistance, and a clear majority supported the Russian military operation in Ukraine based on several representative surveys conducted by the Lewada Center.
Russian law does not classify the conflict as a 'war', and the conflict is referred to as a 'military special operation' in Russia due to propaganda.
Emigration started with the beginning of the war and increased to several hundred thousand people following mobilization in Russia.
Observers evaluate this migration as the largest since the October Revolution, and more than 1% of the working population was included in this migration.
Emigrants included young people, well-educated individuals, members of technical professions, and people from the IT sector.

Putin's war justifications exhibit extreme self-centeredness and contain a grotesque contradiction, which confirmed the openly present Russian fascism.
