== Prison system and torture ==

In 2013, an estimated 600,000 people were held in strict camp detention in Russia, and the human rights organization Memorial believes that some of these detainees were political prisoners.
Approximately 140,000 prisoners were in custody in the spring of 2019 for drug abuse based on Article 228.2, the potential for abuse of which had been known for a long time and which became internationally known due to the scandal involving journalist Ivan Golunov.
The number of imprisoned convicts, suspects, and defendants in Russian penal and pre-trial detention facilities decreased in August 2020 to fewer than 500,000, a drop that the Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) attributed to the use of alternative, non-custodial penalties and to a liberalization of the prison system.
Torture and severe torture are widespread in the Russian prison system, where prison authorities can deliberately expose disliked prisoners to sexualized violence to permanently move them into the caste of Untouchables.
A report states that torture is endemic and that torturers remain almost totally unpunished.

Law enforcement agencies secretly filmed Jehovah's Witnesses in the homes of Jehovah's Witnesses and in Kingdom Halls of Jehovah's Witnesses.

Russian society cultivates 'groups of basic prerequisites' based on the theories of Wilfred Bion.[1036,1037] The author compared the additional projective identification of a nation feeling humiliated after imperialism to the rise of Nazism in Austria, noting that the nation felt humiliated after being post-imperial.[1036,1037] Individuality is rejected and there is a prevailing rejection of the differentiation of personalities, which leads to increased intolerance towards deviations from a single pattern of thought and behavior.[1036,1037] State media and their propaganda fueled hatred in society.[1063,1064] According to Jason Stanley, Putin uses antisemitic key elements that belong to a globally networked right-wing movement which sees Putin as its leader.[1178,1179]

== LGBTQ+ rights and discrimination ==

Russia is considered one of the countries with a strong opposition to homosexuality, and recent polls show that most Russians do not accept homosexuality and have expressed support for discriminatory laws against homosexuals.
In a survey of 450 psychiatrists in the Rostov region, 62.5% considered homosexuality to be a disease and three-quarters considered it to be immoral behavior.

Petersburg are believed to have a thriving LGBT community [4406,4407].
In 2013, Russia under President Vladimir Putin passed a law banning all forms of propaganda regarding homosexuality and same-sex marriage, which banned events that promote homosexuality and events promoting homosexual relationships.

This ban was an effort to promote traditional Russian values and aimed to counter the trend of promoting homosexuality [4409,4410,4411].
Western countries were demanding the legalization of same-sex marriage, and the Russian government believed these demands were corrupting youth, destroying the moral foundation of the family in Russia, and weakening Russia [4409,4410,4411].

Russia's autocratic political system has been variously described as a kleptocracy, an oligarchy, and a plutocracy.

== Oligarchs and asset privatization ==

Valuable companies, banks, and natural resources, including mineral oil reserves, were acquired by oligarchs during auctions at prices significantly below their value [cite: 957].
These oligarchs, such as Sergey Grishin and Roman Abramovich, had good relationships with the ruling elite, paid bribes to the ruling elite, and paid protection money to the ruling elite [cite: 957].
Alisher Usmanov is a co-owner of the metal and mining company Metalloinvest.
The oligarchs engaged in lucrative business deals with the state and became politically influential actors [cite: 958].
The situation is partly explained by the network economy inherited from the 1990s privatization period, which favored certain oligarchs and shaped power dynamics in the highest levels of Russian power [cite: 1793].

== Nepotism and personal enrichment ==

Nepotism occurs in job assignments and contract awards.
Jelena Tschischowa describes how the extent of corruption increases with proximity to power in the Kremlin.
Alexei Nawalny and his anti-corruption organization uncovered numerous cases of personal enrichment that involved nepotism at the highest level, including the existence of so-called Putin's Palace.
Estimates suggest corruption is of an enormous scale, with 22.5% of costs in public contracts estimated to be bribes and total corruption costs in state contracts estimated at 93 billion US dollars.

In the 2022 Corruption Perception Index, which ranked 180 countries, Russia scored 28 out of a possible 100 points.

== State-criminal nexus and sanctions evasion ==

The state and organized crime help each other, with the Russian state using criminal structures to import sanctioned goods while the Kremlin mobilizes these structures for political interests.
The use of criminal income or capabilities can obscure the underlying interests and actions of the Russian state.

The Investigative Committee investigates cases of abuse of power and corruption.
In 2016, President Putin issued an order directed at control authorities that mandated a "control pause".
The alleged security checks rarely served security purposes and were primarily used for enrichment.

== Academic debates on regime classification ==

Gellately considered the term 'fascism' to be highly charged or loaded.
Ulrich Schmid believes the idea of fascism is close to the current Russian system.
Ulrich Schmid argues that labeling the current Russian system simply as fascist blurs things more than it helps us recognize its contours.
Political scientist Marlene Laruelle analyzed the Russian political system.
Marlene Laruelle concluded that the system cannot be called fascist.
Laruelle argues that the regime's power does not rely on mass mobilization.
Laruelle argues that the regime benefits from the atomization of society instead.
Comparative fascism researchers Roger Griffin and Stanley Payne (2022) reject classifying Putin as a fascist in the context of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Payne argues that Putin's ideology is not revolutionary but reactionary.
Payne holds that Putin's regime represents the closest analogue to fascism in a large country since the end of World War II.
Putin did not build a dynamic and charismatic movement in the fascist style.
Payne opposes the comparison of Putin to Mussolini and Hitler.
Payne states that Putin's political system is more of a revival of the creed of Tsar Nicholas I in the 19th century.
Putin's system is not similar to the revolutionary, modernizing regimes of Hitler and Mussolini.
Griffin maintains the view that Putin's regime is an illiberal democracy.
The ultranationalist regime of Japan during World War II adopted some elements of fascism.
The ultranationalist regime of Japan during World War II did not become an authentically fascist regime.
Ulrich Herbert rejects characterizing Putin's system as fascist.
There is no supporting mass movement in Putin's system.

Some people classify Russia as a totalitarian state.
Political scientist Claus Leggewie considers Russia a new type of totalitarian system that identifies a Stalinist core and a fascist outer shell in the Russian system.
Vladimir Putin is accused of corruption, adopted the concept of Russki Mir from fascist sources, and his rule has so far relied on the passivity of society.
The situation leads to family resemblances with fascism and Stalinism caused by radicalization and an intensification of repression.
The system described is a type of recombination of Stalinism and Fascism, though the intensity of this recombined system has not yet been reached.
Comparisons with Hitler are disproportionate.

== Economic impact and shadow economy ==

Corruption prevented Russia from increasing foreign investments during the transition period.
Much money is held in private hands rather than in bank accounts.
The large scale of corruption is caused by the fact that large parts of the Russian economy are in the dark or shadows.
Large parts of the Russian economy involve unreported income or expenses.
Corruption is estimated to cost the Russian economy approximately 2 billion dollars, an amount equivalent to 80 billion rubles.
There are many different estimates of the actual cost of corruption.
Official government statistics were published by Rosstat, which reported that the underground economy represented 15% of Russia's GDP in 2011.
This underground economy included undeclared salaries intended to avoid paying taxes and social contributions, as well as other types of tax evasion.
Rosstat provided estimates regarding corruption in Russia for the year 2011, stating that corruption represented between 3.5% and 7% of Russia's GDP.
Independent experts estimate corruption figures up to 25% of Russia's GDP.
A World Bank report estimates the figure at approximately 48%.
These price increases significantly exceed the inflation rate.
The Russian population pays for this corruption.

Housing, water, gas, and electricity prices have risen rapidly as a direct result of massive corruption at the highest level.
The International Organization of Certified Accountants (ACCA) provides estimates regarding Russia's shadow economy, which is among the top five countries with the highest level of shadow economy.

== Causes and systemic drivers ==

Corruption is based on a historical model of public governance in Russia and is attributed to the general weakness of the rule of law in Russia.
Weak rule of law in the country is one of the reasons for corruption.
Corruption is widespread due to low government funding for ministries, and another reason for the rampant corruption is the level of salaries in the public sector.
Public sector salaries are significantly lower than the average private sector salaries, and low salaries force government employees and officials to accept bribes to supplement income.
This situation weakens the already deficient anti-corruption apparatus in Russia.
There is a lack of political will for real changes.

== Oligarchs and political structure ==

These oligarchs are now an integral part of Russia's socio-economic and political reality, and these corrupt groups had secret links with the mafia.
Examples include authoritarian practices by subject administrators or presidents in republics, manipulation of the police, and control over the judiciary.
The sudden tax fraud involving Yukos is an example that came to light when owner oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky gained political ambitions.
Boris Berezovsky was a co-owner of the oil company Sibneft, fled the country earlier in his life, and died in 2013.
Putin appointed oligarchs as governors in multiple poor regions with the goal of having these oligarchs invest money in these regions.
Russia is described by some commentators as a fascist state, and the Russian variant of fascism is referred to as 'Raschizm'.
Putin's system is characterized by an open and pervasive mixing of public services and business, involves the use of relatives, friends, and acquaintances to benefit from budget expenditures, and involves the use of relatives, friends, and acquaintances to take over state property.

== International rankings and assessments ==

Russia was ranked as the most corrupt country in Europe starting in 2016.
In 2013, Russia was ranked 122nd out of 167 countries and received a score of 29.
Transparency International rated Russia's corruption level at less than 3 points in 2011, a score that indicates a very poor performance.
Russia's position in the Corruption Perceptions Index has remained stable in recent years, though its position in the ranking experienced more significant changes.
In 2015, Russia was ranked 119th, followed by 131st in 2016, 135th in 2017, and 138th in 2018.
The fluctuations in Russia's ranking are linked to changes in the rankings of other countries and to the inclusion or exclusion of certain countries from the index.
In 2021, Russia ranked 136th out of 180 countries on the index.
Russia's ranking on the Transparency International Corruption Perception Index fell at the beginning of Putin's rule.
The Corruption Perceptions Index has not improved despite efforts to fight corruption.

== Business environment and corporate risks ==

The Russia-Norwegian Chamber of Commerce states that corruption is one of the biggest problems facing Russian and international companies.
A study conducted by the British audit firm Ernst & Young in the spring of 2012 included over 1,500 top executives from companies in 43 countries worldwide.
According to the study, corruption risks in Russia decreased significantly in 2011 and became lower than the global average in many parameters.
PWC and Transparency International published reports at the end of 2011 stating that the scale of corruption in Russia is decreasing.

== Anti-corruption laws and institutional efforts ==

Anti-corruption efforts began in 1992 under President Boris Yeltsin.
The first package of anti-corruption laws was adopted in 2008 under President Medvedev to ratify the UN Convention against Corruption and the Council of Europe's Criminal Law Convention on Corruption.
A new law came into effect in 2012 requiring all officials of public organizations to disclose their entire assets and defining conflict of interest for public officials for the first time in this manner.
The General Prosecutor's Office of Russia reported on anti-corruption efforts and dismissals due to corruption investigations.
Existing anti-corruption tools were not developed, systemic anti-corruption efforts were replaced by isolated criminal cases, and spot measures taken by anti-corruption authorities and local amendments to legislation cannot fundamentally change the situation in the country.
Russia has not ratified the Convention on Civil Liability for Corruption.
International anti-corruption commitments were abandoned after 2022, Russia consistently hinders civil society cooperation in the fight against corruption, and Russia withdrew from the criminal convention on corruption.

== Public reaction and civil society ==

Corruption has a strong impact on individual citizens' lives in Russia and has an impact on all aspects of life in Russia.[2477,2478,2479,2480,2481,2482,2483,2484,2485,2486,3169,3170] The reaction to corruption has changed in recent years, and since Putin's second term, very few corruption cases have become the subject of scandals.
Protests against corruption in the Russian federal government took place simultaneously in multiple cities across the country.
These protests were triggered by the release of an investigative film and by the inadequate reaction of Russian authorities.
The investigative film accumulated more than 20 million views on YouTube.
Mikhail Zadornov stated that corruption levels in Russia are currently higher than in the 1990s.[3727,3728] Anton Pominov is the director of the Center 'Transparency International - R'.
The Anti-Corruption Foundation is a non-profit organization founded by opposition politician Alexei Navalny.

== Evolution of bribery practices ==

There has been a change in the main objective of bribery.
Previously, officials took bribes to look the other way at crimes, whereas now officials take bribes only to do their job.
This private money is used to pay bribes to high-ranking government officials.

== Anti-corruption activism and repression ==

The Anti-Corruption Foundation issued multiple reports detailing the involvement of high-ranking officials in corruption.
The legal system ignored the findings and used them only for attempts to discredit the organization.
The organization was labeled as a 'foreign agent' in 2019, labeled as 'extremist' in 2021, and banned in 2021.

== Government rhetoric and enforcement ==

Medvedev focused heavily on the 'war against corruption', which targeted corrupt police specifically.
Some progress was made in fighting corruption, yet problems with corruption still exist despite this progress.
The government failed to curb corruption.

== Oligarchs and the banking sector ==

This situation is assumed to be caused by banks being extremely corrupt, and these banks are owned by oligarchs.
The business model of banks seems to be primarily supporting the other companies of oligarchs.
Putin has occasionally taken controversial actions against oligarchs.
Most current business leaders in Russia are likely guilty of crimes during the transition from a planned economy to an attempt at a market economy.

== The Khodorkovsky case ==

Mikhail Khodorkovsky was Russia's richest man in 2003 and was arrested in 2003.
He was accused of securing companies during Yeltsin's privatization through improper means.
The imprisonment of Mikhail Khodorkovsky is considered politically motivated by several Russian analysts and several foreign analysts.

== Political analysis and legal concerns ==

According to Alexander Motyl, the Putin regime is a variant of fascism.
Concern and worry were regarding the application of selective laws to private enterprises.

== International rankings and economic impact ==

The 2016 Corruption Perceptions Index was published by Transparency International, in which Russia ranked 131st out of 176 countries and scored 29 points.
The damage caused by corruption amounts to up to 50% of Russia's total GDP.

The primary and fundamental statement of laws in Russia is the Constitution of the Russian Federation.
Statutes, like the Russian Civil Code and the Russian Criminal Code, are the predominant legal sources of Russian law.

Russia has the world's second largest illegal arms trade market, after the United States, is ranked first in Europe and 32nd globally in the Global Organized Crime Index, and is among the countries with the highest number of people in prison.

== Constitutional framework and civil rights ==

The Russian Constitution states that judges are independent, subject only to the law, and that constitutional justice in courts is based on the equality of all citizens.
Trials must be open to the public and defendants are guaranteed a defense.
The Russian Constitution guarantees media freedom and freedom of thought and speech, which are guaranteed in Chapter 2, Article 29 of the Russian Constitution.
The Russian Constitution prohibits propaganda and agitation that incites social, racist, national, or religious hatred and prohibits any form of censorship.
There was a lack of Roman legal tradition.

== Judicial structure and appointment ==

Judicial independence is guaranteed by the constitution, and the High Court of Arbitration interprets laws.
Judges in Russia are mostly federal judges, and they are recruited from the judiciary and security agencies rather than from the bar association or legal academia [cite: 1091].
Upon appointment, judges must prove they have a university legal education and five years of professional experience [cite: 1091].
A commission decides on the appointment of judges, a process that requires the President's consent.
The Commission consists of four representatives of the judiciary, seven heads of various departments of the Presidential Administration, the Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs, the First Deputy Director of the Federal Security Service (FSB), and the Prosecutor General [cite: 1092].
The sessions of this Commission are not public, and decisions made by the commission do not need to be justified, are final, and cannot be appealed [cite: 1092].
Judges of the highest courts are selected entirely without the participation of the judiciary [cite: 1092].

Economic courts and arbitration courts are considered competent and handle disputes between companies.
The Supreme Economic Court was attached to the Supreme Court in 2014 and was effectively dissolved as a result.
The selection process for these judges takes place behind closed doors.

== Executive influence and judicial independence ==

Courts and the prosecution are actually under the influence of the executive branch, and there is direct or indirect influence on judgments.
Court presidents play a significant role in the courts by assigning individual cases to judges, deciding on the allocation of service apartments, withdrawing cases from judges during the proceedings, and deciding on the distribution of annual bonus payments.
The executive branch exerts influence within the courts, and influence is exerted on cases of interest to the executive via 'telephone justice'.
The prosecutor's office can intervene in civil cases and propose a verdict.
The executive branch can instruct the prosecutor's office to annul verdicts at its own discretion and to retry cases.
The Russian judiciary has more room to make independent decisions.

== Constitutional Court and political rulings ==

The Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation holds the status of a constitutional body.
Valery Zorkin was the long-serving president of the Constitutional Court and acknowledged that national security interests should be weighted higher than constitutional principles.
The court supported a shift in power towards the office of the President in multiple rulings.
The Constitutional Court opposed President Yeltsin's thirst for power in 1993 and assisted Vladimir Putin in the authoritarian transformation of the country by enabling further presidential terms beyond constitutional permissibility.
There are lay judge courts at the lower level.

== Investigative authorities and political interference ==

The Investigative Committee is directly subordinate to the President, is the most important federal investigative authority, and audits federal agencies.
Police investigations end when they involve influential politicians, prosecutorial investigations end when they involve influential politicians, and investigations are not initiated if they would involve influential politicians.

== Legal remedies and complaints ==

Filing a complaint against this situation is difficult in Russia, and complaint and appeal instances function very limitedly there. These instances particularly struggle with cases against state actions, such as court rulings. Filing complaints involves high administrative costs.

== International law and sovereignty ==

In December 2015, Putin signed a law allowing the Russian government to override international court rulings.
The Russian Constitutional Court can annul judgments of international courts upon request by the government, a power that primarily concerns judgments of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).
The review of civil rights takes place before the Supreme Court of Russia, with examples including cases involving violations of the European Convention on Human Rights.

== Capital punishment ==

The death penalty has not yet been legally abolished in Russia, and it has not been abolished by law.
Russia suspended the death penalty in 1996, and there has been a moratorium on the death penalty since 1996.

== Homicide rates and trends ==

The homicide rate in Russia fluctuated significantly between 1990 and 2017.
The rate was 30.5 per 100,000 people in 1995 and 9.2 per 100,000 people in 2017.
According to Novaya Gazeta, the homicide rate increased by four percent in 2022.
From January to April 2023, the homicide rate increased by 15 percent.
The homicide rate subsequently decreased significantly.
This decrease may be due to official concealment of the true figures.

== Missing persons and domestic violence ==

Between 70,000 and 100,000 people go missing in Russia annually, with 25% permanently classified as missing, resulting in a range of 17,500 to 25,000 permanently missing persons.
Domestic violence is a societal problem in Russia, where 40% of all violent crimes are committed inside the home.
According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, 12,000 to 14,000 women die annually in Russia due to this violence.

== Organized crime and criminal subculture ==

Organized crime plays a major role in the territory of the former Soviet Union, where the well-known 'thieves in law' operate with a strict internal ethics code and their own sublanguage.
This internal ethics code is closely linked to the former Soviet prison system and the Gulag.
The tight cohesion of criminal groups originating from Soviet times no longer exists, as criminal groups previously shared a common fund but different regional groups now claim the names and heritage of these organizations.
Organized crime has become more provincial in nature and more internationalized.

== State-criminal relations and illicit trade ==

The taboo against collaborating with the state and its members has been broken.
Viktor But is a weapons dealer who was formerly a secret service officer and is suspected of acting at least partially on orders.
The electronic expertise of Russian hacker groups is extracted by Russian services.
Criminal group members benefit from relationships with security services and can exchange their services for protection or information from security services.

== Trial procedures and jury courts ==

Lay judge courts were established in 1993.
Acquittals are more likely before lay judge courts than before pure professional courts, occurring in 15% of cases.
Competencies were gradually withdrawn from the courts, as political cases and crimes with high potential prison sentences were transferred from regional juries courts to district courts without juries.
Criminal convictions are usually based on confessions.
Seventy-five percent of defendants agree to a shortened procedure without evidence collection in hope of a lenient sentence, against which no legal appeals are possible.
Only 4% of defendants have a chance at acquittal.

== Legal framework and sources ==

Russian laws and decrees only come into force after publication in Rossijskaja Gaseta.
Laws enacted in 2002 prohibit extremism, and amendments to these laws were made in 2006.
Critics argue that the law grants the government the right to intervene in matters of faith.
Russia has not used the death penalty since 1996, though the death penalty was not legally abolished in Russia.
The Russian constitution guarantees equality of all citizens before the law.
Legal sources most frequently refer to the Civil Code and the Criminal Code.
Law No.
65-FZ was adopted and signed in 2013 and concerns strengthening liability for offenses at mass events.
Some provisions of the law were repealed by the Constitutional Court in 2013.
Law No.
139-FZ concerns the regulation of information on the Internet.
Laws were signed in July 2012.
Law No.
121-FZ concerns non-commercial organizations.

Law No.
121-FZ is known as the 'foreign agents' law.
A law was signed in May 2013 that banned foreign accounts for ministers, members of the Federation Council and State Duma, judges, military personnel, and prosecutors.
The number of convicts in Russia is approaching 900,000.
The judicial branch includes the Arbitration Court.

== Criminal procedure and trials ==

Acquittals are rare in this legal system, and investigative authorities exert significant pressure to obtain confessions. This applies to defendants who completely deny their guilt, while defendants agree to the expedited procedure, among other reasons, to end long pre-trial detention. The Russian Constitution guarantees freedom of opinion and speech in Chapter 2, Article 29. Propaganda and agitation that incites social, racial, national, or religious hostility is prohibited, and the minimization of the role of the armed forces in World War II is prohibited.

== Prison system structure and facilities ==

Officially, eight different types of correctional facilities are distinguished, including investigative detention centers, rehabilitation labor colonies with general penal execution, rehabilitation labor colonies with strict detention conditions, settlement penal colonies, education colonies, medical penitentiary institutions, special colonies, and prisons.
Eighty percent of prisoners are held in correctional labor colonies with general penal execution.
The differences between these two types of detention facilities are minor and relate to the number of allowed visits, the number of packages received, and the number of money transfers received.
Settlement penal colonies are considered the mildest institutions, where prisoners have extensive freedom of movement, may leave their work with permission to go outside, and may even visit or reunite with their family.
Prisons are considered the harshest institutions, and special colonies are considered the harshest institutions.

Juvenile and young adult offenders are imprisoned in educational colonies.
Women can only be imprisoned in educational colonies, medical correctional facilities, general correctional labor colonies, or settlement penal colonies.
The court does not decide on the organization or severity of prison conditions, while the prison administration decides on both the organization and severity of prison conditions.
Male recidivists are imprisoned in correctional labor colonies with strict detention conditions.
Prisoners convicted of special crimes such as terrorism or hostage-taking are imprisoned in prisons and also in special colonies.
Alexei Navalny died in the colony IK-3, which is called Polarwolf and is considered one of the harshest prisons in the country.

== Prison conditions and internal hierarchy ==

Prisons are unofficially divided into red and black facilities.
Black facilities possess a certain degree of self-governance, where professional criminals such as the 'wory w sakone' play a larger role and illegal items or drugs are available.
Red facilities are considered stricter and are dominated by prison administration.
The 'Thieves of the Law' form a self-governance structure from below in prisons they dominate and enforce their values on all prisoners.
Prison administration generally does not intervene in this self-governance.
Prisoners are mostly housed in communal cells.
A rigid caste system exists within Russian prisons.
The 'Fallengelassenen' (those who have been left behind) form the lowest layer of this system and are completely ostracized.

== Prison population and statistics ==

In 2020, there were 523,928 people in detention facilities, and on March 1, 2021, the incarceration rate was 332 per 100,000 inhabitants.
In Germany, approximately 80 people per 100,000 residents are in detention facilities, while in the USA, approximately 650 people per 100,000 residents are in detention facilities.
The number of people in custody has decreased significantly since the year 2000, when there were over one million people in custody facilities.
This decrease is attributed partly to the imposition of penalties without deprivation of liberty, such as house arrest and regular reporting to police stations.
The exact number of prisoners is unknown, though the Ministry of Justice stated in late 2023 that there were still 266,000 prisoners in detention facilities.
The FSIN prison authority provided a figure for the number of prisoners at the beginning of that year, citing 433,006.

== Prison economy and costs ==

The prison system has its own economic enterprises in which prisoners work, and these enterprises generate profits that keep the costs for each prisoner low.
The average daily cost per prisoner in Europe is approximately 68 euros, while the average daily cost per prisoner in Russia is only 2.4 euros.

== Recidivism and reoffending ==

One third of offenders reoffend, and the recidivism rate is approximately 33%.

== Pardons and early release ==

Pardons are issued by presidential decree, and this pardon process operates outside the standard pardon procedure which requires hearing from victims and reconciliation.
No legal basis for pardons was established by the Duma.
An offer was made in exchange for a pardon and the remission of remaining sentences, and violent serious criminals were among those offered this opportunity.
The conditions for release before the end of the war have been significantly tightened, and a prerequisite for release is reaching a certain age limit, receiving a high award, or being wounded.
If none of these prerequisites are met, the contract is automatically extended.

== Mercenaries and returnee crimes ==

After their service ended, criminals returned to Russia and committed further crimes there, some of which included murders.
There is a legal ban on mercenary companies.

== Police organization and structure ==

The Russian police is federally organized and subordinate to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Russia.
The Russian police force was established in 2011 and replaced the militia as a police organization.
The Ministry of Internal Affairs experienced a significant loss of power in 2016 when it lost the Internal Troops to the newly formed National Guard.
In exchange, the Ministry of Internal Affairs received the Drug Enforcement Agency (Federal Service for Supervision of Control over Circulation of Narcotic Drugs), which had up to 40,000 employees, and the Foreigners' Police (Federal Migration Service), which had 42,000 employees.

== Police force size and demographics ==

In early 2023, the Russian police force had 900,000 officers and was one of the largest in the world.
There were 630 officers per 100,000 inhabitants in Russia, a ratio that is more than double that of the United States.

== Police challenges and public perception ==

Poor pay and increased workload contribute to the personnel shortage, with the increased workload due to stricter laws related to the war in Ukraine.
The population traditionally has little trust in the police, and corruption has been complained about regarding the police.
The police have been criticized for mixing with economic interests and for mixing with private security services.
In 2011, only about 40% of crimes were reported.

== Constitutional framework and legal principles ==

The Constitution of the Russian Federation acts as a social public contract with the citizens of the Russian Federation and establishes checks and balances in state administration.
Chapter 2 of the Russian Constitution guarantees civil rights and freedoms, while the document guarantees rights to all its citizens.
The Constitution states that constitutional justice in the court is based on the equality of all citizens, guarantees judicial independence, and ensures that trials are open to the public.
The accused is guaranteed a defense, and the right to a defense is guaranteed to the accused.
Article 15, which is located in Chapter 1 of the Russian Constitution, enables the subordination of the internal legislation of Russia to the mentioned institutions.

== Judicial system and institutions ==

The highest level of the Russian judicial system is the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation, and regional courts exist below the Supreme Court.
The judicial branch includes the Supreme Arbitration Court.
A decision was made in 1996 to introduce a jury system, which was planned sequentially across all federal regions and introduced in all regions by 2010.
FSSP is the Federal Service of Judicial Execution.
SKR is the Investigative Committee.

== Rule of law and human rights assessments ==

Russia lacks certain attributes of a rule of law state, including independent justice, freedom of association, and freedom of the press.
The World Justice Project ranks Russia 80th out of 99 countries in terms of rule of law.
In 2013, Russia was ranked 80th out of 99 countries surveyed in terms of rule of law.
Public security in Russia has aspects of instability.
Approximately 77% of the interviewees stated they do not trust the police.
In 2011, the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg ruled that neither the criminal proceedings nor the trial regarding the arrest of former Yukos chief Mikhail Khodorkovsky had the characteristics of a political process.

== Death penalty status ==

Russia established a moratorium on the application of the death penalty in 1996 and introduced a moratorium on the death penalty in 1998.
The death penalty has not been abolished by law in Russia, and the highest sentencing measure was not abolished by law.
On November 19, 2009, the Constitutional Court issued an order to continue suspending executions, which effectively abolished the death penalty system in Russia.

== Historical crime and mortality trends ==

During the transition crisis period, Russia experienced four times more violent deaths than the United States and ranked second in the world for homicides.
The homicide rate in Russia was 28.4 per 100,000 people in 2000.
At that time, Russia ranked third in the world for suicides, and the suicide rate was 38.4 per 100,000 people in 2002.

== Crime statistics and trends (2017–2020) ==

According to the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs report on the crime situation in Russia in 2017, the total number of registered crimes was approximately 2,058,500, representing a 4.7% decrease from the previous year.
93.0% of these crimes were solved.
There were 37 recognized terrorist acts in Russia in 2017, which is a 48% increase compared to the previous year.
There were 1,871 crimes with terrorist characteristics (including those similar to terrorism) in 2017, representing a 16% decrease compared to the previous year.
The number of deaths caused by crime was 29,300, an increase of 0.5% compared to the previous year.
The number of crimes in public facilities was 738,000, a decrease of 6.6% compared to the previous year.
1,540.2 thousand crimes were registered between January and September 2020, representing a 1.2% increase compared to the same period in 2019.
17,500 people died as a result of criminal offenses, and 27,100 people suffered serious injuries as a result of criminal offenses.
39.3% of the deceased occurred in rural areas, where 6,900 people died.
67.6% of those who suffered serious injuries occurred in cities and urban settlements, where 18,300 people suffered serious injuries.

Internal affairs agencies reviewed 24.6 million applications, reports, and other information about incidents, and a criminal case was filed for almost every twelfth report.
8.1% of reports resulted in the filing of a criminal case.
40,100 people died as a result of criminal attacks, and deaths accounted for 4.5% of the total incidents.

== Common crimes and victimization ==

Crimes targeting foreigners, including robberies, occur frequently in urban areas.
Pickpocketing, burglary, fraud, and the skimming of credit cards and cash cards also occur frequently in urban areas.
Reports indicate that some victims were Japanese.

== Specific criminal and administrative laws ==

One relevant law is Article 242 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation regarding illegal distribution of pornography.
Another relevant law is Article 6.17 of the Code of Administrative Offenses of the Russian Federation regarding protection of children from harmful information.
Employees cannot be dismissed for improper reasons during the first two years after their employment contract is established.

== Prison system overview and demographics ==

The Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) is the fourth largest prison system in the world, with the United States, China, and Brazil having larger prison systems than FSIN.
Russia ranks 16th in the world based on the relative number of prisoners per capita, with 404 prisoners per 100,000 people.
The number of people deprived of liberty in Russia was 1,060,404 in 2000 and decreased to 582,889 in 2018, representing an almost twofold decrease between 2000 and 2018.
During this period, the number of people deprived of liberty increased by 3.1% for the rest of Europe excluding Russia, while globally the number of prisoners increased by 3.7% between 2015 and 2018.
According to 2019 statistical data, there were 558,778 people held in prisons, among whom 44,336 were women.
Of the total number of prisoners, 100,771 were held in pre-trial detention facilities, and among those in pre-trial detention, 8,851 were women.
The number of first-time prisoners decreased from 356,000 in 2002 to 211,000 in 2018.
The number of people serving a second prison sentence decreased significantly.

In 2002, 204,000 people were serving their second prison sentence.
The number of people serving a third or more prison sentences remained stable.

== Penitentiary infrastructure and operations ==

The FSIN consists of 702 correctional colonies housing 432,579 prisoners, including 122 settlement-type colonies with 33,269 people and 7 colonies for those sentenced to life imprisonment containing 2,017 people.
Additionally, 98,301 people were held in 209 pre-trial detention centers, 1,145 people were held in 8 prisons, and 1,182 people were held in 23 educational colonies for minors.
There are 13 children's homes associated with women's colonies that house 437 children.
The FSIN operates 31 industrial and agricultural facilities, 584 employee adaptation centers, and 72 production workshops.
Correctional facilities contain 283 general education institutions and 503 branches of general education institutions, as well as 284 vocational training institutions and 442 branches of vocational training institutions [cite: 2900].
There are 1,554 objects used for religious purposes, and the Russian penal system employs 295,967 people [cite: 2900].

== Crime statistics and trends ==

In 2010, there were 2.63 million crimes in total across the entire population of Russia, which amounted to 1,800 crimes per 100,000 people.
In 2011, more than 3 million crimes were reported, and the number of murders was 12% lower than in 2010.
The intentional homicide rate in Russia in 2016 was 10.82 per 100,000 people.
The murder rate in Russia is four times higher than in the United States.
In 2001, 33,500 people were killed.
Of the deceased, 41.0% occurred in rural areas where 16,400 people died, and 35.8% occurred in cities and settlements that are not centers of federal subjects.
A total of 49,400 people suffered serious injuries as a result of criminal attacks, with 17,700 people suffering serious injuries specifically, and these serious injuries accounted for 2.8% of the total incidents.
The recidivism rate has exceeded 46%.
Twenty percent of former orphanage residents become criminals after leaving.
Robbery and smuggling contributed to the rising crime wave.
The Russian government committed to cracking down on crime, but these actions did not yield significant results.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime reported statistics.

The intentional homicide rate in the United States in 2016 was 5.8 per 100,000 people.
The intentional homicide rate in Russia in 2016 was twice that of the United States.
The global average intentional homicide rate is 6.2 per 100,000 people.
The intentional homicide rate in Russia in 2016 was significantly higher than the global average.

== Counterfeit goods and consumer safety ==

Counterfeit goods are another problem, with the Russian government estimating that up to 90% of goods in circulation have unclear origins and up to 90% of goods in circulation are counterfeit or untraceable.
Toys are imported from China, while electronic devices are mainly imported illegally from Southeast Asia.
Food products, medicines, clothing, and audio and video discs usually have a domestic origin.
Fake medicine and fake alcohol pose the most serious threat to consumers.
Thousands of Russians die every year from drinking fake vodka that contains deadly chemicals.

== Terrorism and violent attacks ==

Between 2008 and 2016, there were 1,088 deaths in terrorist attacks in Russia, while there were 235 deaths in terrorist attacks in the United States, making the number of deaths in Russian terrorist attacks five times higher than in US terrorist attacks during that period [4495,4496,4497,4498,4499].
Apartment bombings occurred in September 1999 between September 4 and September 16 in Moscow, Buynaksk, and Volgodonsk, killing nearly 300 people, with Chechen extremists suspected of being behind these attacks.

Russia has a market economy, with enormous natural resources, particularly oil and natural gas.
It has the world's ninth-largest economy by nominal GDP and the sixth-largest by PPP.
The large service sector accounts for 62% of total GDP, followed by the industrial sector (32%), while the agricultural sector is the smallest, making up only 5% of total GDP.
Russia has a low official unemployment rate of 4.1%.
Its foreign exchange reserves are the world's fifth-largest, worth $540 billion.
It has a labour force of roughly 70 million, which is the world's sixth-largest.

Russia is the world's thirteenth-largest exporter and the 21st-largest importer.
It relies heavily on revenues from oil and gas-related taxes and export tariffs, which accounted for 45% of Russia's federal budget revenues in January 2022, and up to 60% of its exports in 2019.
Russia has one of the lowest levels of external debt among major economies, although its inequality of household income and wealth is one of the highest among developed countries.
High regional disparity is also an issue.

After over a decade of post-Soviet rapid economic growth, backed by high oil-prices and a surge in foreign exchange reserves and investment, Russia's economy was damaged following the start of the Russo-Ukrainian War and the annexation of Crimea in 2014, due to the first wave of international sanctions being imposed.
In the aftermath of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the country has faced revamped sanctions and corporate boycotts, becoming the most sanctioned country in the world, in a move described as an "all-out economic and financial war" to isolate the Russian economy from the Western financial system.
Due to the impact, the Russian government has stopped publishing a raft of economic data since April 2022.

== Currency, Inflation, and Banking ==

The currency of Russia is the Russian Ruble, and one Ruble is equal to 100 Kopeks.
A currency reform was carried out in 1998, during which 1,000 old rubles (RUR) were replaced by one new ruble (RUB).
The Russian ruble was essentially stable against the US dollar and the euro until 2008, and inflation in Russia was 8.2% in 2006.
The Russian Central Bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to prevent a rapid appreciation of the ruble, as such an appreciation would have worsened the price competitiveness of Russian producers.
The Central Bank bought foreign currencies flowing into Russia due to high current account surpluses, and the circulating amount of ruble currency increased significantly.
The rubel lost value during the international economic crisis and lost approximately 20% of its value in the second half of 2008.
The Russian ruble lost more than half its value since the annexation of Crimea.
The Russian ruble is used in everyday life, and prices were often indicated in accounting units until January 2007.
Each accounting unit corresponded to one US dollar.
The use of third-party currencies in Russia is not allowed, and this prohibition took effect in January 2007.
Payments were made in Rubles despite the prohibition on third-party currencies.

== Economic Structure and State Control ==

Putin disempowered the oligarchs to regain control and installed trusted individuals from the Siloviki ranks into key companies, which are primarily in the oil and gas extraction industries, and these leadership figures are sometimes called silovarchs.
The current economic system can be characterized as an oligarchically led 'state capitalism' in which an exclusive elite determines the main priorities in economic and foreign economic policy using extractive political and economic institutions.
This elite earns significant income through the sale of raw materials on world markets and does not desire or prevent market-oriented modernization that would lead to power gains for other actors.
The economy of Russia is strongly characterized by clientelism, where loyalty to the system is rewarded by the ability to extract excessive profits.
Margareta Mommsen estimates there are approximately 13 to 15 clans involved in a permanent struggle for power and property that ruled the country informally as a 'secret oligarchy'.
Vladimir Putin appears as a link between these clans and the visible state power institutions, is described as the 'patron of cliquistic structures', and his role involves balancing the interests of these groups.
Private companies in the energy sector were pushed out, the state expanded its influence outside the energy sector, and the government promoted the formation of state-owned large corporations.

Russia is experiencing an economic recession [cite: 2576], and its economy is still significantly smaller than that of G8 countries [cite: 2590].
The Russian government still intervenes significantly in the economy [cite: 2590], and the economic climate is dominated by oligarchs.
The credit crisis, declining oil revenues, and capital flight suppressed consumption and investment [cite: 2779].
The gross domestic product was 104,000 billion rubles, an amount less than three times the level of the Netherlands [cite: 2779].
Promoting the development of small and medium-sized enterprises is a major challenge for the future.

The banking system is not functioning adequately, as many banks are controlled by entrepreneurs and oligarchs who use bank funds to make loans to companies they are related to.
Making these processes fairer is one of the priorities of the World Trade Organization and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Vladimir Putin has intervened in the economy and has carried out nationalizations.
Since 2005, bidding for concessions to extract energy carriers and strategic metals has been restricted to only enterprises with at least 51% Russian capital participation.

== Metallurgical and heavy industry ==

Russia has massive iron ore production, and its output in 1993 was 42.67 million metric tons, ranking fourth in the world that year.
Large-scale steel industries developed in the Urals, Kursk, and Kuznetsk regions based on this production, with steel factories of various sizes located throughout these areas.
The non-ferrous metal industry is a sector in Russia, which holds significant confirmed reserves of copper, lead, zinc, nickel, beryllium, bauxite, and mercury.
Based on these reserves, Russia's non-ferrous metal industry is world-class.
Major non-ferrous metal industry regions include the Volga region, which produces copper and composite metals.
The Urals are also a major region, producing copper and aluminum.
Kuzbass and the North Caucasus are major regions that produce composite metals and aluminum.
East Siberia is a major region that produces gold and nickel.
The Far Eastern coastal areas are a major region that produces gold and composite metals.

== Chemical and machine manufacturing ==

Russia has abundant raw materials for the chemical industry, including oil, gas, coal, phosphate rock, potash, and sulfur.
The chemical industry sector in Russia is highly developed, having developed significantly in Siberia, while European Russia still holds an absolute advantage in the chemical industry.
Machine manufacturing industry is the core of heavy industry, with important regions including the western part of Russia, the northwestern part of Russia, and the Urals.
The western part of Russia and the northwestern part of Russia produce electrical machinery, precision machinery, vehicles, and ships, while the Urals produce medium-sized machinery.

Silk and wool textile industries exist in Siberia.

== Currency history and denominations ==

The ruble is the currency of Russia and has been in circulation since nearly the beginning of Russia's history.
The currency was introduced in the 13th century in the Republic of Novgorod as an equivalent to a silver fine.
The ruble appeared as a coin in 1654 and entered circulation permanently in 1704 as the result of Peter the Great's monetary reform.
The last monetary reform took place in 1998.
Banknotes with denominations of 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, and 5000 rubles are currently in circulation.
Coins with denominations of 1, 5, 10, and 50 kopecks are currently in circulation.
Coins with denominations of 1, 2, 5, and 10 rubles are currently in circulation.

The 2020s are characterized by the decline of the rural economy.

One of the strategies is to encourage initiatives based on local communities and to promote residential construction.

Real estate costs outside cities are predicted to increase.

== Economic sanctions ==

Russia has been subjected to economic sanctions multiple times since gaining independence.

Foreign investors withdrew approximately 70 billion USD from Russia in the first quarter of 2014, an amount that was more than the total amount withdrawn in all of 2013.
The largest economic sanctions imposed on Russia occurred from 2022 onwards.
These sanctions were implemented in nine packages between February and December 2022 and remain in effect during the year 2023.

== Economic growth drivers ==

Internal consumption and political stability have driven economic growth in Russia.
Russia ended 2008 with nine consecutive years of economic growth, during which the average annual economic growth rate was 7%.
Economic growth was driven primarily by non-tradable services and goods for the domestic market, while profits from oil were not the main driver of economic growth.

== GDP and Growth History ==

The Russian economy was the 12th largest by nominal GDP in 2015 and the 6th largest by purchasing power parity in 2015.
Russia's economic growth was stimulated since the beginning of the 21st century, and the country ended the year 2008 with nine consecutive years of economic growth.
The Russian economy entered stagnation by the end of 2013.

Russia's economy grew in 2021 at a rate of 4.6 percent.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 93.8% between 1999 and 2008, while industrial production grew by 79.1% and agricultural production grew by 39.7% during the same period.
In 1990, industrial production compared to 1989 was 99.9%, and between 1991 and 2004, industrial production decreased by an additional 30%.
In 2008, the country's GDP was 107% of its 1989 level, industrial production was 85% of its 1989 level, and agricultural production was 83.6% of its 1989 level.

== Drivers of Economic Growth ==

The Bank of Russia is the central bank of the country.

== Economic Structure and Growth Drivers ==

Some experts believe that Russia suffers from the 'Dutch disease'.

== Fiscal Policy and Public Finances ==

A simpler tax system came into effect in 2001, and this new tax system reduced the burden on citizens while increasing state revenue.
Russia uses a flat income tax rate of 13% for individuals, making it the second most attractive individual income tax system for executives after the United Arab Emirates.
According to a 2007 survey, the Russian state budget was in surplus since 2001, and by the end of 2007, the Russian state budget surplus was 6% of the GDP.
Oil export revenues allowed Russia's foreign reserves to increase from $12 billion in 1999 to $59.7 billion in 2008, and in 2008, Russia had the third highest foreign reserves in the world.
Russia used oil revenue from the Russian Federation Security Fund to repay Soviet-era debts to the Paris Club and the International Monetary Fund, and Russia significantly reduced its historical foreign debt.

== Income Distribution and Poverty ==

There is some growth in the number of affluent citizens, the highest social group remains relatively closed, the majority of citizens are wage earners with a middle income level, the social group with low and very low incomes makes up about 30% of the total population, representatives of middle social groups have opportunities for vertical social mobility, and the global trend involves an increase in the concentration of public income within the highest social group.
There were 23 million people in Russia with incomes below the subsistence minimum, representing approximately 15.4% of the total population of the country.
Annual surveys by the research holding 'Romir' were conducted to indicate the income required for a conditionally 'normal life' in Russia for an average Russian family of three people in which two members work.
Such a family needs a monthly income between 70,000 and 80,000 rubles, which equates to between 23,000 and 27,000 rubles per month per family member.
The data comes from Rosstat.

Russia ranked 40th in the comfort index for pensioners among 43 countries.

The production and distribution of electricity, gas, and water accounted for 3.1% of the added value structure and 2.7% of GDP.
Net taxes on products accounted for 14.2% of GDP.

== Regional Economic Divisions ==

Russia is divided into eleven major economic regions.
The North-West region, the Northern region, the Central region, the Volga-Vyatka region, the Central Black Earth region, the Volga region, the North Caucasus region, the Ural region, the West Siberian region, the East Siberian region, and the Far Eastern region are the major economic regions of Russia.

== Regional Industrial Specialization ==

Hydroelectric power stations, non-ferrous metallurgy, and the forestry industry are located in Eastern Siberia.
Oil and gas extraction takes place in Western Siberia and Eastern Siberia.
The Far East is distinguished by gold mining, diamond mining, fishing, and the production of seafood.
Mining, coal mining, oil extraction, natural gas extraction, apatite mining, nickel mining, mining of other metals, and logging are main industries in the Northern region.
The Northwestern region, the Central region, and the Volga-Vyatka region are characterized by developed machinery manufacturing.

The Ural and Volga regions are characterized by developed machinery manufacturing, a developed chemical industry, a developed light industry, a developed food industry, and a developed service sector.

== Key Industries and Manufacturing ==

Mining, oil production, oil refining, gas production, metallurgy (both black and non-ferrous), aircraft manufacturing, shipbuilding, machine building, energy equipment manufacturing, food processing, and textile manufacturing are major industries.
Heavy industry plays a leading role in the industrial sector.
There are three black metallurgy bases: the Urals, the Central region, and Siberia.

== Natural Resources and Mineral Wealth ==

Russia extracts all types of mineral fuels.
Large coal deposits exist in the Komi Republic, Eastern Siberia, and the Russian Far East.
Russia is rich in iron ore, bauxite, nickel, tin, gold, diamonds, platinum, lead, and zinc.

== Currency ==

The Russian ruble is the official currency of the Russian Federation and is divided into 100 kopecks.
The ISO 4217 code for the Russian ruble is RUB, while RUR was the code before the 1998 redenomination.
The numerical code for the Russian ruble is 643.

== Economic Overview and Rankings ==

In 2020, the Russian Federation's economy ranked 11th in the world by nominal GDP and 6th globally by purchasing power parity (PPP) [cite: 4390].
The IMF reported Russia's nominal GDP at 1.467 trillion USD [cite: 4390].
The United States, China, Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, and Canada ranked higher than Russia by nominal GDP [cite: 4390].
Russia's economy ranked 13th in the world in 2016 by nominal GDP and 5th in Europe by nominal GDP [cite: 4417].
Russia's economy ranked 6th in the world in 2016 by purchasing power parity (PPP) GDP and 2nd in Europe by purchasing power parity (PPP) GDP [cite: 4417].
Russia's PPP GDP was approximately $3.3 trillion in 2016, and Russia's GDP in 2016 was $3.3 trillion [cite: 4417].
In 2016, Russia was the 6th largest economy in the world and the 2nd largest economy in Europe [cite: 4417].
Russia's GDP in 2021 was $4.02 trillion.
Russia was the 6th largest economy in the world in 2021 and the 2nd largest economy in Europe in 2021.

== Industrial Sectors and Production ==

Many of these resources are located in Siberia.
Russia inherited most of the Soviet manufacturing facilities.
The production of electrical, electronic, and optical equipment, chemical production, processing industries, extraction of fuel and energy-bearing minerals, cellulose and paper production, publishing and printing activities, metallurgical production and the manufacture of finished metal products, and the production and distribution of electricity, gas, and water are among the strongest sectors.
Russia relies primarily on the export of goods.
The main exported goods are oil, gas, metals, and wood.
These goods account for more than 80% of Russia's export volume.

== Trade Balance and External Commerce ==

Exports amounted to $301.7 billion and the import value was $167.4 billion.
External trade significantly decreased following the attack and sanctions, with the decrease primarily occurring with Ukraine.
The volume of international trade in 2016 was $424.4 billion.
The US trade balance was positive and amounted to 94.2 billion dollars, with an export volume of 259.3 billion dollars and an import volume of 165.1 billion dollars.
Russia is vulnerable to international market price fluctuations.

== Income, Inequality, and Living Standards ==

The average per capita income in Russia was 18,721 Russian rubles in April 2010, while the average monthly gross salary was 21,597 rubles in June 2010.
The subsistence minimum was 5,144 rubles per month in the fourth quarter of 2009, and the share of the population with incomes below the subsistence minimum was 13.1% as of 2009.
This is due to significant inequality in income distribution, and the average income of the Russian population does not determine the standard of living for the majority of Russians.
As of the mid-2010s, 1% of Russia's wealthiest citizens owned 43% of all household assets, a level of asset concentration that is one of the highest among industrialized countries worldwide, while income inequality in Russia was increasing rapidly during this period.
Russia's estimated per capita income in 2020 was $9,972 based on nominal values and $27,394 based on purchasing power parity.
Russia ranked 61st in the world for per capita income based on nominal values in 2020 and 50th in the world for per capita income based on purchasing power parity in 2020.

== Economic History and Growth Trends ==

Russia inherited control of the Soviet Union's foreign assets and has a mixed economy.
In recent years, the Russian economy has focused more on domestic consumer goods demand, and the domestic consumer goods sector grew by over 12% per year between 2000 and 2004.
Higher domestic consumption in subsequent years boosted economic growth in Russia, and greater political stability in subsequent years boosted economic growth in Russia.
The Russian economy experienced strong growth continuously from 1999 to 2008.

== Banking System and Structural Challenges ==

The biggest challenge for Russia is promoting the development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
The Russian banking system is controlled by Russian oligarchs who typically use bank deposits to lend money to their own businesses.
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and the World Bank (WB) made efforts to normalize banking activities.

== Economic Overview and Growth Trends ==

Russia's average annual economic growth rate was 5% during the period 2000-2009 and dropped to 1.8% during the period 2010-2019.
Russia experienced a recession in 2015 and in 2016.
After 2015, Russia's average annual economic growth rate decreased to 0.4%.
The main reason for Russia's economic inefficiency during 2010-2019 was the exhaustion of previous growth drivers, and during this period the Russian government chose to increase reserve funds instead of improving economic efficiency.
Russia has been experiencing a financial crisis since 2014.
As of 2015, Russia was the 13th largest economy in the world by GDP and the 6th largest economy in the world by purchasing power parity.
Russia has a relatively low economic level.

== Industrial Structure and Competitiveness ==

Russia inherited a very strong industrial foundation from the Soviet Union, with approximately 60% of the Soviet Union's industrial facilities located on Russian territory, though the industrial base of Russia is aging.
Russia's light industrial goods have relatively weak competitiveness in the global market, while Russia's weapons industry is the most modern sector and is oriented towards exports.
Russia currently inherited three basic industrial groups from the Soviet regime [cite: 4428], which have extremely high competitiveness [cite: 4428]: the industrial-defense complexes [cite: 4428], the space technology industry [cite: 4428], and machine manufacturing and nuclear technology equipment [cite: 4428].
Defense-industrial complexes and the aerospace industry experienced a decline [cite: 4428] that lasted for approximately 20 years [cite: 4428].
It became very difficult to see Russian civilian industrial brands after the dissolution of the Soviet Union [cite: 4434], and even light industrial brands were not visible [cite: 4434].
The most common areas where Russian goods can be found are vodka and military products [cite: 4434].
Russia is a leading global exporter of heavy industrial goods [cite: 4456], but Russian consumer products lack competitiveness in the international market [cite: 4456] due to monotonous product designs [cite: 4456].

== Import Dependence and Supply Chains ==

Russia imports up to 90% of its industrial machine tools, approximately 60–80% of its heavy machinery engineering, and 80–90% of its electronics industry.
Russia aims to reduce its dependence on Western suppliers in most key industries and plans to reduce import indices from 70–90% to 50–60% by the year 2020.
China began selling products to Russia, including diesel engines.
The rate of imports grew rapidly, and revenue continued to increase by 2017.
Russia will purchase more technological equipment from China in the future.
Russia did not like the idea of buying products from China and preferred to buy Western products.
Immediately after the sanctions, Russia had to turn to China for purchases.

== Economic Transformation and Policy Goals ==

The transformation aims to shift from being simply a raw material exporter and to become a more diverse nation based on high-tech products and services.
The Putin administration has not yet demonstrated effectiveness in this transformation.
Directing consumers and promoting spending on consumer goods is quite difficult, and consumer demand in these rural areas is very simple.
Significant commendable progress has been made in large cities, especially in sectors such as clothing, food, and the entertainment industry.

== Corporate Expansion and Market Outlook ==

A 2013 survey conducted by the Macro Research Center (CMR), which belongs to Sberbank of Russia, found that 36% of surveyed enterprises have no plans to expand production within the next 5 years, 38% plan to possibly expand in the domestic market, 19% target nearby markets specifically member countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and only 9% have long-term plans to expand business into the global market.
The upgrades are needed within the next 3 years.
Sergei Tsyb is the Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade of Russia.

== Social Conditions and Living Standards ==

The wealth gap is increasing and inflation rates in Russia remained high.
Many Russians live in houses built during the Soviet era that are now deteriorating.
A survey conducted by the Russian Engineers Association found that 12% of people in cities do not have a heating system and must use manual stoves.
Data provided by the World Bank indicates that more than 15 million Russians currently live below an income level of less than 150 USD per person per month, representing approximately 11% of the population.

Poverty reached over 40% of the population by 1999 and decreased noticeably after 1999.
In 2002, the poverty rate was 19.6%, and by 2011, the poverty rate decreased to 12.8%.
The number of people living in poverty in 2011 was 18 million Russians.
The official subsistence minimum was 170 euros for a person of working age, while the minimum subsistence value for children is slightly lower than the standard and the minimum subsistence value for pensioners is 125 Euros.

More than half of the people lived in poverty in Chechnya and in Dagestan.
Ingushetia, Tuva, Kabardino-Balkaria, Mari El, Kalmykia, Buryatia, and Altai are poor regions.

Mordovia is a poor region.

Russia was widely described as an energy superpower.
It has the world's largest proven gas reserves, the second-largest coal reserves, the eighth-largest oil reserves, and the largest oil shale reserves in Europe.
Russia is also the world's leading natural gas exporter, the second-largest natural gas producer, and the second-largest oil producer and exporter.
Russia's oil and gas production led to deep economic relationships with the European Union, China, and former Soviet and Eastern Bloc states.
For example, over the last decade, Russia's share of supplies to total European Union (including the United Kingdom) gas demand increased from 25% in 2009 to 32% in the weeks before the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In the mid-2000s, the share of the oil and gas sector in GDP was around 20%, and in 2013 it was 20–21% of GDP.
The share of oil and gas in Russia's exports (about 50%) and federal budget revenues (about 50%) is large, and the dynamics of Russia's GDP are highly dependent on oil and gas prices, but the share in GDP is much less than 50%.
According to the first such comprehensive assessment published by the Russian statistics agency Rosstat in 2021, the maximum total share of the oil and gas sector in Russia's GDP, including extraction, refining, transport, sale of oil and gas, all goods and services used, and all supporting activities, amounts to 19.2% in 2019 and 15.2% in 2020.
This is comparable to the share of GDP in Norway and Kazakhstan.
It is much lower than the share of GDP in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Russia ratified the Paris Agreement in 2019.
Greenhouse gas emissions by Russia are the world's fourth-largest.
Russia is the world's fourth-largest electricity producer.
It was also the world's first country to develop civilian nuclear power, and to construct the world's first nuclear power plant.
Russia was also the world's fourth-largest nuclear energy producer in 2019, and was the fifth-largest hydroelectric producer in 2021.

== Railway infrastructure and history ==

Russia's railway transport network formed mainly during the late 19th century and until the early 20th century.
The construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway was completed in the early 20th century, connected Russia's European part to the Pacific coast, and included Chelyabinsk, Irkutsk, and Vladivostok on its route.
Many railways were built in the northern and eastern regions of European Russia after 1917.
The construction of the Baikal-Amur Mainline (BAM) has been completed in recent years, and its length is more than 3,000 km.
Railways in Russia use a broad gauge track that reaches up to 1,520 mm (4 feet 11 and 5/6 inches) [552,553].
957 kilometers of railway lines are located on Sakhalin Island, where the lines use a narrow gauge track approximately 1,067 mm (3 feet 6 inches) wide [552,553].
Russia ranks second in the world for the length of diesel-operated railway lines, while the United States ranks first.
This network is the largest in the world [550,551].

By 2006, the total length of roads in Russia was 933,000 kilometers, of which 755,000 kilometers were paved [554,555].

The road density in Russia is the lowest among G8 countries [556,557].

Railways are used as a mass transport method, cover long distances in Russia, and hold an important share of the transportation market in Russia.

The Baikal-Amur Mainline runs from Lake Baikal to the Amur River, was built in the late 20th century, and was constructed to develop the Far East of Siberia.
The country is developed in a west-east direction through the two main lines and their branching routes.
The transportation of goods between Pusan and Helsinki can be reduced by these routes, and transport via the railway routes takes about 16 days.
The railway on Sakhalin has a gauge of 1,067 mm.

Rivers flowing into the Arctic Ocean lose their importance in transportation.
All rivers in Siberia freeze for a period between 7 and 9 months per year.
Most rivers freeze for most months of the year.

Large cascades of hydroelectric power plants are located in the European part of Russia on large rivers such as the Volga, while the potential for hydropower in Eastern Siberia remains mostly untapped.

== Energy policy and state control ==

The Russian government has plans to increase energy efficiency and planned to double the share of nuclear energy in electricity generation to approximately one-third by 2020, while also aiming to export more oil and natural gas.
Russian policy was aimed at increasing state control over the energy sector to benefit from revenues in the energy sector and to push private companies out of the energy sector.
The goal of increasing state control over the energy sector was achieved through the breakup of the oil company Yukos and Gazprom taking over the oil company Sibneft.
Gazprom is a semi-state natural gas company, and Surgutneftegas is one of the largest gas and oil production corporations in which Vladimir Putin controls 37% of the shares.
All Russian nuclear power plants are owned by the state-owned company Rosatom.

== Gas pipeline projects ==

South Stream was planned to run under the Black Sea and pass through Bulgaria, but it was not built due to disagreement by the European Commission.
Representatives of the Austrian company OMV and the Russian company Gazprom signed a Memorandum of Understanding on June 18, 2015, which was a preliminary agreement stating that Austrians would participate in the construction of two additional pipelines under the Baltic Sea that are part of the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline project.
On the same day, at the edge of an economic conference in St.
Petersburg, it was announced that German company EON joined the group of companies participating in the construction, and Royal Dutch Shell, a Dutch-British company, also joined the group of companies participating in the construction.
The first pipeline was scheduled to be put into operation by 2019, which would make a total of four pipelines.
The total cost of the project will reach at least 9.5 billion euros, while the costs of the first phase of the project were 7.4 billion euros, and the total cost of the project is likely to exceed the costs of its first phase.
Two new pipelines are planned to transport an additional 55 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually to the European Union.
Russia intended to stop transporting gas to Western Europe via Ukraine starting in 2020, as the gas was originally transported from Russia to Western Europe through Ukraine.
The estimated completion date was the beginning of 2021.

Presidents Putin and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan put the Turkstream gas pipeline into operation on January 8, 2020, at an inauguration ceremony held in Istanbul.
Turkstream is a new gas pipeline and the successor to the cancelled South Stream project.
Natural gas flows from Russia to Turkey through Turkstream under the Black Sea.
Bulgaria was originally intended to be connected to the pipeline, but the pipeline now continues through Greece, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Hungary before ending in Austria.
Germany did not allow the Nord Stream 2 pipeline to operate due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
