== Energy infrastructure and policy ==

All Russian nuclear power plants are operated by the state-owned company Rosenergoatom.
The Unified Energy System, which was owned more than 50% by the Russian state and had the largest share of electricity production until 2008, has since been split into smaller companies.
The gas supply program for Russian regions has been running since 2005 with a plan intended to be completed in ten years by the target year 2015 to supply gas to every village.
The program was extended until the year 2030, changing the goal from supplying all settlements to supplying 85% of the country's settlements.
In 2022, schools and hospitals in Russia were heated with firewood, which was reportedly more expensive in Russia than in Germany according to Novaya Gazeta.

== Transport strategy and investment ==

Traffic volume in Russia decreased after the political transition, primarily due to economic decline, but subsequently experienced strong growth.
The current infrastructure largely dates back to the Soviet era and requires modernization, while existing transport systems generate few network effects.
The Russian government considers the expansion and modernization of transport infrastructure a high priority and adopted a strategy in 2005.
This strategy aimed at renewing transport routes and focused on continued modernization and improvements in rail, road, and air transport, as well as the renovation of the country's ports.
Concessions and other public-private partnership models are to be promoted in the transport sector with the goal of mobilizing financing from private investors.

== Geographic challenges and logistics ==

Russia aims to establish itself as a key transit hub in Asia-Europe transport and also aims to be part of the North-South axis from Northern Europe towards India.
Logistics infrastructure is to be expanded, with the expansion focusing primarily on key hubs in Moscow and St.
Petersburg.
Russia's transportation infrastructure west of the Urals is generally well-developed, while the road and railway infrastructure in Trans-Ural and Siberia is technically at best outdated and not competitive.
The largest transportation obstacle to the economic connection of Siberia's vast territories with booming South and Southeast Asian states is the lack of north-south transport routes.
Russia ranked 75th in the Logistics Performance Index in 2018, which is created by the World Bank, measures infrastructure quality, and included 160 countries.
Transport costs account for up to 20% of production costs, and poor road conditions are the reason for high transport costs.
Poor infrastructure costs the country up to 9% of its economic output.
Transport experts estimate that at least 32 billion euros would need to be invested annually for road expansion.

== Road network characteristics ==

A trend towards road transport has been clearly visible in Russia since 2000.
The road density is 40 meters of road per square kilometer.
The road network in Russia varies significantly in quality, and the expansion of the road network cannot keep pace with the increasingly heavy road traffic.
The density of the road network decreases from west to east, and road conditions worsen as one moves eastward from Moscow.
The Russian highway and long-distance road network covers approximately 540,000 km, a figure referring to the year 2001.
Two-thirds of the network is paved.
A continuous road connection from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean existed starting in 2003, and this road connection was seasonally continuous.
Long-distance roads outside urban areas are generally not developed as motorways or expressways, and even on wider long-distance roads, the carriageways in each direction are not separated by guardrails.
The most important highway in Russia is European Route 30, which ends in Siberia.

== Road freight and international transit ==

Most freight traffic between Western Europe and Russia is handled by road, including transit through Poland and Belarus, a northern route via Poland and the Baltic Republics, and a route via Finland.
The difference in railway track gauges contributes to the situation.
Trucks in Russia only started to catch up with other modes of transport since 2000.

== Road safety and vehicle fleet ==

Traffic accidents are relatively frequent in Russia, and many of these accidents result in fatalities.
In 2013, there were 18.9 traffic fatalities per 100,000 people in Russia, and 27,000 people died in road traffic.
The motorization rate of the country is in the upper middle range globally, with 324 motor vehicles per 1,000 inhabitants in 2017.
Russia has approximately 46.9 million vehicles and possesses the fifth-largest vehicle fleet of all countries.
There were 60 car brands previously available in Russia, but only 14 car brands are officially distributed in Russia as of early 2024.
The three Russian car brands are Lada, GAZ, and UAZ.

== Urban public transport ==

The bus network exists in 120 cities, and almost half of passenger transport takes place in local transit, which is primarily conducted via the bus network.
90 Russian cities have a trolleybus network, 66 cities have trams and suburban trains, 7 cities have a metro system, and 4 cities have S-Bahn lines.
Many good public transport networks declined in the 1990s and were increasingly supplemented or replaced by private bus companies and private taxi line operators.
In recent times, tram or trolleybus systems were discontinued in several major cities and replaced by buses, including the trolleybus system in Archangelsk in 2008 and the tram system in Voronezh in 2009.
Buses are the most common type of vehicle in these systems.
Seven Russian cities have metro systems, including Moscow, Saint Petersburg, Nizhny Novgorod, and Novosibirsk.

== Railway reform and market structure ==

The Russian government decided to implement the railway reform in May 2001 with the main goals of liberalizing the railway market and releasing tariffs in railway transport.
The railway reform took place in October 2003, when the former Railway Ministry (MPS) was dissolved and Rossijskije schelesnyje dorogi (RZhD) was founded.
RZhD is Russia's second-largest state-owned enterprise.
In recent years, 85 private railway companies have emerged in Russia, and these companies transport more than 25% of goods today.
These private railway companies own approximately 30% of the total freight wagon stock in Russia, a stock that amounts to about 200,000 freight wagons.

== Inland waterways ==

Russia has a considerable number of ports, and the Kama, Nizhny Novgorod Oka, Vyatka, and Don are important waterways that are connected to each other by canals.
There are 24,000 kilometers of navigable waterways in Siberia, but there is no east-west waterway development due to this drainage pattern.
The polar route is only possible for a few months in the summer due to ice formation, though climate change is extending this period of navigability.
The navigability of rivers and canals is significantly impaired, and poor infrastructure development affects the navigability of rivers and canals.
A decline in the inland ship fleet has been observed in Russia since 1990, and of these vessels, 8,000 were cargo ships and 800 were passenger ships.
Archangelsk, Perm, Jaroslavl, and Saratov are among the most important Russian inland ports.

Russia has 102,000 km of waterways that consist mostly of natural rivers and lakes.
The country has a network of canals that connects the basins of major rivers in the European part of the country.
Moscow has waterway connections to the Baltic Sea, the White Sea, the Caspian Sea, the Azov Sea, and the Black Sea, and is sometimes referred to as the 'port of five seas'.
Cheboksary is one of the most important Russian inland ports.
River transport carries a portion of the cargo.

== Maritime transport ==

Maritime shipping is one of the rapidly growing transportation sectors in Russia, and the increase in exports of crude oil and petroleum products is a major reason for the growth.
The most important seaports are located in St.
Petersburg and Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea, include Noworossijsk and Sotschi on the Black Sea, and include Vladivostok, Nakhodka, Magadan, and Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky on the Pacific Ocean.
Murmansk is a port on the North Atlantic and is kept ice-free year-round.
The cargo turnover in Russian ports was 285.7 million tons.
Ferry transport is significant for freight traffic between the Russian core territory and the exclave of Kaliningrad.
The country possessed 1,448 commercial vessels.
The Russian fleet is the only one in the world promoting economic exploitation of the Arctic Ocean and develops sea trade between Europe and East Asia.
In 2010, sea transport accounted for 2.1% of the freight turnover.

== Aviation infrastructure and history ==

Aviation has been of great importance in Russia and the Soviet Union, an importance that arose early on due to the size of the country.
National air transport connects remote regions where developing by land was never worthwhile.
Aeroflot was a state-owned airline that was the largest airline in the world during the Soviet era, and its fares were sometimes cheaper than train fares.
The number of airports in Russia decreased from 1302 in 1992 to 496 in 2011, while 55 airfields had a paved runway longer than 3000 meters.
The number of international airports in Russia increased from 19 in 1992 to 70 in 2011.
Multiple international airlines fly to Russian cities and operate flights to destinations other than Moscow.
Sheremetyevo-2 and Domodedovo are located near Moscow and are among the largest airports in Russia.

Sheremetyevo-2 and Domodedovo are the most important airports in Russia.
Russia's aircraft fleet included approximately 6,000 aircraft in 2011, of which approximately 2,000 were cargo planes.
Only the United States, Brazil, Canada, and Mexico have more airports than Russia.

== Aviation policy and operations ==

State subsidies and regulations support the Russian aviation industry.
Flight tickets to the far east of Russia are subsidized.
Aeroflot is a semi-state airline, while Rossija, S7 Airlines, and UTair are major airlines connected to the state.
In autumn 2018, the government issued an order directed to the banks Sberbank and VTB, tasking them with founding a large regional airline to upgrade regional airports and relieve pressure on Moscow as a hub.
In January 2020, President Putin issued an instruction to the government to form a company for developing remote eastern regions with a fleet consisting entirely of Russian aircraft.
A new company was subsequently established based on Red Wings.

Russian authorities granted permission to 21 airlines to operate foreign aircraft without valid airworthiness certificates, a situation that led to a flight ban over the European Union.
Russia closed its airspace and eleven airports along the war zone, including Anapa, Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Gelendzhik, Krasnodar, Kursk, Lipetsk, Rostov-on-Don, Simferopol, and Elista.
The closure of airspace and airports was initially for seven days, and the measures were extended multiple times after the initial period.
China denied the use of its airspace to double-registered aircraft.
Russian airlines transported 105 million passengers in 2023, four-fifths of whom were domestic travelers.
Flights to 40 countries were planned for 2024, compared to 32 countries that had flights in 2022.

== Energy consumption and production ==

Russia is the ninth largest producer of renewable energy in the world.
Sixty percent of the power capacity in the electricity and gas industry is currently in use, and 80% of the oil processing capacity is currently in use.
Russia's total energy consumption in 2018 was 800 Mtoe.
Russia is among the ten countries with the highest energy consumption, ranking fourth in 2018 behind China, the United States, and India.
Russia's energy consumption relative to its GDP is higher than that of any other top energy-consuming country, a high ratio caused by outdated production and transmission capacity.

== Electricity sector ==

Electricity production, transmission, and distribution were under the control of a state-owned monopoly company called RAO UES Rossii until the beginning of the 2000s.
The company ceased its operations in 2008.
After 2008, the Russian electricity sector began to open up to competition.
Hydroelectric and nuclear power companies remained state-owned.
The privatization of electricity generation is part of an ongoing plan.
Russia's wholesale electricity markets were liberalized.

== Nuclear and renewable energy ==

Russia has invested in nuclear power for over 50 years, and the energy company Rosenergoatom operates Russia's nuclear power plants.
In 2018, there were 38 nuclear reactors in the country, eight of which were commissioned in the 2000s.
All nuclear power in Russia is managed by Rosatom State Corporation, the nuclear sector is growing very rapidly, and the government plans to increase the share of nuclear energy in the market from the current 16.9% to 23% by 2020.[1963,1964] The amount allocated was 127 billion Rubles for a federal program aimed at developing the latest nuclear technology.[1963,1964] Renewable energy has great potential, yet very little renewable energy is currently used.
The share of wind and solar energy in the country's energy budget is not expected to exceed one percent, a projection that extends at least until the year 2040.
Russia is the fifth-largest renewable energy producer in the world and develops a large number of hydroelectric power plants.[1959,1960,1961,1962]

== Energy production and exports ==

Russia possesses specialized expertise in the field of energy.
Russia was the third-largest energy exporter in the world in 2021 and the third-largest energy consumer in the world in 2021.
In 2021, 42% of Russia's energy production came from natural gas, 39% came from oil, and 14% came from coal.
Russia has several of the world's most powerful hydroelectric power plants and several of the world's most powerful nuclear power plants.
Nuclear and renewable energies were minor compared to natural gas, oil, and coal.
Russia was the world's largest producer of oil in 2012, the world's largest producer of natural gas in 2012, the world's largest producer of nuclear electricity in 2011, and the world's largest producer of hydroelectricity.
Russia was the world's largest oil producer in 2011, the world's largest natural gas producer in 2012, and the world's largest coal producer in 2012.
45.6% of this production is exported.
48% of the oil production is exported, 30% of the natural gas production is exported, and 45% of the coal production is exported.

== Energy consumption and emissions ==

Russia has a very high energy consumption.
In 2011, Russia's per capita energy consumption was higher than France's (3.88), and its per capita greenhouse gas emissions were higher than France's (5.04 tCO2/hab).
The per capita greenhouse gas emissions in the United States were 16.94 tCO2, while China's per capita greenhouse gas emissions were 5.92 tCO2/hab.

== Railway networks and lines ==

The Baikal-Amur Railway is 3,500 kilometers long.
The Russian Railway Company (RJD) connects all major cities in Russia.
The Allegro is a fast train that connects Helsinki to Saint Petersburg and has been operating since 2010.
The regional railway network is called 'Elektritschka'.
Turksib, known as the Turkestan-Siberia Railway, connects Tashkent to Novosibirsk and links the Trans-Caspian Railway and the Trans-Siberian Railway.
The railway line starts in Tashkent, separates from the Trans-Caspian Railway in Tashkent, heads northeast, reaches Almaty, passes through the city of Shymkent, passes through the city of Taraz, passes through the city of Bishkek, crosses the Russian border, passes through Barnaul, arrives in Novosibirsk, and connects with the Trans-Siberian Railway in Novosibirsk.

The Trans-Siberian Railway provides east-west connections between major Siberian basins, including the agricultural basin of Omsk on the Irtych River and the coal basin of Kuzbass on the Tom River.
The main railway axis crosses the Ob at Novosibirsk and the Irtych at Omsk.
The Turksib railway connects Central Asia to Siberia, terminates in Novosibirsk, and crosses the upper Ob at Barnaul.

== Inland waterways and canals ==

The Volga-Baltic waterway is a system of rivers, lakes, and canals located in northwestern Russia that connects the Volga River to the Baltic Sea.
The system was built in the early 20th century and reconstructed in the 1960s to accommodate larger tonnage boats.
Commercial exchanges are now conducted by sea, and the river has been abandoned for commercial use.
The Northern Dvina is a navigable waterway that is navigable from end to end and freezes from December to April.
The river is used intensively for timber transport and serves as an important communication route.
The Northern Dvina Canal connects the Northern Dvina River to the Volga River.
Another canal connects the Northern Dvina River to the Black Sea.
Another canal allows boats traveling on the Northern Dvina to reach the Gulf of Finland via a route that passes through Lake Ladoga and Lake Onega.
The White Sea is connected to the North Sea via the Dvina River.
The White Sea is connected to the Mediterranean Sea via the Dvina River.

The Northern Dvina is located in northern Russia.
The Don-Volga Canal is part of the Unified Deep Water System, which is located in European Russia.
The Volga River, the Don River, and the Lenin Canal form a route together that is the most direct path connecting the Caspian Sea to the Sea of Azov, which connects to the Black Sea, which connects to the oceans.
The Ob is a major communication route for Western Siberia but is navigable only about once a year on average in its upper course.
The canals utilized the Ket River, but the canal system has since been abandoned due to the canals being uncompetitive compared to railway transport.
River transport in Russia is not very effective.
The Lena River serves as a major transportation route, and the Yenisei River serves as a major transportation route.
The Volga-Don Canal connects the Volga River and the Don River, is 101 kilometers long, and was completed in 1952.
Moscow was connected to the Black Sea via waterways, and the completion of the canal connected cities in the Volga River basin to the Black Sea via waterways.

The total length of Russia's inland waterways is 102,000 km, and most of these are natural rivers or lakes.
72,000 km of these waterways run through the European part of Russia, where a network of canals connects with the basins of major rivers.
These waterways provide connections to the Sea of Azov, the Baltic Sea, the White Sea, and the Black Sea.
Industrial cities in the Volga River basin and Saint Petersburg were connected to the Black Sea via waterways.
Moscow is sometimes called "the port of five seas" because the waterway connects to the Baltic Sea, the White Sea, the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov.

Russia has a network of canals in its European territory that connect the basins of major rivers.
The Volga River is Russia's most important inland waterway.
The Moscow Canal and the Volga-Don Canal were constructed.
These canals allow access to the White Sea, Baltic Sea, Azov Sea, Black Sea, and Caspian Sea.

== Northern Sea Route and Arctic navigation ==

The Northern Sea Route passes through the Arctic and is the shortest path from Europe to Asia.
This route has been known since 1648, when a Cossack navigator named Simon Dejnev identified it.
The waterway is only navigable in the summer, but navigation channels are opened on this strategic route by powerful Russian nuclear icebreakers to maximize the navigation period.
Sea transport uses icebreakers, and goods subsequently transit via the Northern Sea Route.

River transport acts in complementarity with the Trans-Siberian Railway.

Air transport is the most expensive means of transportation, and passenger transport plays a significant role in air transport.

The passenger turnover of public transport in 2010 was 484 billion passenger-kilometers [3558,3559], with air transport accounting for 30% of the passenger turnover [3558,3559].
The share of air transport in passenger turnover has increased [3558,3559], and air transport passenger turnover grew almost three times compared to the year 2000 [3558,3559].

Moscow is a major hub for connecting flights and has the largest airports, while Saint Petersburg has the largest airports.

Domodedovo is one of the largest airports in Moscow, Sheremetyevo is one of the largest airports in Moscow, and Vnukovo is one of the largest airports in Moscow.

One of the platforms is Moscow-Cheremetyevo Airport, which serves Aeroflot.

Transaero's operating license was revoked in October 2015.
The Il-96-400M is a large wide-body passenger aircraft [2346,2347,2348,2349].

The vast territory of the Russian Federation causes difficulties in travel across the country, and most travel across the country is conducted by train.
Great distances have significantly influenced the development of transport infrastructure in Russia, and harsh climatic conditions have significantly influenced the development of transport infrastructure in Russia.
Railways play a dominant role in cargo transport and in passenger transport.
The railway network has 87,000 km of tracks in public use and 63,000 km of industrial tracks.
The share of railways in total freight transport is 83.2%, and the share of railways in total passenger transport is 40.9%.
Russian Railways holds approximately 3.6% of Russia's GDP, accounts for 39% of total freight traffic, and accounts for more than 42% of passenger traffic.
Russia uses wide-gauge tracks, with an exception to the wide-gauge rule on Sakhalin Island.
Rossijskie železnye dorogi manage the system as a monopoly, produces more than 3.6% of the country's GDP, manages 39% of total freight traffic, and manages more than 42% of passenger traffic.
Freight traffic includes gas pipelines.

All-weather ground transport is of primary importance for Russia.
Russia has over 124,000 km of railways [cite: 3555].
Russia has the longest electrified railway network of any single country in the world [cite: 550,2141].
This is the largest number of electrified lines in the world [cite: 550,2141].

The Moscow-Vladivostok railway route exists [cite: 1966,1967].
The Moscow-Pyongyang railway route exists [cite: 1966,1967].
The Kiev-Vladivostok railway route exists [cite: 1966,1967].

The company represents more than 3.6% of Russia's GDP [cite: 549].

The company manages more than 42% of passenger traffic [cite: 549].
In 2010, rail transport accounted for 42% of the freight turnover [cite: 3556,3557].
Rail transport accounted for 29% of the passenger turnover [cite: 3558,3559].

Railway transport in Russia is largely a monopoly held by Russian Railways.
Railway company accounts constitute 3.6% of Russia's GDP, 39% of total freight traffic including pipelines, and more than 42% of passenger traffic.
The total length of shared railway tracks exceeds 85,500 km, with more than 44,000 km of railway lines electrified, which is the largest number in the world.

== The Trans-Siberian Railway ==

Russia contains the longest railway line in the world, the Trans-Siberian Railway, which is 9,289 km long and connects Moscow and Vladivostok, where Vladivostok is located on the Pacific Ocean.
The Trans-Siberian Railway spans seven time zones [1966,1967] and holds the record for the most time zones crossed, crossing 7 time zones.
It serves the world's longest single train service [1966,1967], provides the world's longest continuous service [1966,1967], and holds the record for the longest permanently served line in the world.
The Moscow-Vladivostok route is served by the Trans-Siberian Railway [1966,1967], is part of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and the railway operates between Moscow and Vladivostok (9,259 km) [1966,1967].
The Moscow-Pyongyang route is served by the Trans-Siberian Railway [1966,1967], is part of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and the railway operates between Moscow and Pyongyang (10,267 km) [1966,1967].
The Kiev-Vladivostok route is served by the Trans-Siberian Railway [1966,1967], is part of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and the railway operates between Kiev and Vladivostok (11,085 km) [1966,1967].

== Railway services and operations ==

The Rossiya train travels the entire length of the Trans-Siberian Railway in 7 days and its route ends at Yaroslavsky Station.
The Ocean train is operated by Russian Railways and its route ends at Khabarovsk Station.
Rail accounts for 40% of freight transport and 50% of passenger transport in Russia.

== Maritime and river transport ==

Sea transport holds the second place in terms of cargo transportation and accounts for the largest share of international cargo turnover.
The sea-river transport network covers 115,000 kilometers, though sea transport has a short navigation period and ports freeze during winter.
Russia has more than 500 navigable rivers, and the Volga-Kama river basin accounts for 40% of waterway cargo turnover.
Kaliningrad, Saint Petersburg, and Vladivostok are Russian ports.
Baltiysk is a Russian port located on the Baltic Sea, Arkhangelsk is a Russian port located on the White Sea, and Port Vostochny is a Russian port located on the Sea of Japan.
Murmansk, Makhachkala, and Novorossiysk are ice-free ports in Russia.
Vladivostok is a port in Russia, and Russia has major seaports in cities such as Vladivostok on the Sea of Japan.
The country utilizes the Northern Sea Route.
The Pacific coastline allows for maritime connections with all countries in the Asia-Pacific region.

Astrakhan and Makhaqal are major Russian seaports located on the Caspian Sea.
Kaliningrad and Svetlogorsk are major Russian seaports located on the Baltic Sea.
Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky and Vladivostok are major Russian seaports located on the Pacific Ocean.
Russia is the only country in the world that possesses nuclear-powered icebreakers.
These icebreakers have helped promote Russia's transport and economic sectors along the Northern Sea Route.
The total length of inland waterways (lakes and rivers) in Russia is 102,000 km.

== Transport challenges and characteristics ==

Land transport is primarily used due to the country's harsh climatic conditions.
The state of the modern transport network has deteriorated and has not been updated for a considerable time.
All types of transport in Russia are almost well developed, yet the distribution frequency of transport modes, the share of freight transport, and the share of passenger transport are uneven.
This situation depends on the vastness of the republic's territory, certain characteristics of the natural conditions, the degree of development of each region, the economic level of each region, and the social level of each region.
One evaluation metric is the amount of cargo transported in million tons, one is the number of passengers transported in million people, and one is the cargo and passenger turnover.
Vehicle speed, cargo capacity, and the impact of natural conditions on transport operations are considered when selecting transport modes.

== Postal and communication services ==

Federal post offices are managed by the state-owned company named Počta Rossii.
Russia's communication systems consist of two main sectors, one being the postal service and the other being electrical communication.
The development level of postal communication in Russia is comparable to that of highly developed European countries.
Telephone network coverage is not uniform across all areas, with the highest level of coverage characteristic of the Central Economic Region.
A unified automatic communication system was built, and the Trans-Russian fiber optic network is being built to join the global communication system with a length reaching 18,000 kilometers.
The rapid development of the internet system has been observed in recent years.
Moscow and Saint Petersburg are major centers of the communication system.

A branch line of the East Siberia–Pacific Ocean oil pipeline was extended to the Daqing Oil Field.
Approximately 20% of electricity in Russia comes from nuclear power.
Russia is building the world's first series of mobile nuclear power plants.
The recoverable coal reserves of the entire Soviet Union were approximately 240 billion tons.
The air transport network covers more than 600,000 kilometers.

== Coal resources and production ==

The Soviet Union held the world's number one position in coal reserves, and coal production in the Soviet Union reached 340 million tons in 1993.
The Kuznetsk coal mine plays an absolute role in Russia's coal supply, while the Pechora, Irkutsk, Tunguska, Lena, and South Yakutia coal mines are other major coal mines.

== Oil reserves and extraction ==

Russia's oil production has been decreasing annually in recent years.
Until the 1970s, the Volga-Ural oil fields were the largest production sites and accounted for 70% of the Soviet Union's total extraction volume.
Recently, the Volga-Ural oil fields account for about 12% of Russia's total production volume.
The Tyumen oil field is located in the West Siberian Lowland and produces more than 70% of Russia's total oil production.
One of these oil fields is located in the North Caucasus region, and another is located in the Sakhalin area in the Russian Far East.

== Natural gas reserves and infrastructure ==

Russia has the largest natural gas extraction volume in the world.
More than 70% of Russia's proven natural gas reserves are concentrated in Western Siberia.
Major natural gas production areas include the North Caucasus, Volga, Urals, and Western Siberia.
Gas pipelines are concentrated from gas fields towards the Moscow region and the Urals region.
There are 185,000 km of gas pipelines installed in Russia.
These pipelines account for approximately 35% of the country's freight transport volume.
Most pipelines originating in or passing through Russia are directed westward.

== Electricity generation and demand ==

In 1991, the total electricity production of the Soviet Union was 17,129 billion kWh and ranked second in the world.
Almost all of the Soviet Union's electricity production in 1991 was generated by thermal power plants, while hydropower in the Volga and Yenisei river basins previously accounted for a significant portion of power generation.
Electricity demand has increased over time, and power generation now relies heavily on thermal power plants utilizing abundant fossil fuels.
Thermal power generation accounts for more than 70% of Russia's electricity production, hydroelectric power generation accounts for approximately 15%, and nuclear power generation accounts for approximately 10%.

== Railway network overview ==

The Russian railway network has a total length of 87,157 km and a density of 4.5 km per km.
Russia has a total of 85,000 kilometers of railway tracks.
A significant portion of the railway network is aging, and this aging infrastructure has led to reduced transportation efficiency.
The container transport rate accounts for less than 1% of total freight.
The railway system operates as a single unified system that includes countries belonging to the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the three Baltic states: Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania.
The Russian state railway company manages a monopoly on the railways and is responsible for approximately 40% of all freight and passenger transport.
The American railway network is ranked first in the world by total length.

== Trans-Siberian Railway ==

The Trans-Siberian Railway is a transcontinental railway that connects Chelyabinsk to Vladivostok over a distance of approximately 7,400 km and was completed in 1905.
The Moscow-Vladivostok route connects Europe and the Far East and is 9,334 km long.
The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world.
The journey from Moscow to Vladivostok takes seven days.
The railway line serves destinations in Mongolia, China, and North Korea.

In 2006, Russia had a total road length of 933,000 kilometers, and by 2010 the total length of roads in Russia exceeded 1 million kilometers.
The length of paved roads in Russia was 786,000 kilometers by 2010, while the length of federal roads in Russia is 50,000 km.
Russia has the longest total road network of any European country except France, with approximately 5.3 kilometers of paved roads per 1,000 residents.
Russia has a network of M-roads that are mainly found in European Russia, and these secondary roads are called A-roads.
There are often no grade-separated intersections on these roads, and few M-roads have highway status.
Only the M-11, M-12, and parts of the M-2 and M-4 are officially highways.
Many major Russian roads consist of two lanes in each direction and are usually not separated by a median strip.
The MKAD ring road is located around the capital city of Moscow, and the full name of the MKAD is Moskovskaja Koltsevaja Avtomobilnaja Doroga.

== Railway history and infrastructure ==

Railway transport in Russia began to develop actively in the mid-19th century.
The first major railway line in Russia was the St.
Petersburg–Moscow route, which opened in 1851.
The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway in Russia and the longest railway in the world.
As of 2012, railways were present in 78 out of 83 Russian regions.[490,3566,3567,3568] The total length of operational railway tracks was 124,000 km, of which 86,000 km were for public use and 38,000 km were for non-public use.[490,3566,3567,3568] Of the public-use tracks, 43,000 km were electrified.[490,3566,3567,3568] Non-public-use tracks are located on enterprise territories and at mineral extraction sites.[490,3566,3567,3568] The average density of railways is 7.3 km per 1,000 km².[3569,3570] Only the United States has a longer total railway track length than Russia, with 194,700 km of railway tracks.[3566,3571,3572,3573,3574] Russia ranks first in electrified railway track length.[3566,3571,3572,3573,3574] Russia has adopted a standard railway gauge width of 1520 mm.
The island of Sakhalin uses a different railway gauge width due to historical reasons, with a width of 1067 mm.[18,19] Railways converge towards Moscow.

The railway network in the European part of Russia has a radial layout and relatively high density.
The railway network in the Asian part of Russia has a latitudinal orientation and low density.
The length of Russia's railway network is 85,500 kilometers.
Most European countries do not have a broad-gauge railway system.
The total length of standard-gauge railway tracks in Russia exceeds 87,000 kilometers (54,100 miles).

Russia's agriculture sector contributes about 5% of the country's total GDP, although the sector employs about one-eighth of the total labour force.

== Historical development and institutions ==

Science as a social institution emerged in Russia only at the beginning of the 18th century under the reign of Peter the Great.
The Academy of Sciences was founded in 1724, and the first scientific institutions of the Russian Empire were established at that time.
The first university in Russia was founded in Moscow in 1755, and the institution founded is the current Lomonosov University.
In 1916, there were approximately 100 higher education institutions in Russia, of which 10 were universities, and there were several dozen research facilities in Russia in 1916.
The science of the Russian Empire was at a low level of development, yet certain areas of Russian science enjoyed international prestige at that time.
Two Russian academics were among the first Nobel Prize winners: Ivan Pavlov won the Nobel Prize in 1904, and Ilya Mechnikov won the Nobel Prize in 1908.

== Soviet science system and achievements ==

Russian science received a significant development boost during the Soviet era, when the Soviet Union possessed a well-developed research and development system.
Research was highly centralized during this period, with most scientists employed by the Academy of Sciences and its regional departments.
The Academy of Sciences of the USSR dominated basic research and applied research.
A key characteristic was the separation of research and production, while the university sector had low significance in research.
All enterprises in the economic sector were state-owned and conducted very little research themselves.
A large portion of research was conducted by specialized research institutes that were generally organizationally separate from state-owned enterprises.
The Soviet state prioritized military superiority, and research and development was world-leading in certain areas.

== The 1990s crisis and brain drain ==

Science experienced a severe crisis in the Russian Federation during the 1990s, which was caused by a permanent lack of financial funds.
The crisis in the 1990s led to a drastic reduction in state support for science and a brain drain from Russia.
The lack of funds prevented the support of existing research institutions, and development stopped in many fields.
Qualified researchers and teachers emigrated to the USA.

== Modern research structure and funding ==

Institutions and working methods in Russian research and development have retained many features of the former Soviet system, and the state has overwhelming power in Russian research.
The majority of research organizations are separated from the economic sector, while research institutions within companies are generally underdeveloped and typically poorly trained.
The Russian Academy of Sciences holds a dominant position and is the leading institution in Russian research.
Russian research is primarily led by large research institutes, whereas small organizations have only minor significance.
As of April 2012, two-thirds of all research institutions were state-owned, and state-owned research institutions employed 78% of the research personnel.
The majority of research institutions are state-owned, while 14% of the research institutions are privately organized.
In 2008, the largest Russian research institutions employed 53% of all research personnel and were responsible for 44% of total research expenditures.
State budget funding dominates research and development financing, and government subsidies are the primary source of R&D funding.

== Role of universities in research ==

In the early 2010s, the government attempted to increase the research contribution of universities.
The university sector accounts for only 6% to 7% of the total research funding, 12% of the teaching staff are classified as researchers, and almost half of all universities and other higher education institutions do not participate in research activities.

== Government modernization and innovation programs ==

The government launched a campaign focused on modernization and innovation.
After the year 2000, the situation of Russian science and technology improved amidst a new economic boom.
Special national target programs were designed to promote domestic research and development starting in 2000, and these programs included plans to increase salaries for employees in science, support young academics, and establish technology parks nationwide.
One of the key areas is natural sciences, and another key area is the defense industry.
One of the key projects is the City of Innovations (Innograd), which is located in Skolkovo.
The new research and development complex was intended to focus primarily on five areas: energy, information technology, telecommunications, biomedicine, and nuclear technology.
The Russian government planned to enter the production of microelectronics.
Russia intends to strengthen its market share in satellite navigation and plans to prioritize the use of its domestic GLONASS system.

== Semiconductor manufacturing and processors ==

The semiconductor microfabrication technology level is at the 65nm process rule.
The Elbrus-4S CPU is based on 65nm semiconductor process technology, is designed for general-purpose applications, features four cores, contains 986 million transistors, operates at a frequency of 800MHz per core, and has a combined computational capability of 25 GFLOPS.
Mapper LLC is a semiconductor exposure equipment (stepper) manufacturer based in Moscow.
Around 2008, Mapper LLC was researching the mass production of fine processing technologies for processes after 22nm in collaboration with TSMC of Taiwan.
As of 2023, the production status of certain 16nm process semiconductor chips developed by Mapper LLC is one-of-a-kind and experimental small-scale production.
One such chip is the 'Elbrus-16S', a 16-core CPU for general-purpose use based on the 16nm process that has a total transistor count of 12 billion, operates at a frequency of 2GHz per core across 16 cores, and has a total computing capability of 1500 GFLOPS.
The Elbrus-2S3 is a general-purpose semiconductor chip that uses a 16nm process and is a 9-core CPU containing two CPU cores with 3D capabilities, one GPU core with 2D capabilities, and two GPU cores with 2D capabilities.

The Elbrus-2S3 contains four VPU cores.
The Baikal-S Processor is a semiconductor chip with the model number BE-S1000 that uses a 16nm process rule, is designed for general-purpose applications, and has 48 CPU cores.
Efforts are being made to establish fully domestic mass production technology for 16nm process semiconductor chips.
Russia has reached full domestic production levels for legacy semiconductor processes (90nm/65nm), and even if foreign CPU supply is completely halted, Russia can maintain CPU production domestically.
Russian semiconductor manufacturing companies like Mikron have facilities that handle both design and manufacturing, and these domestic facilities can produce CPUs sufficient for running practical application software on IoT devices such as smart home appliances as well as CPUs suitable for embedded control computers used in industrial machinery.
As of March 26, 2024, Russia has achieved full domestic mass production of semiconductor chips through the active use of reverse engineering technology.
The produced chips include the 'Baikal-M Processor' (BE-M1000), which is designed for general-purpose applications, utilizes a 28nm process rule, and features 8 CPU cores.
The Elbrus-8SV is a general-purpose CPU that uses a 28nm process semiconductor technology.

The Elbrus-8SV has 8 cores, a total of 3.5 billion transistors, an operating frequency of 1.5 GHz per core, a total computational capability of 576 GFLOPS, and a computational capability of 72 GFLOPS per core.
An initial production batch of 130,000 units has been produced.
More than half of the 28nm process semiconductor chips were defective, and the defect rate was high enough to cause production issues.
High-purity hydrofluoric acid is used in the semiconductor manufacturing process.
These chips follow a 40nm process rule.

== Post-Soviet crisis and structural reforms ==

This transition occurred during post-Soviet reforms.
Russian science experienced a severe crisis at the end of the 20th century.
In 1987, applied research and development were recognized as commodities, a year considered the starting point for the transformation of scientific institutions and the escalation of the crisis in science.
In 1987, a decree by the Central Committee of the CPSU and the Council of Ministers of the USSR titled 'On transferring scientific organizations to full economic accounting and self-financing' was adopted.
In 1987, a transition to paying for scientific and technical products at contractual prices was implemented and the reduction in the number of scientific workers began for the first time.
Science funding was drastically reduced.
Tens of thousands of scientists left the country and now work abroad.
The Russian Academy of Sciences underwent a reform conducted by the government of Dmitry A.
Medvedev that caused significant criticism from scientists.
The Ministry of Education and Science planned to lay off approximately 8,000 scientists by 2019, a plan linked to a reduction in the share of the state program 'Development of Science and Technology' in the total budget expenditures.
The share of the state program 'Development of Science and Technology' in total budget expenditures was projected to be 0.87% in 2019.

== Soviet institutional structure and expansion ==

The number of scientific institutions increased significantly during the Soviet era.

== The post-Soviet scientific crisis ==

Russian science experienced a severe crisis at the end of the 20th century, with 1987 considered the starting point for the transformation of scientific institutions and the growth of the crisis in science.
This transfer occurred during post-Soviet reforms in sectors that were previously part of the state sector.
In 1987, a decree titled 'On transferring scientific organizations to full economic accounting and self-financing' was adopted by the Central Committee of the CPSU and the Council of Ministers of the USSR.
Under this decree, applied research and developments were recognized as commodities, and a transition occurred to paying for scientific and technical products at contractual prices.
Research was not updated, equipment was not updated, and human resources potential was not updated.
The process of conserving the technological backwardness of industrial sectors deepened, affecting the technological base of national economy industries.
Science funding was sharply reduced, and state funding for science decreased significantly due to this crisis.
Tens of thousands of scientists left the country, and many Russian scientists and skilled professionals migrated to Europe or the United States.

== Modernization efforts and government priorities ==

The situation of science and technology in Russia improved during the 2000s, an improvement accompanied by an economic boom wave.
The Russian government launched a campaign with the goal of modernization and improvement.
Russian President Dmitry Medvedev established five top priorities for the country's technological development, including energy efficiency, IT (including both standard products and those combined with space technology), nuclear energy, and pharmaceuticals.

== GLONASS satellite navigation system ==

Russia has completed the GLONASS system, which is one of four global satellite navigation systems alongside the Global Positioning System (GPS) operated by the United States and the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System operated by China.
Between 75% and 80% of electronic components for Glonass-M satellites were purchased from Western countries.
The Russian government considered stopping the production of GLONASS-K satellites due to a lack of synchronous components from abroad after Western countries banned the export of components to Russia.
In 2016, Russia planned to produce all satellite components domestically by 2024 with the goal of avoiding dependence on imported components.
The Glonass-K2 satellites were developed by ISS Reshetnev, and Russia began producing them in 2019.
While GLONASS-K satellites had 90% of their electronic equipment imported from abroad, GLONASS-K2 satellites will use all components manufactured in Russia.

== Superheavy element research ==

Russia leads the world in research on superheavy elements.
Experts from the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Physics, which is located at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, successfully synthesized six of the heaviest elements for the first time.
The atomic numbers of these elements range from 113 to 118.
This achievement was the result of 10 years of research that spanned from 2000 to 2010.

== High-energy physics achievements ==

In 2006, Russian scientists created the world's strongest light emission based on PEARL technology (Petawatt Parametric Laser), which was developed at the Nizhny Novgorod Applied Physics Institute belonging to the Russian Academy of Sciences.
This technology relies on parametric optical amplification in nonlinear optical crystals and can generate an electric pulse as strong as 0.56 petawatts, a power hundreds of times greater than the combined capacity of all power plants in the world.
Russian scientists also created an unprecedentedly strong artificial magnetic field reaching 28 megagausses, a strength hundreds of millions of times stronger than Earth's magnetic field.

== Propulsion and energy claims ==

In 2015, a Russian scientist named Vladimir Leonov claimed to have successfully tested an experimental quantum engine that he stated was 5,000 times stronger than conventional rocket engines.
The quantum engine was claimed to propel aircraft at speeds of 1,000 km/s, allowing spacecraft equipped with it to reach the Moon in 3.6 hours and Mars in 42 hours.
The engine is powered by cold nuclear fusion, where one kilogram of nickel provides energy equivalent to one million kilograms of gasoline, and a single refueling would allow the aircraft to fly for several years.
This technical achievement is the result of applying the theory of super-linkage, which was developed by Russian scientists.

Russian government agencies and state-owned companies must purchase 700,000 PCs and 300,000 servers annually.
The cost of purchasing these PCs is 500 million USD per year, while the cost of purchasing these servers is 300 million USD per year.

Russia plans to replace Intel and AMD microprocessors with the domestic Baikal microprocessor soon.
Russia had to order the production of these microprocessors at TSMC's factory in Taiwan.
The Mikron enterprise is located in Zelenograd and is the most developed enterprise in Russia regarding this aspect.
Mikron can only mass-produce 90 nm microprocessors.

== Strategic plans and future missions ==

Roscosmos is developing a new spacecraft named Orjol, which is intended to gradually replace the aging Soyuz spacecraft starting in 2025, is designed to transport a crew to lunar orbit, and is scheduled to reach lunar orbit by 2029.
Russia announced its plans in February 2019 for its first crewed mission to the lunar surface, which was scheduled for the year 2031.
A new space program was approved by the Russian government in July 2005 to cover the years 2005 to 2015 with the goal to secure the world-class level of Russian spaceflight and to solidify Russia's position among leading global space powers.
The program prioritized the development and use of space technology and services, the construction of spacecraft for manned flights, the construction of spacecraft for transport missions, the construction of spacecraft for interplanetary missions, and a reusable space system.
Since the discontinuation of the Space Shuttle program, Russia has increasingly used the Soyuz rocket for ISS resupply, carrying the Soyuz spacecraft and the Progress space transporter to the ISS.

Scientific and technical foundations are to be established for a manned flight to Mars and a new generation space station.

The first unmanned launches were to take place from the new Wostotschny cosmodrome in the Amur region using modernized versions of existing launch vehicles.
Manned launches were planned for 2020 to originate from Vostochny with spacecraft carrying crew members, though the new launch date is the mid-2020s.
Missions are planned for the 2020s to conduct in-depth exploration of the Moon and the planet Venus.

Roscosmos is producing a new spacecraft named Orel to replace the aging Soyuz.

== Launch capabilities and international cooperation ==

Russia is the largest satellite launcher and the only country capable of independently launching rockets into space to transport cargo to the International Space Station (ISS), a capability it has held since after 2010.
Between 1999 and 2009, Russia launched the most rockets, successfully placing 245 payloads into orbit compared to the 218 payloads successfully launched by the United States during the same period.
Russia is currently one of the providers of space rocket engines to the United States, which will purchase 18 RD-180 rocket engines from Russia until 2022 for the purpose of transporting cargo into space.
The United States requires at least two launch systems for national security reasons, and the US Air Force and NASA currently rely primarily on three types of rockets: the Delta IV, the Atlas V, and the Falcon 9.
The Delta IV and Atlas V are operated by ULA, while the Falcon 9 is operated by SpaceX.
The Atlas V rocket uses the RD-180 engine, which is designed and manufactured in Russia.
The operating cost of the Atlas V is lower than that of the Delta IV, which is reserved for heavier payloads and more difficult orbits.

Atlas V cannot handle the payloads and orbits assigned to Delta IV.

== Rocket engine supply and dependencies ==

Russia is developing the Angara super-heavy launch vehicle, which may currently use foreign components. If Western countries stop supplying Russia, Russia can switch to buying components from China. New components may still require a period of operation with the Russian platform, the features of the products may not be able to completely replace similar Western products, and the variety of components may not be entirely sufficient.
One advantage is guaranteed supply, and another advantage is relatively favorable pricing.
Energomash believes the time from testing to successful production is very long. The United States will need more than 3 billion USD to produce replacement engines and will need approximately 10 years to produce replacement engines. The United States will continue to import rocket engines from Russia even if it is banned, and an upgraded version of the Antares rocket will be equipped with these Russian engines.

Russia is one of the world's most sparsely populated and urbanised countries, with the vast majority of its population concentrated within its western part.
It had a population of 142.8 million according to the 2010 census, which rose to 144.7 million as of the 2021 census (excluding Crimea and Sevastopol).
Russia is the most populous country in Europe, and the world's ninth most populous country, with a population density of .

Since the 1990s, Russia's death rate has exceeded its birth rate, which some analysts have called a demographic crisis.
In 2022, the total fertility rate across Russia was estimated to be 1.42 children born per woman, which is below the replacement rate of 2.1, and is one of the world's lowest fertility rates.
Subsequently, the nation has one of the world's oldest populations, with a median age of 40.3 years.
In 2009, it recorded annual population growth for the first time in fifteen years, and subsequently experienced annual population growth due to declining death rates, increased birth rates, and increased immigration.

However, since 2020, Russia's population gains have been reversed, as excessive deaths from the COVID-19 pandemic resulted in its largest peacetime decline in history.
Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the demographic crisis in the country has deepened, as the country has reportedly suffered high military fatalities while facing renewed brain drain and human capital flight caused by Western mass-sanctions and boycotts.

Russia is a multinational state with many subnational entities associated with different minorities.
There are over 193 ethnic groups nationwide.
In the 2010 census, roughly 81% of the population were ethnic Russians, and the remaining 19% of the population were ethnic minorities; while over four-fifths of Russia's population was of European descent—of whom the vast majority were Slavs, with a substantial minority of Finno-Ugric and Germanic peoples.
According to the United Nations, Russia's immigrant population is the world's third-largest, numbering over 11.6 million; most of which are from post-Soviet states, mainly from Central Asia.

== Geographic distribution ==

The average population density is 8.4 inhabitants per square kilometer, which is low due to the country's large land area.[70,487] Approximately 70 percent of Russia's population lives in the European part, while 15% of the population lives in the Asian part.
The main region where the Russian population lives is west of the Ural Mountains, where approximately 110 million people reside.
The area of highest population density is near the Ural Mountains and in Southwest Siberia, where the majority of the population resides.[70,487] A significant part of the Russian population lives in North-Western Siberia.
Large areas in Siberia are virtually uninhabited, and vast areas of Siberia are nearly uninhabited.

Population density varies significantly across Russia, with an average of 8.3 people per square kilometer and a reported figure of 9 people per square kilometer [cite: 1374,2032].
Approximately 77% of the population lives in western Russia, while three-quarters of the population lives in the European part of the country, which has the most favorable natural conditions.
Approximately 75% of the population lives west of the Ural Mountains, whereas less than 25% of the population lives in Siberia and further eastern regions.
The population density in the European part of Russia is higher than in the Asian part [cite: 2628], where approximately 22 million people live and where 39 million of these inhabitants lived [cite: 3996].
The population density is lowest in northeastern Russia [cite: 2628], where the population in the northern part of Russia is sparse and the density is less than 1 person per square kilometer.
The population density in the Russian Far East is also less than 1 person per square kilometer, and the population increases as one moves south from the north.
In the capital and its surroundings (Moscow region), the population density is 362 people per square kilometer.
In many cases, a considerable proportion of the population lives in the respective regional capital.
The population density in rural areas rarely exceeds 40 to 50 inhabitants per square kilometer, a low density that applies even in relatively densely populated central Russian administrative regions.

== Immigration ==

In 2006, 186,380 immigrants entered Russia, 95% of whom were from CIS countries.
Illegal immigrants come from former Soviet republics.
The Russian Federation has the most liberal immigration laws in the world.

Immigrants can acquire citizenship of the Russian Federation after five years of permanent residence in the country, provided they are proficient in the Russian language and pass a corresponding language test.

== Emigration ==

Emigration is a decisive factor in the country's demographic development.
Millions of Russians have settled in European and overseas countries since the 1990s.
Germany is the main destination for Russian emigrants, where a Russian-speaking community of about four million people resides.
This community is the largest outside of Russia.
The number of Russian emigrants decreased steadily, falling from 359,000 in the year 2000 to 32,000 in the year 2009 [cite: 491].
It is estimated that nearly 20 million Russians live outside of Russia, with most residing in former Soviet countries.
The Russian Federation is a country with a shrinking population, and migration was a cause of the population decrease.
Russia experienced the highest birth rate in 2009, which was the highest birth rate since the dissolution of the Soviet Union [cite: 490,503,504].
The 2002 census was the basis for the data, and 80% of Russia's population lives in the European part.

== Regional population dynamics ==

Western European regions are depopulating the most, including the Pskov, Smolensk, and Novgorod regions.
Population growth is currently continuing in some southern regions, such as Chechnya, Ingushetia, and Dagestan, and is also occurring in the northeast.

== Fertility and mortality rates ==

The birth rate in Russia was 13.3 per 1,000 people in 2014, while the average birth rate in the European Union was 10.1 per 1,000 people in 2014.[490,802] The mortality rate in Russia was 13.1 per 1,000 people in 2014, and the average mortality rate in the European Union was 9.7 per 1,000 people in 2014.[490,802] The prediction was that the mortality rate would equal the birth rate by 2011.

== Government policies and incentives ==

The Russian Ministry of Health and Social Affairs predicted that the death rate would equal the birth rate by 2011.
The Russian government has launched several national programs to increase the birth rate.
Parents received a one-time state grant known as Maternity Capital since 2007, which was available starting from the birth of the second child and amounted to nearly 10,000 euros in 2012.
Women who had their second child since 2007 received a one-time payment of 9,200 dollars.
Monthly government child allowances were doubled to an amount of 55 dollars.
Families received preferential mortgages and subsidies in 2018, with subsidies available starting from the first child for some families.
Nine billion dollars were budgeted for a period of 3 years for these measures.
President Vladimir Putin made a statement in February 2019 stating that he could not accept the declining birth rate and announced further relief measures for families with children.

The increase in fertility and the decrease in mortality were expected to cause the death rate to equal the birth rate.
The government is implementing a series of programs to increase the birth rate and to attract more migrants.

A one-time payment of 9,200 dollars has been offered since 2007 for women who have a second child.
The Russian government began simplifying immigration laws in 2006 with the goal of compensating for the country's demographic decline.
The Russian government launched a state program in 2006 that provided assistance for the voluntary immigration of ethnic Russians from former Soviet republics.
Maternity capital was introduced in 2007 as a form of stimulating birth rates and supporting large families.[3422,3423] Maternity capital played a significant role in stabilizing the demographic sphere in Russia and contributed to the transition to expanded population reproduction.[3422,3423]

== Population trends and projections ==

Russia's population decreased to 142.2 million by 2007, and the rate of population decline slowed down after 2007.[847,848] The correction was based on the results of the 2010 census.
The fertility rate declined between 1988 and 1999, falling from two births per woman in 1988 to 1.16 births per woman in 1999.
The number of births was 1.48 million in 2006 and 1.9 million in 2012, as the number of births in Russia increased.[856,857] Statistics indicate there were only 1.3 million births in 2022.
Russia's population is expected to continue declining in the coming decades, a decline similar to that of other European countries.
The International Labour Organization (ILO) forecasts a population drop to 130 million by 2050.
The population decline would be mild, assuming a net migration of 300,000 people per year.
The population increased slightly by 2012, reaching approximately 143.5 million, and the demographic situation stabilized somewhat by 2012.
A deterioration of the demographic situation was expected starting from 2015 due to low birth cohorts in the 1990s.

This population growth trend reversed during the later part of the 2010s.
According to Rosstat, the decline in 2020 exceeded 500,000 people, which was the first time since 2005 that the annual population decline surpassed 500,000.
Russian authorities made projections in 2021 covering the period until 2024, with a projected population decline of 1.2 million people.
The population shrank by at least 524,000 people after the war began.
Between January and April 2023, 3.1% fewer children were born compared to the previous year's period, a birth rate decline that represents a negative record.

The majority of immigrants are descendants of Russians who were settled in other constituent republics during the Empire and Soviet eras and mostly returned to Russia together with their families.
The influx of immigrants decreased after the annexation of Crimea, a decrease to which economic recession, protectionism, and nationalism contributed.

== Social structure and values ==

Russian society is traditionally shaped by collectivism, a value system based on the lifestyle of peasant village communities known as the Mir.
Land and soil were communal property for a long time in Russia, and people in Russia have traditionally defined themselves through the community.
People in Russia value consistency between their own behavior and that of the collective, as well as consistency between their own opinions and those of the collective.
The family is an important reference group for many Russians, where multiple generations often live together.
Families support each other financially, help each other with childcare, and help each other with elderly care.
Domestic violence is widespread.
Collective orientation is sometimes still evident in the professional world, where the faculty is experienced as a community.
Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, educated social strata in major cities have oriented themselves towards principles of individualism [911,912,913].
These educated social strata were able to benefit from newly gained travel freedom [911,912,913].
This shift resulted in massive internal societal tension [911,912,913].

== Family policy and state programs ==

The state emphasizes the ideal of 'traditional family values' in light of the demographic crisis and suggests that every woman should have three children, though in reality, families with only one child are common.
The state government has implemented several programs that aim to increase birth rates and boost immigration.
In 2007, the monthly state child allowance was raised to $55, and a one-time payment of $9,200 is given to every woman who decides to have a second child.

== Economic status and class ==

The United Nations Development Programme classifies the Russian Federation as a country with very high human development.
More than 70% of Russia's population is classified as middle class.
The country has 75.41 million people of working age.
In the year 2000, there were 8 million people in the middle class, and by 2006, there were 55 million people in the middle class.
The subsistence level is less than 135 euros per month.

== Gender and labor ==

In 2014, 43% of all management positions in Russia were held by women.

== Religious history ==

This conversion took place in the late 8th century or early 9th century.
After the destruction of the Khazar Empire, Judaism was essentially limited to Kiev, Crimea, and the Caucasus.
Jews were first mentioned in the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1471.
Jews were tolerated until the time of Ivan the Terrible, though Jewish tolerance was subject to some laws directed against them.
Jews were expelled from the Russian Empire starting in 1721, but the expulsion of Jews became impossible after the incorporation of eastern parts of Poland in 1793 and 1795.
Jews were required to live within a designated settlement zone starting in 1791, and this settlement zone was located in the area of present-day Ukraine, Belarus, and the Baltic states.
Leading officials supported antisemitic trends in the population during the 19th century, including Konstantin Pobedonoszew.
Many pogroms occurred in southern Russia in 1881.
The proportion of Muslims in the general population is increasing significantly.
Moscow has 12 million residents.

== Birth and death rates ==

In 2007, the death rate exceeded the birth rate by 477,700 people, although the death toll in the previous year was higher.
