== Historical context ==

Russia's population was half of the Soviet Union's population at the time of the dissolution.
The population of Russia was only half that of the Soviet Union when the union collapsed.

== Vital statistics ==

The main reasons for the decline in Russia's population are a high mortality rate and a low birth rate.[490,802] Russia's birth rate is equal to that of European countries, while its mortality rate is significantly higher than that of European countries.[490,802] In 2014, Russia had 13.3 births per 1,000 people and a mortality rate of 13.1 deaths per 1,000 people.[490,802] The average birth rate in the European Union in 2014 was 10.1 per 1,000 people, and the average mortality rate in the European Union in 2014 was 9.7 per 1,000 people.[490,802] The birth rate in Russia increased by 8.3% annually, with an estimated 1.6 million births in Russia.
Approximately 2 million people died in Russia in 2007, and the mortality rate in Russia decreased by 4% in 2007 compared to 2006.
The number of deaths was 687,100 in 2006 and decreased from 477,700 in 2007.[490,1662] The decline is due to a decrease in the death rate, an increase in the birth rate, and increased immigration.[490,1662]

== Ukrainian population ==

In 1719, the number of Ukrainians in Russia was 262,900, and by 1795, this number increased to 810,900.
According to census data, the number of Ukrainians in Russia reached 3.6211 million in 1897 and 7.873 million in 1926.
The number of Ukrainians in post-war years was 3.359 million, and the number of Ukrainians in Russia was 4.4 million in 1989.
The largest number of Ukrainians live in Moscow and St.
Petersburg.
A large number of Ukrainians live in the Kursk region, the Voronezh region, the Saratov region, Samara, Astrakhan, Vladivostok, Kuban (Krasnodar Krai), the Don region, from Orenburg to the Pacific Ocean, the Primorsky Krai along the Ussuri River, and the Amur region (known as the 'Green Belt').
Several authors and organizations believe official estimates of the Ukrainian population in Russia are underestimated.

Ukrainians are undergoing rapid assimilation.
The oldest compact settlements of Ukrainians are located in the Voronezh region, the Kursk region, and the Belgorod region, where the number of Ukrainians today is 200,000.
There are 460,000 Ukrainians living in the North Caucasus region, where the population of Ukrainians is approximately 460,000, and they live most compactly in this region in the Krasnodar Krai and the Rostov Oblast.
1.5 million Ukrainians live in Siberia and the Russian Far East.
There are 800,000 Ukrainians living in the Chelyabinsk, Orenburg, and Saratov regions.
Up to 500,000 Ukrainians live in Moscow and up to 500,000 Ukrainians live in the Moscow region.
There are up to 250,000 Ukrainians in Saint Petersburg and up to 250,000 Ukrainians in the Leningrad Oblast.
Estimates suggest that 7 million to 10 million residents of Russia are of Ukrainian origin.
Ukrainian cultural and national organizations were established in practically all regions, and all these regional organizations belong to the 'Union of Ukrainians in Russia' (OUR).

== Homelessness and orphanage issues ==

The army of homeless children increases by 130,000 annually, and 731,000 homeless children are officially registered.
By the beginning of 2011, there were already 4 million homeless people in Russia, 3 million beggars in Russia, and approximately 5 million homeless children in Russia.
Almost every fifth Russian child is a resident of an orphanage or homeless, and these children are typically born to living parents.
Thirty percent of former orphanage residents become homeless after leaving, and almost 10% of former orphanage residents commit suicide after leaving.
Kabardino-Balkaria, Chuvashia, and Kaliningrad Oblast are one of these regions.
The population density in the Far Eastern Federal District is 1.01 people per square kilometer.

== Fertility trends and government measures ==

The Russian government provides subsidies to families with children, and these programs are designed to increase the birth rate.[502,804] Starting in 2007, the government doubled the monthly child allowance and provided a one-time payment of 250,000 Rubles (approximately US$10,000) to women giving birth to their second child.[502,804] Russia had the highest birth rate in 2007, which was the highest birth rate since the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Most Russian families choose to have only one child.

== Immigration policy ==

Immigration is increasingly considered necessary, and the goal of immigration is to maintain the national population level.
These programs are designed to attract more immigrants.[502,804]

== Emigration and data reliability ==

The number of Russians leaving the country in 2013 was significantly higher than in 2012, when only 122,751 Russians left the country.
Some experts doubt the authenticity of Rosstat's data and allege that the actual number of emigrants is much higher than reported.
Among those who left Russia are Pavel Durov, who founded the Russian social network VKontakte; Sergei Guriyev, an economic expert; and Garry Kasparov, a world chess champion.

== Urbanization and Cities ==

Cities appeared as isolated phenomena outside of agglomerations and formed a sparse network.
Industrialization took place in all regions of the country and provided a significant impetus for subsequent urbanization.
This industrialization led to the creation of numerous new cities and caused rapid growth in existing cities.
Many Russian cities were formed as a result of administrative restructuring.
New foundations of cities and elevations of towns to city status are characteristics of Russian urbanization that persist until today.
More than half of all Russian cities were founded in the last 90 years, with most of these cities founded especially in the 1960s.
There are 160 large cities in Russia, and half of the Russian population lives in these 160 large cities.
Many of these large cities are new cities, and approximately one quarter of these large cities are new cities.
Major Russian cities are primarily industrial centers and primarily administrative centers.
Magnitogorsk and Nowokusnezk are examples of new major cities.

New types of cities emerged during the Soviet era, including the capital of small national republics and the science city.
Tscheboksary and Naltschik are examples of capitals of small national republics, while Dubna is an example of a science city.
Bratsk is an example of a new major city, whereas Samara and Tambow are examples of established major cities.
Cities emerged as independent entities.

Russian is the official and the predominantly spoken language in Russia.
It is the most spoken native language in Europe, the most geographically widespread language of Eurasia, as well as the world's most widely spoken Slavic language.
Russian is one of two official languages aboard the International Space Station, as well as one of the six official languages of the United Nations.

Russia is a multilingual nation; approximately 100–150 minority languages are spoken across the country.
According to the Russian Census of 2010, 137.5 million across the country spoke Russian, 4.3 million spoke Tatar, and 1.1 million spoke Ukrainian.
The constitution gives the country's individual republics the right to establish their own state languages in addition to Russian, as well as guarantee its citizens the right to preserve their native language and to create conditions for its study and development.
However, various experts have claimed Russia's linguistic diversity is rapidly declining due to many languages becoming endangered.

== Linguistic classification and history ==

Russian belongs to the Indo-European language family and is part of the East Slavic branch of Slavic languages, which also includes White Russian, Ukrainian, and Ruthenian.[1467,1468][1692,1693][1468,2049]
Russian is one of the three most important East Slavic languages, with the other two major East Slavic languages being Belarusian and Ukrainian.[1467,1468][1692,1693]
Written examples of ancient East Slavic exist and are dated to the 10th century, while written records of Old East Slavic Russian date back to the 9th century.[1467,1468][1692,1693]
The earliest known writings in the Russian language date back to the 10th century, and written Old Russian existed as early as the 10th century.[1467,1468][1468,2049]

The Russian language belongs to the Indo-European language group, as do Belarusian and Ukrainian.
Old Russian was spoken from the 10th century to the 14th century.
The East Slavic languages originated from Old Russian.

== Official status and legal framework ==

Russian is the only official state language, a classification based on a law from 1997.
Official documents must be written in Cyrillic, which is the only official script, a requirement that applies to languages that also use the Latin alphabet.
Russia officially speaks 31 languages in total, including 27 other official languages that exist within the republics and autonomous regions of Russia.
Russian is the only official language of the central government.
There are 15 other languages with an official status and 27 recognized minority languages.
Approximately 27 other languages are spoken in some regions of Russia due to its vast size.
Republics and autonomous districts have the right to use one or more languages as official languages in addition to Russian.

== Usage statistics and demographics ==

Russian is spoken by 142.6 million people, and approximately 80% of people in Russia speak Russian.
The Russian language is extremely dominant, with 98% of the population using the Russian language and 99.1% of the population able to speak Russian.
Russian is understood almost completely throughout the entire region, including the national republics.
The Cyrillic alphabet is the only one used by the population in Russia.
Russian is the second most used language on the internet.
There are 100 different languages spoken in Russia.
Tatar is the second most spoken language.
Ukrainian is the third most spoken language in Russia.
German is the third most spoken language with 2.9 million speakers.
The third largest language group consists of German speakers.
There are 2.9 million German speakers.
Tatar, Ukrainian, Chuvash, and German are examples of such local languages.
The Chuvash Republic belongs to the group of Turkic-speaking peoples.
Several Central European languages, including German, Polish, and Yiddish, are also spoken in Russia.
Many people speak the Romani language in Russia.
Populations not belonging to the Russian ethnicity are often bilingual.

The ethnic groups of Russia belong to four language families and speak approximately 100 languages.[84,2738] The Indo-European language family accounts for 89% of the population, the Altaic language family accounts for 7% of the population, the Caucasian language family accounts for 2% of the population, and the Uralic language family accounts for 2% of the population.
The Yakuts speak a Turkic language.
Russian is the most popular language in Eurasia, the largest language in the Balto-Slavic group, and the second most used language on the internet after English.[2052,2548,2549,2550,2551] Russian is the second most spoken language on the internet.[2050,2051,2052] The Russian language is uniform throughout the territory of the Russian Federation.
According to a 2002 survey, 6.95 million people speak English, 2.9 million people speak German, and 49,020 people speak Lithuanian.[84,2630]

== Regional languages and republics ==

These ethnic groups speak approximately 100 languages [310,505].
More than one hundred languages are spoken by these ethnic groups.
Representatives of these ethnic groups speak approximately 100 different languages.
Non-Russian minorities speak languages predominantly from the Turkic language family, Caucasian languages, Uralic languages (including Samoyedic languages), Altaic languages, and Paleo-Siberian languages.
Some of these languages have regional co-official status, such as Chechen, Chuvash, Kalmyk, Kabardian, Komi, Mari, Mordvin, Ossetian, Tatar, Tuvin, Udmurt, Yakut, Avar, Buryat, and Bashkir.
Some republics have three or more official languages.
Dagestan is a republic located within the territory of Russia.
The official languages of Dagestan are Azerbaijani and Russian.
There are 14 official languages in Dagestan.
Karelian, Finnish, and Vepsian are used in Karelia.
Karelian, Finnish, and Vepsian have only a subordinate official status in Karelia.
Yiddish is used in the Jewish Autonomous Oblast.

== Script and alphabet policies ==

Almost all regional official languages in Russia are written in the Cyrillic alphabet, and there is a guideline that all respective languages should be written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
The Cyrillic alphabet is the only official form of writing, and these languages are all written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
Some of these languages have other alphabets besides Cyrillic, including the Tatar language and the Chechen language, which have non-Cyrillic alphabets that do not have official status.
Tatar was written exclusively in the Latin script in Tatarstan from 2001 to 2004, a practice that the Russian-speaking population residing in Tatarstan opposed.
The Russian Constitutional Court banned this practice in November 2004, stating that a unified script is necessary for the unity of Russia.

== Language preservation and education ==

The use of regional languages is promoted in cultural policy, education, and mass media.
The governments and parliaments of the republics consider this an indispensable prerequisite to prevent the extinction of ethnic groups.
The mastery of indigenous mother tongues is declining, and Yiddish has not been spoken for decades in the Jewish Autonomous Oblast.
In 2015, the Duma discussed a ban on foreign language instruction intended to prevent emigration.

== Dialects and external influences ==

Russian has three main regional dialects.
The Russian language is used uniformly across the entire country and is quite homogeneous throughout the country.
The Arabic language has added many words to the Russian language.
Written examples of Church Slavonic have been preserved in the Russian Federation since the 10th century.
Russian is a politically significant language in the 20th century.
More than one quarter of scientific publications worldwide are published in Russian.
The subject is a country from the Russian-speaking area.

== Status and Constitution ==

Russian is the only official state language, a status established by Article 68 of the Constitution of the Russian Federation [cite: 86].
Official texts must be written using the Cyrillic alphabet, and the use of other alphabets for official texts is not permitted [cite: 2969,2970].
The Cyrillic alphabet is the only allowed script in the country, and Russian is written with the Cyrillic alphabet, which has 33 letters.
The Constitution of the Russian Federation does not mention the right of autonomous okrugs and oblasts to establish their own state languages, yet in practice, autonomous okrugs and oblasts declare their languages as state languages through their own charters.

== Linguistic Classification and History ==

Russian belongs to the Slavic branch of the Indo-European language family and is one of the three most important East Slavic languages.[1692,1693]
Russian belongs to the Indo-European language family and is a member of the East Slavic languages group.[1468,3197]
Russian is one of the last three living members of the East Slavic languages, and the other two living East Slavic languages are Belarusian and Ukrainian.
Russian is one of the still-spoken languages of the East Slavic group, and other languages in the East Slavic group include Belarusian and Ukrainian.[1468,2548,2549,3197]
The Rusyn language may also be included in the East Slavic group.[1468,2548,2549,3197]
Old Church Slavonic is the ancestor of all Slavic languages.
Written examples of Old East Slavic (Old Russian) have been proven to date back to at least the 10th century.[1468,2548,2549,3197]
The literary language developed directly from Old Russian and was codified in the 18th century.
New literary languages emerged in the 19th century, and these new languages were based on West Russian dialects.
The new languages include Ukrainian and Belarusian, and Ukrainian and Belarusian drew upon traditions from the former Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

The other two major East Slavic languages are Belarusian and Ukrainian, and written examples of these date back to the 10th century.

== Speakers and Demographics ==

Approximately 145 million people speak Russian as their first language, and the total number of Russian speakers is between 250 and 300 million according to various sources.
Approximately 92% of the population of Russia speaks Russian as their native language, while more than 99.4% of Russians speak the Russian language.
Approximately 99.4% of the population speaks Russian as their state language.
There are over 100 languages and dialects spoken in Russia, which are spoken by 160 ethnic groups.
There are eight languages in Russia with more than one million speakers.

== Regional Official Languages ==

The main local languages are spoken in the republics.
An exceptional situation exists in the multi-ethnic Republic of Dagestan, where Russian is an official language alongside 13 additional official languages: Aguul, Avar, Azerbaijani, Chechen, Dargin, Kumyk, Laki, Lezgian, Nogai, Rutul, Tabasaran, and Tat.
Languages other than official languages can be introduced with official status in any region of Russia [cite: 2971].
There are 27 other languages with regional official status in Russia, bringing the total to 35 languages officially recognized in Russia, which are recognized in different regions by local governments.

In the Karachay-Cherkess Republic, several languages have state status in addition to Russian, including the Abazin, Karachay, Nogai, and Circassian languages.
All state languages of the federal subjects must have a written form based on the Cyrillic script, and regions using a second official language must write it using Cyrillic characters.
There are 13 official languages in the Republic of Dagestan besides Russian, 4 official languages in the Karachay-Cherkessia Republic besides Russian, and 2 official languages in the Kabardino-Balkaria Republic besides Russian.

== International and Scientific Usage ==

Russian is the official language of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Transnistria, Gagauzia, Abkhazia, and South Ossetia.
The Russian language was widely used in global scientific literature, and its usage peaked in 1970 when 20% of all publications worldwide were in Russian.
Currently, the Russian language is used in less than 2% of global scientific publications.
In the last decade, English was used in more than 90% of scientific publications, while Russian was used in less than 9% of scientific publications.
More than one quarter of scientific publications worldwide are published in Russian.
Russian is the second most used language on the Internet and is one of the six official and working languages of UNESCO.
Russian is a politically significant language in the 20th century.

== Linguistic Diversity and Families ==

These ethnic groups speak approximately 100 languages.
These languages and dialects belong to the Indo-European, Altaic, and Uralic language families, as well as the Caucasian and Paleo-Asian language groups.
Chechen, Bashkir, and Chuvash are among the most common languages in Russia.

== Script and Orthography ==

Graždanka is a variant of the Cyrillic script that was created as a result of simplifying the Cyrillic script.

== Foreign Languages ==

English is the most well-known foreign language, while German, French, and Spanish are also well-known but to a lesser extent.
The popularity of the Chinese and Japanese languages has increased since 2021.

== Endangered Languages ==

In 2009, UNESCO recognized 136 languages located within the territory of Russia as endangered.

== Language Homogeneity ==

The Russian language is homogeneous throughout Russia, and it is the same dialect throughout the country despite wide regional spread.
Russian was the prioritized language of the union, and 35 languages are officially recognized.

== Language families and classification ==

Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Armenian, Ossetian, and German belong to the Indo-European language family.
Tatar, Chuvash, and Bashkir belong to the Altaic language family.
Udmurt, Mari, and Erzya belong to the Uralic language family.
Chechen, Avar, and Dargin are Nakh-Dagestani languages.
Kabardian-Circassian belongs to the Abkhazo-Adyghe language family.
These languages and dialects belong to the Paleo-Asian language group.
Russian belongs to the Indo-European language family and is one of the surviving East Slavic languages.
Belarusian and Ukrainian are other East Slavic languages, and Rusyn may also be an East Slavic language.
Russian belongs to the East Slavic branch of the Slavic language family.

== Major minority languages ==

Belarusian, Armenian, Ossetian, German, Chuvash, Bashkir, Udmurt, Mari, Erzya, Chechen, Avar, Dargin, and Kabardian-Circassian are among the most common spoken languages.

== Demographics and census data ==

Russian speakers represent 85.7% of Russia's population, and the number of native speakers for seven other languages exceeded one million according to the 2001 census.
The largest number of Russian speakers was in 1991, and the number of Russian speakers began to decline sharply in the early 1990s.
A census was conducted in 2002, which found that 142.6 million people spoke Russian, 5.3 million people spoke Tatar, and 1.8 million people spoke Ukrainian.

== Historical development and script ==

Examples of texts using Old East Slavic script (Old Russian) have been proven to exist and date back to the 10th century or later.

== International and regional usage ==

Russian is primarily used in Russia and other former Soviet member states, especially for communication between these countries.
In Warsaw Pact member countries, Russian was taught as a first foreign language in schools.
Many former Soviet republics today prioritize their own languages, yet Russian is still widely used in these regions.

== Legal status and endangerment ==

UNESCO recognized 136 languages in Russia as endangered.
All state languages of the subjects of the federation must have Cyrillic script.

Russia is a secular state by constitution, and its largest religion is Eastern Orthodox Christianity, chiefly represented by the Russian Orthodox Church.
Orthodox Christianity, together with Islam, Buddhism, and Paganism (either preserved or revived), are recognised by Russian law as the traditional religions of the country, part of its "historical heritage".

Islam is the second-largest religion in Russia, and is the traditional religion among the majority of the peoples of the North Caucasus, and among some Turkic peoples scattered along the Volga-Ural region.
Large populations of Buddhists are found in Kalmykia, Buryatia, Zabaykalsky Krai, and they are the vast majority of the population in Tuva.
Many Russians practise other religions, including Rodnovery (Slavic Neopaganism), Assianism (Scythian Neopaganism), other ethnic Paganisms, and inter-Pagan movements such as Ringing Cedars' Anastasianism, various movements of Hinduism, Siberian shamanism and Tengrism, various Neo-Theosophical movements such as Roerichism, and other faiths.
Some religious minorities have faced oppression and some have been banned in the country; notably, in 2017 the Jehovah's Witnesses were outlawed in Russia, facing persecution ever since, after having been declared an "extremist" and "nontraditional" faith.

In 2012, the research organisation Sreda, in cooperation with the Ministry of Justice, published the Arena Atlas, an adjunct to the 2010 census, enumerating in detail the religious populations and nationalities of Russia, based on a large-sample country-wide survey.
The results showed that 47.3% of Russians declared themselves Christians—including 41% Russian Orthodox, 1.5% simply Orthodox or members of non-Russian Orthodox churches, 4.1% unaffiliated Christians, and less than 1% Old Believers, Catholics or Protestants—25% were believers without affiliation to any specific religion, 13% were atheists, 6.5% were Muslims, 1.2% were followers of "traditional religions honouring gods and ancestors" (Rodnovery, other Paganisms, Siberian shamanism and Tengrism), 0.5% were Buddhists, 0.1% were religious Jews and 0.1% were Hindus.

== Demographic estimates and methodology ==

Estimates of the number of believers vary significantly between sources.
Some sources believe that between 16% and 48% of the population is non-believing.
Estimates of religious affiliation vary significantly between sources.
Some sources indicate that the number of non-religious people ranges from 16% to 48% of the population.
There is no official census of religion in Russia.
Estimates of religious affiliation are based solely on survey studies.
A 2010 survey was conducted by the American Research Center.
According to this survey, approximately 73.6% of Russia's population are Christians.
The CIA World Factbook contains information about the religious demographics of Russia.
The version of the CIA World Factbook cited was published in 2011.
According to the 2011 CIA World Factbook, 70.3% of Russians are Christians.
A Levada Center survey was conducted in 2012.
The survey indicated that approximately 76% of Russia's population are Christians.
There are no reliable statistics regarding membership in individual religious groups.
Surveys often differ significantly from one another.
25 percent of respondents stated they believe in a higher god-like power.
The All-Russian Center for Public Opinion Research (VCIOM) estimated that 75 percent of the population were Orthodox in 2010.
The All-Russian Center for Public Opinion Research (VCIOM) estimated that only 8 percent of the population were atheists in 2010.
The VCIOM's figures are also cited by the Russian Embassy in Germany.
The proportion of Orthodox Christians is usually stated between 51% and 72%.

The proportion of other Christians combined is less than 2%, the proportion of Buddhists is approximately 1%, and the proportion of Jews is about 0.35%.
The Fischer World Almanach and the US Department of State's Religious Freedom Report both report 14% Muslims.
The CIA World Factbook provided estimates in 2006 for practicing believers, defined as those who actively practice their faith.
According to these estimates, 15% to 20% of practicing believers were Russian Orthodox, 10% to 15% were Muslims, and 2% belonged to other Christian denominations.

== Eastern Orthodox Christianity ==

Christianity was adopted as the state religion of Russia starting in 988, and this dominance dates back to the Christianization of Kievan Rus' in the 10th century [519,520].
A separate patriarchate was established in 1589.
Approximately 100 million Russian citizens identify themselves as Orthodox Christians [519,520], and approximately half of the population belongs to the Russian Orthodox Church.
Orthodox Slavs are overwhelmingly Christian [310,529].
95% of registered Orthodox parishes belong to the Russian Orthodox Church [521,522], and there are fewer non-Russian Orthodox churches than those belonging to the Russian Orthodox Church [521,522].
The majority of Orthodox believers do not attend church regularly [523,524].
The church was brutally persecuted during the anti-religious era of the Soviet Union, yet the influence of Christianity was not completely suppressed during the Soviet era.
The influence of Christianity rose significantly again after the collapse of the USSR.
Between 1991 and 2010, 23,000 Orthodox churches were rebuilt, and the number of active churches in Russia increased fourfold.
The Orthodox Church forms a fundamental pillar of Russian society, and the values of the Orthodox Church form a fundamental pillar of Russian society.
This has been true up to the present day.
Greek Orthodox Church culture has permeated every aspect of Russian people's lives.

Orthodox Slavic culture adds to the diversity of Russia.

Orthodoxy was adopted through Southern Slavs and Byzantium when Prince Vladimir I the Great of Kiev adopted Orthodoxy.

In 1991, only 37% of the Russian population identified as Russian Orthodox believers, but the percentage of Russian Orthodox believers in Russia increased significantly after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The baptism of Rus in 988 is widely considered the beginning of the Russian Orthodox Church. The Russian Orthodox Church is also known as the Moscow Patriarchate and ranks fifth among autocephalous Eastern Orthodox churches. The Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople governed the Rus' Church for six centuries, with the position of the Metropolitan of Kiev and All Rus' under his jurisdiction until 1686.
Orthodoxy regained a leading position within the Russian Federation after the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

The Synod convenes as needed with the participation of all bishops, and when not in session, it is led by the Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia.
Since February 2009, Kirill I has held this position.
Cyril I visited Cuba on February 12, 2016, representing the Russian Orthodox Church, where he met with Pope Francis at Jose Marti International Airport.
A joint statement was signed calling for all parties to cooperate against terrorism and against the persecution of Christians.
The Russian Orthodox Church, the Serbian Orthodox Church, and the Georgian Orthodox Church boycotted the Ecumenical Council.

The population in the political center of Russia predominantly follows Orthodoxy.

== Islam ==

Estimates of the number of Muslims in Russia range between 7 and 9 million based on local sources, while other estimates range between 15 and 20 million based on Western and Islamic sources.
There are between 3 and 4 million Muslim migrants who live in post-Soviet countries.

== Other religious groups ==

Small Christian faiths include Armenian Apostolic churches and various Protestant churches.
The smallest Christian denominations in Russia are Catholics, Armenians, and Protestants.
There are three traditional regions for Buddhism in the Russian Federation, one of which is Tuva and another is Kalmykia.
Judaism and Buddhism are major religions in Russia.

== Historical development ==

Atheism was enforced by force in Russia during the Soviet era and the rule of the Communist Party.
The collapse of the Soviet Union led to the disappearance of the Marxist-Leninist state ideology.
A return to religious values occurred after these events.

== Legal status and state relations ==

Widespread religious liberalism prevailed immediately after the end of the Soviet Union and facilitated successful missionary activities for foreign and well-funded religious communities. The 1997 Religious Law privileges so-called 'traditional religions'. Restrictions on missionary activities have existed since 2016 and were initially targeted at Islam, while also affecting independent churches and new religious movements. Regulations to protect religious feelings were established in 2012 and are applied in practice according to the Russian Orthodox Church. Religious incitement often arises on ethnic grounds. [310,529] No church tax is levied in Russia.
The Council for Interreligious Dialogue of Russia unites leading representatives from the four most significant confessions in the country, which include Islam, Judaism, and Buddhism. The Council is led by Patriarch Kirill of the Russian Orthodox Church, provides advisory input on relevant legislative processes and decisions, and serves to coordinate the President's work with religions. The Council for Cooperation with Religious Associations under the President of the Russian Federation is located in the Presidential Chancellery.

A religious reference was added to Article 67 of the Russian Constitution in 2020, stating that the Russian state should preserve its thousand-year history and unity, preserve the memory of ancestors, and acknowledge that ancestors transmitted belief in God and ensured continuity in the development of the Russian state.
The Constitution guarantees freedom of worship.
The 1997 Russian Parliament Law on Religion defines the four religions of Russia as the Russian Orthodox Church, Islam, Buddhism, and Judaism, while all other religions must meet a series of requirements for registration and the right to preach.
In 1997, the Russian Orthodox Church became part of Russia's cultural heritage.
The Russian Orthodox Church is semi-state in nature, has a close relationship with the state, and is seen as a symbol of Russia's cultural heritage.

== Future projections ==

By the year 2050, Muslims are projected to form a majority in Russia.

== Historical status and restrictions of the Russian Orthodox Church ==

Peter I abolished the Patriarchate and established the Most Holy Governing Synod at the head of the Church in 1721.
Before 1917, followers of the Russian Orthodox Church were not allowed to convert to another confession or to marry non-Christians, a restriction that applied even if the other confession was Christian.
Only this church was permitted to engage in missionary work and was the only religion allowed to proselytize.
Children from mixed marriages with non-Orthodox individuals were considered Orthodox.
These laws were relaxed only with the Revolution of 1905.

== Soviet persecution and decline of the Russian Orthodox Church ==

The Most Holy Governing Synod was abolished in Soviet Russia in 1918.
The Soviets initially restored the Patriarchate.
Members of the Russian Orthodox Church were mainly suppressed after the Communists took power.
The Russian Orthodox Church was considered a symbol of autocracy.
Between 1918 and 1939, approximately 40,000 Orthodox clergy were executed.
There were 77,800 communities in 1917.
The number of communities was reduced to approximately 3,100 by 1941.

== Post-Soviet revival and state relations ==

A Holy Synod of the Russian Orthodox Church was re-established in 1988.
The Russian Orthodox Church is experiencing a state-sponsored revival that is particularly evident in rural areas [cite: 886].
Many monasteries were founded and many monasteries were rebuilt.
Only 5 to 10 percent of these members are regular churchgoers.
Religious education was reintroduced in schools in 2006.
The Russian Orthodox Church sees itself as a representative of the people's interests and does not stand in opposition to the government [cite: 886].
The state views the church as a guarantor of social cohesion and believes the church ensures societal unity [cite: 886].
Theologian Thomas Bremer assessed the situation in 2008 [cite: 886].
The majority viewed the church as an institution that conveys values and as an institution that strengthens internal social cohesion [cite: 886].
This close relationship fits into historical patterns.
The community is always preferred over individuals and over particular identities [cite: 887].
Traditionally, the state and the church are not truly separated [cite: 887].

The West is perceived as threateningly individualistic and decadent.
Traditional values such as nation, family, and marriage between a man and a woman are affirmed and protected in Russia after the end of the Soviet Union.

== Political influence and contemporary controversies ==

The Russian Orthodox Church provides Putin with a basis for rule and provides a religious basis for the political separation of Russia from the West.
Andreas Heinemann-Grüder assesses the Russian Orthodox Church as part of Putinist power structures in 2023.
The concept of Russki Mir is advocated militantly by the Russian Orthodox Church.
The war against Ukraine is glorified as a form of worship.
There is a symbiotic closeness between the Russian Orthodox Church and Putin's regime.
This closeness shows parallels to clerical-fascist movements of the 1920s and 1930s.
Faith is merely declaimed rather than actually lived.

== Orthodox schisms and dissenting groups ==

Schisms have occurred from Orthodox Christianity throughout history, with the oldest being that of the Old Believers (Altorthodoxen).
The Molokans are a religious direction that emerged from Orthodoxy.
Both religious communities reject wealth, seek a truly biblical community, and strive to live a life of simplicity.
Some serfs founded the Subbotniki community, which bases itself primarily on the Old Testament.
Many of these sects or groups were subjected to arbitrary persecution in the Russian Empire.

== History and status of Roman Catholicism ==

The Roman Catholic Church in Russia was unpopular, and Byzantine influences contributed to this unpopularity.
Peter I allowed the construction of a Roman Catholic church for the first time in 1705.
Catholics were subject to strict state control.
The Bolsheviks focused primarily on controlling the Orthodox Church after the October Revolution.
Catholics were later monitored more strictly.
All structures of the church were dissolved by 1930.
After 1945, there were only 20 communities in the Russian part of the Soviet Union, and these communities were forbidden from establishing connections with each other.
There are approximately 200 Catholic communities in Russia.
The Catholic population in Russia consists of about 400,000 to 800,000 members.
The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception is located in Moscow, was restored, and has been returned to its intended use.
An Apostolic Nuncio has been present in Moscow since 2010.
The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church was banned.

== History and status of Protestantism ==

The Protestant church in Russia was historically widespread primarily among ethnic Germans and concentrated in German colonies.
Other confessions were legalized for Russians and Ukrainians only after the Revolution of 1905.
Russian German Adventists and Baptists conducted missionary activities directed towards the local population before religious laws were relaxed in Russia.
Protestantism experienced a boom in the 1920s that included Baptists, Seventh-day Adventists, and Pentecostals.
The atheist Soviet government forced Baptists, Evangelical Christians, and Pentecostals into centralized structures to better control these groups.
Many evangelical Christians of all denominations were executed and persecuted during the Stalinist era.
It was impossible for the New Apostolic Church (NAC) to missionize in Russia before the fall of the Berlin Wall.

New Apostolic Christians are present in Russia, and the New Apostolic Church has been officially recognized by the state since the early 1990s.
The number of New Apostolic Christians in Russia has been growing steadily since then.

== Jehovah's Witnesses ==

As of April 2017, there were approximately 170,000 active Jehovah's Witnesses in Russia.
Many Jehovah's Witnesses were imprisoned in the Soviet Union.

== History and demographics of Islam ==

Islam has been present in the North Caucasus since the 7th century and is older than the first establishment of the Russian state on current Russian territory.
The Volga Bulgars converted to Islam in the year 922 and passed Islam on to the Tatars in the 13th century.
Tatars, Chechens, and labor migrants from Central Asia are among the ethnic origins of Muslims in Russia.
The indigenous peoples of the Caucasus and Turkic peoples are mostly Sunni believers, and 90% of these Muslims are Sunni [cite: 900].
At the end of the 19th century, 11.1% of the total population in the Russian Empire was of Muslim origin, a proportion that is roughly the same as it was in the Soviet Union.
Kazan, Moscow, Ufa, and Dagestan are centers of Islam in Russia [cite: 901].
The increasing importance of Islam in the Caucasus is linked to a loss of trust in the state, a link that was reported by Nowaja gaseta in 2018 [cite: 901].

== State control and regulation of Islam ==

The state attempts to institutionalize and control Islam through the Russian Muftiate and the Central Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Russia.
Persecution and suppression were chosen by authorities as a means of response following the fight against terrorist Salafist and Wahhabi groups against the state.
These measures have not proven effective in regions with larger Muslim populations and instead led to Islamist radicalization.
The state increasingly chose the means of regional power participation.
Religious organizations are organized regionally within and by their republics, must register in their home republics, and are legally required to report the names of their members.
It is forbidden for religious organizations to expand beyond their assigned geographical limitations.
Religious organizations receive financial support, for example for construction activities.
Foreign support is administratively banned or made difficult, and the state scrutinizes the finances of these organizations very closely.
The state aims to control influences from Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
Missionary activities require a permit and are limited to registered personnel.
Certain Muslim texts are banned, including the text of the Turkish Sufi master Şefik Can.

Mosques that resist inclusion are gradually closed or taken over by umbrella organizations, and those that resist inclusion and self-finance through donations are targeted for closure or takeover.
Umbrella organizations oversee training institutions such as the Russian Islamic University in Ufa.
Friday sermons are prescribed, and their content is predetermined by authorities.
These strategies function better in the Volga Republics than in the North Caucasus.
Moscow reached an agreement with a group of the resistance and appointed this resistance group as loyal leadership.
Ramsan Kadyrow is the current leader of the Caucasus republic, rules Chechnya with an iron hand, and receives significant payments from Moscow for his rule.
Security agencies work closely with the Muftiates.

== Demographics and distribution of Islam ==

Islam has a special extent in Russia, and its followers include approximately 40 ethnic groups.
Several larger minority groups are predominantly Muslim, including Tatars, Chechens, and Bashkirs.
Regions with the largest Muslim populations include the North Caucasus, the Volga region, Ural, and Western Siberia.
Most Muslims live in the Republic of Adygea, Kabardino-Balkaria, the Bashkortostan Republic, the Republic of Dagestan, the Republic of Ingushetia, and the Tatarstan Republic.
Many Muslims live in the Central Federal District, Moscow, and St.
Petersburg.

Muslims make up more than 20 million people in the population of Russia, though there is no accurate statistic on Muslims reported in censuses.
Most Muslims in Russia are Sunni, and the majority of Russian Muslims follow the Sunni branch of Islam.
The Chechen Republic and the Tatarstan Republic are major centers for Sunni Muslims in Russia.
The Republic of Dagestan is located in southern Russia, borders the Republic of Azerbaijan, and is the most important Shia Muslim region in Russia.
People of Azerbaijani descent residing in Russia are counted among the Shia Muslims of that country.

== Judaism in Russia ==

Judaism has many followers in Russia, which is the fourth country in the world by number of Jewish residents.
Jewish people in Russia mainly reside in western Russia, where most are Ashkenazi, while some Bukharian Jews live east of European Russia.
Mountain Jews and Bukharian Jews are classified as Mizrahi.
There are 87 synagogues in Russia, most of which are located in St.
Petersburg and Moscow.
Two rabbis are recognized as the Chief Rabbis of Russia [cite: 907].
Pinchas Goldschmidt is the Chief Rabbi of Moscow [cite: 907].
The invasion of Ukraine began before Pinchas Goldschmidt left Russia in 2022 in protest [cite: 907].
According to Pinchas Goldschmidt, community leaders are being pressured to support the war [cite: 907].
Many Jews have left the country [cite: 907].

== Buddhism and Shamanism ==

The Tibetan form of Buddhism is widespread in Russia, particularly among the Asian peoples of Kalmyks and Tuvinians.
Kalmykia is a republic with a Buddhist majority.
Buddhist communities have recorded membership growth since the political transition in Russia and the successor states of the Soviet Union.
Buddhism has many followers in eastern Russia.
Shamanism is widespread again, particularly among the indigenous population in Siberia and the small peoples of northern Russia.
Altai shamanism is practiced by the Altai people, while Burkhanism is practiced by people in the Altai Republic, a region where Burkhanism is found.
Most residents of Siberia are Christians today, yet they do not view it as a contradiction to practice the rituals of their ancestors.
Nomadic Buryat culture and Paganism in the Far East add to the diversity of Russia.
Turco-Mongolic and Altaic populations living in Siberia and the Far East regions of Russia, including specific regions such as Yakutia and Chukotka, practice Tengrism.

Some residents of eastern Russia practice shamanism, pantheism, and pagan rituals alongside major religions.
Residents of Siberia and Far Eastern regions practice shamanism, pantheism, and pagan rituals alongside their main religions.
Residents of Yakutia practice shamanism, pantheism, and pagan rituals alongside their main religions.
Residents of Chukotka practice shamanism, pantheism, and pagan rituals alongside their main religions.

== Historical development and Orthodox Christianity ==

This connection originally stems from the Orthodox Church, where the community of believers played a much larger role than the individual responsible to God.
The Great Schism led to Orthodox Christianity developing in a completely different way, accompanied by a growing rejection of Catholicism within Orthodox Christianity.
Saint Andrew brought Christianity to Belarus and brought Christianity to Russia.
Russia became a strongly religious country during the spread of Christianity, and culture and power in Russia were based on religion.
Orthodox Russians consider religious objects and artifacts very important, and bowing before icons is characteristic of Russian Orthodox churches.
The Soviet Union was governed under state atheism, and Communism had significant cultural and religious impacts on Russia.
Communists never succeeded in eradicating religions in Russia.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union and the dissolution of communist rule, religion regained a special role in Russia.
Religions experienced a resurgence in Russia after the collapse of the Soviet Union, traditional beliefs reappeared in Russia, and new forms emerged within traditional beliefs in Russia.
Freedom of worship is guaranteed by the Constitution.
The head of the Russian Orthodox Church is Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia, and in reality, cooperation between the government and the Russian Orthodox Church is very close.

The Eastern Orthodox Church recovered a large portion of its followers.
Communism caused Russia to become one of the largest countries in the world with an irreligious population.

== Contemporary religious landscape and statistics ==

The Russian state strongly emphasizes 'traditional values'.
As a result of this emphasis, the Orthodox Church and organized Islam are deliberately drawing closer to each other.
The Central Mosque of Moscow was opened in 2015, an event attended by Vladimir Putin.
The Central Mosque of Moscow can accommodate more than 10,000 people and is considered the largest mosque in Europe.
These religions are defined in the 'Law on Historical Heritage' established by Russia in 1997.
Twelve percent of people said they believe in God.
Religious organizations are privileged.

== Demographics and ethnic distribution ==

Religious affiliation is distributed primarily along ethnic lines, and ethnicity is a main factor in determining religious group membership [cite: 116].
These religions have become part of the identity of different ethnic groups [cite: 116,488].
A person's religion is generally dependent on their ethnicity.
Slavs are generally Orthodox, and Orthodoxy is an ethnically defining religion for Slavic ethnic groups in Russia [cite: 116,1701,1702].
The Russian Orthodox Church belongs to the Slavic population [cite: 1835].
Speakers of Turkic languages are generally Muslims, and people of Turkish descent are Muslim [cite: 116].
Sunni Islam is the traditional religion of most Turkic-speaking peoples, and it plays a similar role for Turkic-speaking peoples as Orthodoxy does for Slavic groups in Russia [cite: 1701,1702].
The Islamic community includes some peoples of Turkish origin, such as Tatars and Bashkirs [cite: 1835].
Most peoples of the North Caucasus, such as Chechens and Ingush, belong to the Islamic community [cite: 1835].
There are also groups of Turkish-speaking people in the country who do not represent Islam, and the Yakuts are an example of a Turkish-speaking group that does not represent Islam [cite: 116].
This religious distribution is especially true in the regions of Adygea, Bashkortostan, Tatarstan, Kabardino-Balkaria, Ingushetia, Dagestan, Karachay-Cherkessia, and Chechnya.
Buddhism is generally practiced by the population of Altai.

== Orthodox Christianity ==

Ethnic Russians identify themselves as Orthodox even when they do not actually practice their religion or believe in its teachings.
Among the movements within the Orthodox Church, Old Believers have been historically significant and were supported by up to 10 percent of the population in the early 20th century.
Most Orthodox believers do not attend church regularly, though 15% of Orthodox Christians claim to be practicing.
According to the 2006 assessment, Russian Orthodox Christians made up between 15% and 20% of the population.
Levada believes that 76% of the population in Russia is Christian, while POF reports 65% and PRC reports 73.6%.
Approximately 95% of Orthodox parishes in Russia are affiliated with the Russian Orthodox Church, and there are smaller Orthodox churches in addition to the main church.
There are approximately 90 million Russian Orthodox believers.
Armenian Orthodox communities exist in Russia.
Mormon communities exist in Russia.

== Judaism ==

Russia has the fourth largest Jewish population in the world, while Israel and the United States have larger Jewish populations than Russia.
The estimated number of Jews in the Soviet Union in 1970 was approximately 2.15 million, making the Soviet Union the third country in the world by number of Jewish citizens, though the United States and Israel had more Jewish citizens than the Soviet Union.
Russian Jews left Russia after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, with most emigrating to the United States, Israel, and Germany.
Approximately 156,000 Jews are officially registered in Russia, while the estimated number of unregistered Jews in Russia is around one million, and there is an unknown number of Jews in Russia who do not know about their Jewish heritage or do not declare it.
Many unregistered Jews hide their identity due to fear of anti-Semitic incidents.
Half of the registered Jewish population in Russia lives in Moscow, and one-fifth of the registered Jewish population in Russia lives in St.
Petersburg.
The Union of Jewish Communities in Russia is one of the largest Jewish organizations in the country, led by Rabbi Berel Lazar as the Chief Rabbi of Russia and by Israeli billionaire Lev Leviev.
The organization has budgets amounting to millions of dollars and funded the construction of synagogues, schools, orphanages, community centers, and other institutions across Russia and the former Soviet Union.

Putin called on Jews suffering from antisemitism in Europe to emigrate to Russia.

According to some sources, 16% to 48% of the population is non-religious, while 12 percent do not practice any religion.

According to the 2006 assessment, atheists or agnostics made up between 63% and 73% of the population.
The Soviet past contributed to this high percentage of atheism, as Soviet texts based on Karl Marx discouraged religion.
Religion is not surveyed in population censuses, and data on religious composition is unreliable.
Traditional religious communities dominate, yet only a small portion of the population is actively religious.

Free directions emerged after the collapse of the Soviet Union, including evangelical Christian activity.
