== Other Religions and Ethnicity ==

Religious affiliation and motivation primarily follow ethnic origin.
Slavic people are typically Orthodox Christians, though there is a strong revival of pre-Christian Slavic religion among ethnic Russians.
Mongolic populations generally practice Buddhism.
There are also many believers in Judaism, which is a traditional religion of the Russian Federation and has been important in Russian history.
Judaism is the smallest religion within Russia compared to other religions in the country, yet the Jewish community in Russia is very large compared to other European countries. [2560,2561,2562,2563]
Recently, the number of Hindus has increased significantly. [2560,2561,2562,2563]

== Legal Status and Persecution ==

A law was adopted in 1997 regarding these religions.
The Supreme Court of Russia ruled against the Jehovah's Witnesses congregation at the request of the Ministry of Justice.
The court held multiple hearings before making the decision and accepted the argument presented by the Ministry of Justice on March 15, 2017.
The court ordered the closure of the national administrative center located in St.
Petersburg and the dissolution of 395 local religious associations of Jehovah's Witnesses in Russia.

== Buddhism and Indigenous Faiths ==

Buddhism is traditionally found in three regions of the Russian Federation, including Irkutsk Oblast, where most Russian Buddhists follow the Tibetan form of Buddhism.
Mongolic peoples are Buddhist.
Shamanistic and animistic practices and beliefs are found in the Russian Far East, where some residents of the Siberia and Far East regions practice shamanism, pantheism, and pagan rituals alongside major religions.
Traditional Mari religion, a polytheistic religion that has been continuously functioning in Europe, is practiced in Mari El.
Taoism is practiced in Russia, and other religions include Mormons.

== Historical Context and Soviet Era ==

The period of socialism lasted 72 years and had a significant impact on the level of religiosity [cite: 2863].
During this period, religion was combated [cite: 2863].
The Soviet Union proclaimed the elimination of religion as an ideological goal and aimed to replace religion with universal atheism [cite: 3200,3201,3202].
Every form of religion was suppressed during the communist regime, and many residents became atheists.
The communist government ridiculed religions and believers while promoting atheism in schools [cite: 3131].
Ecclesiastical properties were confiscated, often based on accusations of illegal accumulation of wealth.

== Legal Framework and Ethnicity ==

The Russian Constitution of 1993 establishes Russia as a secular state and guarantees freedom of conscience and religion.
A Russian's religion often aligns with their ethnicity, and religious induction occurs primarily along ethnic lines [cite: 3046].
Questions regarding religious affiliation are not asked during population censuses in Russia [cite: 2863].

== Constitutional framework and legal status ==

Judaism and ethnic religions are recognized as traditional religions of Russia.
The Constitution guarantees freedom of conscience and freedom of religion.
Individuals have the right to profess any religion individually or jointly with others, not to profess any religion, freely choose religious and other beliefs, hold religious and other beliefs, spread religious and other beliefs, and act in accordance with their beliefs.
Liability applies to illegal obstruction of the activities of religious organizations and to the performance of religious rites.

== Soviet-era repression and state atheism ==

State atheism in the Soviet Union was based on Marxist–Leninist ideology and was known as gosateizm.
State atheism constantly supported the control, suppression, and elimination of religion.
The state expropriated all church properties, including the churches themselves, within approximately one year of the revolution.
Between 1922 and 1926, 28 Russian Orthodox bishops and more than 1,200 priests were killed.
A study mentioned that religious repression was widespread during the communist regime.
The Russian Orthodox Church was the state church and state religion of Russia before the revolution.
The church was once heavily repressed.

== Post-Soviet religious revival and demographics ==

Religious renewal occurred in Russia after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
There is currently no official census of religions in Russia, and estimates of religious affiliation in Russia are based solely on surveys.
In June 2013, the Public Opinion Foundation estimated that 65% of the population was Christian, and later that year, an estimate suggested that 76% of Russians were Christians.
The VCIOM survey from 2010 estimated approximately 77% of the population were Christians, 2011 estimates stated that 73.6% of Russians were Christians, and the Ipsos MORI survey from 2011 estimated 69% of the population were Christians.
A recent study found that 71% of the Russian population identified as Orthodox in 2015, 15% of the Russian population was unaffiliated with any religion in 2015, 10% of the Russian population identified as Muslim in 2015, 2% of the Russian population identified as other Christians in 2015, and 1% of the Russian population belonged to other religions in 2015.
The unaffiliated category includes atheists, agnostics, and those who describe their religion as 'none'.
One percent of unaffiliated religious people were agnostics, and 10% of unaffiliated religious people fell into another unspecified category.
In 1991, 37% of Russia's population identified as Orthodox.
Orthodox Church membership increased substantially after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, and approximately 71% of the Russian population identified as Orthodox in 2015.
Zero point five percent of Russians were Tibetan Buddhists.

The proportion of religiously unaffiliated people was 61% in 1991 and 18% in 2008.
The proportion of non-religious people in Russia is between 16% and 48%.
Recent studies indicate that the percentage of atheists has decreased significantly over the decades.
Russia is the country with the largest Orthodox population in the world.
According to a VCIOM survey conducted between August and September 2007, half of Russia's citizens considered themselves believers.
Among those who consider themselves believers, 10% regularly attend church and observe all rituals and ceremonies, while 43% only attend church on holidays and do not observe all rituals and ceremonies.
Surveys from 2007 to 2008 were conducted, and 66% to 67% of respondents identified themselves as Orthodox Christians.
The number of Eastern Orthodox Christians has increased in recent years.
The percentage of Russian citizens who consider themselves Orthodox increased during 2009, rising from 70% to 75%.
A survey conducted in January 2010 found that one-third of the respondents admitted the existence of God, while 31% of the respondents admitted the existence of God.
The respondents showed little interest in church life, committed atheists make up only 6% of the surveyed respondents, and 8% of the respondents did not consider the topic of their relationship with religion.
A survey took place on August 25–26, 2007.

There have been many atheists in the country since the Soviet era.
12% of respondents do not believe in any religion, yet 12% of respondents believe in God despite not believing in any religion.
Approximately 100 million citizens identify themselves as Russian Orthodox Christians.

== The Russian Orthodox Church ==

An estimated 95% of registered Orthodox parishes belong to the Russian Orthodox Church, and 95% of registered churches are under the protection of the Russian Orthodox Church [521,4228].
The majority of Orthodox believers do not attend church regularly.
Patriarch Kirill of Moscow is the head of the Russian Orthodox Church [3211,3212].
The church emerged from the Soviet collapse as one of the most respected institutions [3211,3212].
Patriarch Kirill led the faithful directly into an alliance with the state [3211,3212].
Mark Woods provides concrete examples of how the Church under Patriarch Kirill supported the expansion of Russian power in Crimea and eastern Ukraine [3211,3212].
The Church's policy supports the Kremlin's appeal to social conservatives.
The Russian Orthodox Church is a fierce enemy of homosexuality.
The Russian Orthodox Church opposes any attempt to prioritize individual rights over family, community, or national privileges.
The Russian Orthodox Church helps project the image of Russia as a natural ally for those longing for an illiberal world.
This illiberal world is described as being free from the waves of globalization, multiculturalism, women's rights, and homosexual rights.

Saint Mary, Saint Nicholas, Saint Andrew, Saint George, Saint Alexander Nevsky, and Saint Seraphim of Sarov are patron saints of Russia.
Kazan presents a mix of Russian Christian culture and Tatar Muslim culture.
The Orthodox Church contributed to spreading Byzantine culture to Slavic peoples.

A large portion of people belonging to the Orthodox faith do not regularly attend church.

== Islam in Russia ==

There are approximately 20 million Muslims in Russia.
These groups include Chechens, Ingush, and Circassians.
These Turkic peoples include Tatars and Bashkirs.
Most of the Muslim population lives in the North Caucasus region.
There are approximately 3 to 4 million temporary Muslim migrants in Russia.
These migrants come from former Soviet Union states.
The Pilgrimage Mission in Russia stated that 12,000 people applied to go on pilgrimage.

== Buddhism and other traditional religions ==

Buddhism is traditional in three regions of the Russian Federation and is widespread in Russia.
Judaism is widespread in Russia.
Other religions are widespread in Russia.

== Minority Christian denominations ==

Gregorian Armenians, Catholicism, the Armenian Gregorian Church, and various Protestant churches are among the smaller Christian denominations in Russia.

== New religious movements and Paganism ==

Rodnoveria is a reconstructionist form of Slavic paganism.
Hinduism emerged as one of these new religious movements.

== Church-state relations and politics ==

Vladimir Putin collaborated closely with the Russian Orthodox Church in cultural and social matters.
Patriarch Kirill supported Vladimir Putin's candidacy in 2012.
More than half of Russian citizens (55%) believe the future president should prioritize the Russian Orthodox Church among all religious organizations.
Respondents believe the future president should show a respectful attitude towards the Russian Orthodox Church, help the Russian Orthodox Church, and attend festive church services.
45% of respondents believe the future president does not need to be personally religious.
A public debate has been ongoing since the late 1990s concerning the permissibility of introducing 'Fundamentals of Orthodox Culture' into state school curricula.
The subject was introduced on April 1, 2010, in an experimental mode in 19 regions.

== Buddhism ==

Buddhism is a major religion in Russia.
Mongols are generally Buddhist.
There is a Buddhist-influenced culture among the nomadic Buryat and Kalmyk tribes.

== Other Religions and Beliefs ==

Some inhabitants of Siberia and the Russian Far East practice Shamanist, Panteist, and Pagan rituals, which are specifically practiced in the Sakha Republic and Chukotka [cite: 116].
A Shamanist culture exists in the far north and Siberia, while a Finno-Ugric culture is present in the northwest region of Russia and the Volga region.
Judaism is prevalent in the Jewish Autonomous Oblast, and Catholicism, Protestantism, and Judaism are major religions.
Less than 1% of respondents identified as Buddhist, Catholic, Protestant, or Jewish believers [cite: 1696].

== Legal Framework and History ==

The Russian Constitution guarantees religious freedom and allows individuals in Russia to be free to choose their own faith.
The Soviet era involved strict suppression.
The 2007 International Religious Freedom Report was published by the US Department of State.

== Religion in Chechnya ==

Kadyrov uses funds to finance Islamic structures within and outside the republic, implements Sharia regulations that deviate from Russian laws, and permits polygamy and morality police-style control under these regulations.[900,903,904,905] Kadyrov's Islam significantly impacts the lives of Chechnya's residents, is oriented towards Sufism which represents the traditional Islam of the region, and combats Salafism and Wahabism.[900,903,904,905] Salafist influences and connections to the Gulf region have flowed into the ideology and politics developed by Kadyrov, leading to discussions of a type of 'state Salafism'.
Kadyrov adopted traditional concepts of clan and family ties, embraced Chechen nationalism, linked Chechen nationalism with Russian nationalism, and combined these elements with a puritanical conception of Islam that originated from the Gulf region.

Russia has an adult literacy rate of 100%, and has compulsory education for a duration of 11 years, exclusively for children aged 7 to 17–18.
It grants free education to its citizens by constitution.
The Ministry of Education of Russia is responsible for primary and secondary education, as well as vocational education; while the Ministry of Education and Science of Russia is responsible for science and higher education.
Regional authorities regulate education within their jurisdictions within the prevailing framework of federal laws.
Russia is among the world's most educated countries, and has the sixth-highest proportion of tertiary-level graduates in terms of percentage of population, at 62.1%.
It spent roughly 4.7% of its GDP on education in 2018.

Russia's pre-school education system is highly developed and optional, some four-fifths of children aged 3 to 6 attend day nurseries or kindergartens.
Primary school is compulsory for eleven years, starting from age 6 to 7, and leads to a basic general education certificate.
An additional two or three years of schooling are required for the secondary-level certificate, and some seven-eighths of Russians continue their education past this level.

Admission to an institute of higher education is selective and highly competitive: first-degree courses usually take five years.
The oldest and largest universities in Russia are Moscow State University and Saint Petersburg State University.
There are ten highly prestigious federal universities across the country.
Russia was the world's fifth-leading destination for international students in 2019, hosting roughly 300 thousand.

== Structure and Stages of General Education ==

The Russian education system is divided into four sections, one of which is general school education [cite: 1338].
General school education is divided into sections that are the basic level, intermediate level, and upper level.
The education system is divided into three stages [cite: 810].
The first stage is basic education and lasts 4 years [cite: 810].
The second stage is secondary education and lasts 5 years [cite: 810].
The third stage is higher secondary education and lasts 2 years [cite: 810].
School entry takes place at the age of seven.
The primary level of the elementary or initial school lasts four years.
Children who start school at age seven complete this primary level within three years.
Students transition from the third year to the fifth school year.
A mandatory secondary school level follows.
This secondary school level lasts six years.
This acquisition typically occurs at the end of the ninth grade.
This acquisition typically occurs after reaching the mandatory school age of 15 years.
This qualification allows access to the upper secondary level.
The upper secondary level lasts two years.
Middle school education lasts for 2 years.
After middle school, students choose between high school or vocational schools.

After completing compulsory education, one can pursue vocational training instead of upper secondary school.
The completion of the upper secondary level is achieved through a certificate of complete secondary education.

== Vocational and Technical Training ==

The goal of vocational schools is to train students for professional work.
Vocational training can be undertaken at a middle-level technical college (Berufsschule) or at a technical institute (Technikum).
These institutions are available throughout the entire permeable vocational education system and allow for the acquisition of complete secondary education.
This educational path is a dual training program in which vocational-specific subjects and general education subjects are taught, with the content of the general education subjects oriented towards vocational training.

== Higher Education System and Degrees ==

The higher education system in Russia is diverse, featuring various colleges and academies in addition to classical universities.
Russia has a large number of universities that focus on technical fields.
Until 1991, the diploma was the only degree available, but the Bachelor degree is now a possible qualification alongside the Diploma.
Bakalavr is a level of higher education with a duration of 4 years, where the first two years of the program serve as a general basic study.
Many faculties in Russian universities offer a two-level master's training program, the duration of this stage is 2 years, and the graduates obtain a 'Magister' degree.
The education is specialized in the 'Mütəxəssis' field, and the duration of the education is 3 years.
A candidate defends a scientific research work at the dissertation council, the degree is confirmed by the RF AAK (Academy of Sciences of the Russian Federation), and after these steps, the degree of 'Candidate of Sciences' is awarded.
A doctoral degree is awarded after defending a dissertation at the dissertation council, and the degree awarded is Doctor of Sciences.
This division was introduced around 2009.

The Master degree is a possible qualification alongside the Diploma.
Four categories of higher education institutions can be established, with universities as the highest category and institutes (colleges) as the third category.
The State University of Kazan and the State Technical University of Novosibirsk are among the most famous Russian universities.

== School Calendar, Grading, and Daily Routine ==

The academic year in Russia begins on September 1st, and the start date for the academic and school years is uniform across all of Russia.
The academic year begins in September and ends in June, while the school year runs from September to May.
School starts at 8:30, and June is the exam month when students in the ninth and eleventh grades take various exams.
A grade of one indicates insufficient performance, and a grade of five indicates excellent performance.

== Admission, Age, and Enrollment ==

Students who pass the entrance exams properly are eligible for free education.
An early school entry age of six years exists, and this early entry is recommended for approximately 35% of children on average based on a psychological assessment.

== Funding, Budget, and Statistics ==

Government spending on the education sector in 2004 reached 3.6% of GDP and accounted for 13% of the state budget.
In 2005, the share of government spending from GDP for education was 3.8%.
The state allocated 4% of the central budget to education around 2017.
There were 1,061 universities and colleges in Russia in 2005, of which 413 were private colleges.
The government distributes funding to state educational institutions based on a fixed quota amount and the number of students to ensure that all eligible students receive an education place.
According to the 2002 census, 54% of the Russian workforce has a higher education degree, which is the highest rate of higher education attainment in the world.

== Student Support and Financial Aid ==

Students with excellent results receive a monthly scholarship and studying is free for high-achieving students.
Studying is fee-based for an increasingly large portion of the population, a change that occurred after 1992.
Students receive a small stipend and free accommodation.

== International Performance and Assessments ==

Russian students ranked 23rd out of 72 countries in mathematics, 32nd in science, and 26th in reading comprehension on the 2015 PISA ranking.
The PIRLS study was conducted in 2006 and measured reading comprehension skills of fourth graders.

== Curriculum, Ideology, and Reform ==

English is the foreign language learned by Russians.
Education in Russia has traditionally focused heavily on science and technology.
During the Soviet era, education was highly centralized and used as a means to spread socialism, with Marxist-Leninist theory serving as a major component of the curriculum in every school.
There is a trend to change the school curriculum to prepare students to adapt to new economic trends and to meet the desires and interests of different Russian nationalities.
The organization of mega-events is justified by the development of youth work.

== Legal Framework and Governance ==

Article 43 of the Russian Constitution guarantees this right, which is also guaranteed by Federal Law No.
273-FZ, the Federal Law on Education in the Russian Federation.

== Alternative Education and Private Sector ==

The establishment of private schools and private universities in Russia is permitted, and there is an opportunity to establish private schools.
Public education has been free as in the past.
Parents can request home schooling for their child if the child's knowledge level matches the school curriculum, and this knowledge level is assessed twice a year.
One section is postgraduate education.

== Structure and Compulsory Education ==

The Russian education system has been in place since the Soviet era.
Since 1990, an 11-year compulsory school system has been implemented in Russia [1669,1981,1985,2564].
This duration has been in effect since 1990 [1669,1985].
The education system in Russia includes middle school, which starts at age 7 and lasts 5 years.
Elementary school lasts 3 to 4 years.
The education system in Russia includes gimnasium, a type of middle school with a broader curriculum.
There are specialized secondary schools that prioritize specific subjects, including language, mathematics, and physics.

== Examinations and Curriculum ==

An exam called the OGE (Main State Exam) is required upon completion of compulsory education.
Students choose the subjects in which they want to be examined, though Russian and Mathematics are not subjects that students can choose for examination because they are mandatory examination subjects.
Students must choose a post-OGE study path if they wish to continue their education, with an individual school study path lasting two years and a high school (liceo) lasting three years.
Students must pass the Unified State Exam (EGE) upon completing secondary education, which includes two mandatory subjects and elective subjects.
Russian language and Mathematics are mandatory subjects in the EGE.
A unified national history textbook was introduced for students aged 16 to 18 and will be used starting from the new school terms in August and September 2023.
Korean is a newly established regular subject as a second foreign language, and plans are underway to add Asian languages such as Chinese and Japanese as second foreign language subjects.

== Funding and Budget ==

Funding for educational institutions is provided entirely from state or regional budgets, which are the sole sources of funding for education.
In 2004, national spending on education reached 3.6% of GDP and 13% of the national budget.[547,1986] In 2004, state spending on education was equal to 3.6% of GDP and corresponded to 13% of the consolidated state budget.
The government provides funds to cover tuition fees.[1668,1669,1985]

== Higher Education Institutions ==

Higher education institutions in Russia include institutes, universities, and academies.
In 1994, there were more than 40 state universities and 80 specialized universities in technical, medical, teacher training, and agricultural fields that were previously only at the institute level.
There were also more than 30 private universities.
Saint Petersburg State University is the second largest and second oldest university in Russia.
Moscow State University was founded in 1755 by Empress Elizabeth of Russia through a decree issued on January 25, 1755, which accepted the requests of Ivan Shuvalov and Mikhail Lomonosov, and the university is named after Mikhail Lomonosov.
Far Eastern Federal University and Peoples' Friendship University of Russia are major universities in Russia.

== Federal Universities Program ==

In the 2000s, the government launched a program to establish federal universities with the goal of achieving equality in higher education and research institutions across various regions and creating institutions on a scale comparable to Russian regions.
Most of these federal universities were formed by merging existing regional universities with research institutions and received special funding.
The new federal universities include the Higher School of Economics, Southern Federal University, Siberian Federal University, Kazan Volga Federal University, North-Eastern Federal University, and Far Eastern Federal University.

In the 2000s, the Russian government launched a program to create federal universities of similar size across the country with the goal of establishing higher education and research institutions of comparable scale throughout Russia.
Most existing large universities and research institutes were incorporated into this program, which provided special funding to these institutions.

== Higher Education Systems and Degrees ==

Some higher education institutions follow the Western system and have two degree levels: BA and MA.
A BA degree takes 4 years to complete, while an MA degree takes 2 years to complete.
Most of these institutions still follow the old system, which does not award BA or MA degrees.
Graduates in the old system receive qualifications instead of degrees, with examples including school teachers, translators, and engineers.
The duration of study under the old system is 5 to 6 years.

== Access, Enrollment, and Literacy ==

The literacy rate is average among OECD countries.
Between 2003 and 2008, the gross enrollment rate was 96% and the net enrollment rate was 91%.
During the same period, 21% of enrolled children used internet access, the secondary school enrollment rate for men was 85%, and the secondary school enrollment rate for women was 83%.
Russia has the best university graduation rate in the world, which is 54%.

== Tuition, Stipends, and Commercialization ==

Russia offers free university education, though there are exceptions for students who register by paying full fees. [1669,1981,1985,2564] Admission to subsidized higher education is highly competitive. [542,1981,1982] Many state institutions have opened positions funded by external sources, and the number of these externally funded positions has been increasing. [1669,1670] Many private higher education institutions have emerged to meet this demand. Many state universities have become commercial in recent years, and many institutions are beginning to offer paid positions. [1669,1985] The government allocates funds to pay university tuition fees and school fees based on quotas or the number of students per institution. [1987,1988] Students attending higher education institutions receive a small stipend and get free accommodation if they come from outside the city. [1987,1988]

== Quality and Specialization ==

Russia has a science and technology-oriented education system.
Medical, mathematics, natural sciences, and aviation education in Russia are generally of good quality.

== Structure and Governance ==

The country has used an eleven-year school formation system since 1990.
Receiving basic general education is mandatory according to the Constitution of Russia, which mandates that parents or those replacing them must ensure children receive basic general education.
Parents are obligated to ensure their children receive basic general education, and persons replacing parents are obligated to ensure their charges receive basic general education.
The second level of general education is basic general education, and the third level of general education is secondary (complete) general education.
Vocational education is divided into levels, including secondary vocational education and higher vocational education.
Vocational education includes postgraduate education and additional professional education.
Educational institutions for professional training must undergo periodic assessment, licensing, and state accreditation.
Educational institutions without state accreditation cannot issue official state education documents, and educational institutions without a license are not allowed to conduct educational activities.

== Enrollment and Statistics ==

Russia has the highest number of college graduates in the world and a larger absolute number of university graduates than other European countries [cite: 1979,2680,2681,3071].
No other country in Eurasia has a higher proportion of university graduates [cite: 1979].
Russia belongs to the countries with the lowest illiteracy rate in the world [cite: 2804].
There are currently 1,304 higher education institutions in Russia, of which 685 are state schools and 619 are private schools [cite: 2972].
There are currently 48 state universities in Russia [cite: 2972].
In 2003-2004, 5,228,700 students attended state schools and 718,800 students attended private schools [cite: 2972].
There are 31.5 million people studying in Russia [cite: 3733,3734].
In the 2005/06 academic year, there were 60,500 general education institutions in Russia, a number that was 46,794 according to 2015 data [cite: 3735,3736].
More than 15.6 million students were enrolled in these institutions [cite: 3737,3738].
There are approximately 2,000 special schools designed for children with limited health and development capabilities that educate approximately 300,000 students.
There are approximately 3,500 institutions of initial vocational education in which more than 1.5 million people are enrolled.

Approximately 300 educational institutions attached to penal labor institutions belonging to the Ministry of Justice were established.
The number of students has been decreasing in recent years due to a demographic decline.
The country has approximately 7 million students, 3.5 million of whom are enrolled in day programs.
There are 1,068 universities, 413 of which are non-governmental.
There are 2,900 secondary vocational education institutions, 217 of which are non-state funded, with approximately 2.5 million people enrolled in these institutions.

== Funding and Costs ==

Tuition fee coverage is limited to a specific quota, a small stipend is paid to students for a certain number per state institution, and free accommodation is provided to students.
Many state institutions began introducing paid study places.
Educational institutions are unable to provide appropriate teacher salaries, unable to provide scholarships for students, and unable to maintain their buildings.
The first phase of higher education at the university level is free, though there are reservations regarding the free status of the first phase of higher education.
A significant portion of students are enrolled to pay full fees, and state institutions have started opening commercial positions in recent years.
In 2004, state spending on education reached 3.6% of the Russian GDP and 13% of the State budget.
The government allocates funds to pay tuition fees, which are based on an established quota and also on the number of students at each state institution.
Students in higher education institutions receive a small salary and free accommodation.
Secondary education in state secondary schools is free, and university education is free.

There are some exceptions to the free university education, a substantial portion of students are enrolled in fully subsidized studies, and many state institutions have started offering paid places as well.[1669,1985] The number of free (budget) places in higher education institutions in Russia increased from 2010 to 2017, with the percentage of free places in Russian higher education being 43.43% in 2010 and 49.91% in 2017.[3747,3748,3749] The cost of paid tuition in Russia increased significantly between 2010 and 2017, an increase that contradicts the global trend of decreasing fees in higher education, and some researchers believe the rise in tuition costs reduces the overall accessibility of higher education in Russia.[3747,3748,3749] In 2004, the education budget was 3.6% of GDP and 13% of the consolidated state budget.[547,1986] The funds are intended to pay tuition fees within a set quota or student count.[1987,4234]

== Higher Education Reform ==

In the 2000s, the Russian government launched a program to establish 'federal universities' with the goal of creating higher education and research institutions on a comparable scale in multiple regions of the Russian Federation and developing universities and education across the entire country.
Most of these federal universities were created by merging existing regional universities with large research institutes, though there are new institutions among these, such as the Volga Federal University, and these merged institutions received special funding.
A mass transition to a two-level higher education system consisting of bachelor's and master's degrees occurred in 2008, a transition associated with the Bologna Process which aims to increase mobility and transparency between educational systems in different countries.
While Russian universities and colleges have been part of the Bologna Process since the turn of the millennium, the single-level system involving obtaining the qualification of 'specialist' was retained and is primarily used for medical education and defense and security needs.

== Curriculum and Emphasis ==

The Russian government strongly emphasized the promotion of natural sciences and technology in education, and Russia places a strong emphasis on science and technology in education.
New schools and universities were established and organized in a modern European style.
Education focused on socially desirable fields, and Russia ranks first in the world in the number of citizens receiving engineering education.
General education includes special (correctional) education for children and additional education for children.
Sexual education is absent in Russia.

== International Rankings and Performance ==

Moscow State University had the highest ranking among Russian institutions in the 2018 QS World University Rankings and was ranked 95th in the world.
Russia ranked 33rd in the national higher education systems ranking conducted by Universitas 21.
Russia ranked 32nd in the world according to the Education Index, which is a combined indicator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).
Russia ranked 34th in the Global Index of Cognitive Skills and Educational Attainment.
Many private higher education institutions emerged, admission to state-funded higher education institutions in Russia is extremely competitive, and there are some exceptions to the free university education.
School education has lasted for 11 years since 1990.

== Legal framework and administration ==

A law titled 'On Education in the Russian Federation' was adopted in December 2012.
The Russian education administrative system implements a centralized administration.
The Federal Department of General and Vocational Education was established in 1996 and is the highest-level administrative body in Russia.
The Ministry of Education and Science designs and approves standard curricula, approves teaching aids, and approves methodological manuals.
The Federal Ministry of Education and Science participates in investigations involving educational, scientific, and cultural organizations and the International Bureau of Education.
This cooperation involves estimating the number of students in preschool education, primary education, and secondary education.
The State Department of Education directly manages all subordinate educational institutions at various levels and guarantees citizens' legal right to education.

== Historical development and structure ==

Before 1990, the duration of study in the Soviet Union was 10 years, and in late 1990, the duration of study was officially changed to 11 years.
Russia currently has nearly 2,000 universities and nearly 2,000 academies.
Investment in education has increased, while the quality of education has decreased.
Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that the current national exam system may only select students who memorize information and does not encourage scientific thinking among students.

== Funding and expenditure ==

In 2004, national spending on education in Russia accounted for 3.6% of GDP and 13% of the total state budget.[547,4468]
In the United States, national spending on education accounted for 7.2% of GDP in 2004.[547,4468]
Russia's national spending on education as a percentage of GDP was lower than Vietnam's in 2004, when Vietnam's spending accounted for 8.3% of GDP.[547,4468]
The government allocated funds to pay tuition fees based on a predetermined quota determined by the number of students per state school.

== Higher education access and support ==

Secondary education in state schools was free, and initial tertiary education at the university level was also free. [1669,1670]
A significant portion of admitted students were fully sponsored by the state. [1669,1670]
The system provides access to higher education for capable students and does not limit access only to those who can pay.
Students received a small scholarship and were provided with free housing.
Free accommodation is provided to students in higher education institutions, and scholarships are provided to students in higher education institutions. [1987,4234]

== Federal university program ==

In the 2000s, the Russian government initiated a program to create federal universities with the goal of establishing higher education and research institutions on a comparable scale in Russia's regions.
The government primarily achieved this by merging existing large regional universities and research institutes and provided special funding for the program.
The new institutions include the Southern Federal University, the Siberian Federal University, the Kazan Volga Federal University, the North-Eastern Federal University, and the Far Eastern Federal University.

== Private sector and staffing ==

Many state institutions began opening commercial courses in recent years, and private higher education institutions have emerged to serve the high technology, new technology, and economy sectors.
There are more than 3 million teachers and research staff in Russian universities, nearly 45% of whom are professors or associate professors.
Moscow State University is currently rated as the best university in Russia.

Russia, by constitution, guarantees free, universal health care for all Russian citizens, through a compulsory state health insurance program.
The Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation oversees the Russian public healthcare system, and the sector employs more than two million people.
Federal regions also have their own departments of health that oversee local administration.
A separate private health insurance plan is needed to access private healthcare in Russia.

Russia spent 5.65% of its GDP on healthcare in 2019.
Its healthcare expenditure is notably lower than other developed nations.
Russia has one of the world's most female-biased sex ratios, with 0.859 males to every female, due to its high male mortality rate.
In 2021, the overall life expectancy in Russia at birth was 70.06 years (65.51 years for males and 74.51 years for females), and it had a very low infant mortality rate (5 per 1,000 live births).

The principal cause of death in Russia are cardiovascular diseases.
Obesity is a prevalent health issue in Russia; most adults are overweight or obese.
However, Russia's historically high alcohol consumption rate is the biggest health issue in the country, as it remains one of the world's highest, despite a stark decrease in the last decade.
Smoking is another health issue in the country.
The country's high suicide rate, although on the decline, remains a significant social issue.

== Healthcare System Structure and Funding ==

Article 41 of the Constitution of Russia guarantees citizens the right to free basic medical care, a principle that is partially the cause of Russia having a relatively high number of doctors and hospitals per capita compared to other countries internationally.
Healthcare was free in the former Soviet Union, and free healthcare is partially limited due to the propiska system.
Russia has more healthcare workers than almost any other country in the world, and Russia has more doctors, hospitals, and healthcare workers than almost any other country.
A health insurance program to fund healthcare began in Russia in 1993.
The healthcare sector in Russia is organized in a decentralized manner, with this responsibility operating at the federal level.
Specific medical services are the responsibility of federal subjects and municipalities, which cover approximately two-thirds of total budget expenditures.
The Russian healthcare system is financed by a mix of budget funds and social insurance funds.
In 2006, the share of government spending from GDP for health was 5.3%.
Admission restrictions for medical devices from abroad were implemented starting in 2015.
There are 7,000 hospitals in the country, and one-third of these hospitals require urgent renovation.
State funds are being invested in the establishment of new clinics and in the modernization of existing clinics.

== Historical Origins and Cultural Identity ==

This event marked the beginning of the blending of Slavic and Byzantine cultures, and these blended cultures formed the characteristics of Russian culture for the following millennium.
Russian culture consists of a European high culture and an indigenous Russian folk culture.
Russia sometimes viewed itself as the radical Other of the West, and Russian culture followed a different development compared to Western European culture over a long period.
This different development was caused by Russia's location on the periphery of Western cultural development.
Russian state and legal concepts originated from Byzantine Caesaropapism, while Western Roman legal tradition differed from the Byzantine model, and these differences contributed to the distinction between Russian culture and Western European culture.
The development of nation-states in the rest of Europe differed from that in Russia.
Russia underwent a transition to a multi-ethnic empire starting in 1550, and this transition influenced Russia's cultural development.
Russian culture is still shaped by temporally distinct developmental phases that relate to Western European culture.
Russia's geographic peripheral location explains its cultural development patterns, and Russia's simultaneous expansion eastward contributes to its cultural evolution.
These factors created a varied pace of evolution in Russia, and this evolutionary process involved alternating phases of slowed catch-up and accelerated development.
Russia can be considered a translation culture.

This process is not based on passive imitation but is driven by the need to catch up and surpass others.
It creates productive interactions by modeling one's own culture after the imitated foreign culture, which generates something new.
Traditional Russian folk culture continued among the people while a westernized high culture existed among the upper class.
These two cultures coexisted side by side until 1914.
This cultural synthesis defined Russian culture for the next millennium.

The sarafan is a sign of Russian culture and a traditional garment [cite: 448].

The creation of communal farms contributed to the popularity of the sarafan, and in the 20th century, the sarafan became a popular garment.
The kokoshnik was first used in the 16th century by Russian Slavs and covers all of the hair.

== Historical Origins and Influences ==

Byzantine and Slavic culture defined Russian culture until today, and a completely independent Russian culture was formed through this influence.
The formation of Russian culture was closely related to the conquest of a vast territory inhabited by many ethnic groups and peoples, establishing Orthodoxy as a unique branch of Christianity based on spirituality and traditional customs, avoiding isolation from Western European civilization processes even if temporary, and subordinating individual interests to state interests.
Ancient Rus' culture is part of Russian culture and drew nourishment from its national source, while Russian culture found harmony with the cultures of Byzantium, Bulgaria, Serbia, Armenia, and Georgia.
The state blended Byzantine and Slavic cultures to create Russian culture, which was formed from ancient European culture and Russian folk culture.
Russia considered itself a different radical Western culture during a certain period, with the country's geographical location, the origins of the state, and the Great Schism of 1054 serving as factors.
After the Schism, Orthodox Russia drifted away from Catholic Western Europe.

Byzantine culture was adapted into a Slavic form that dominated Russia for nearly seven hundred years.
A native script, art, and architecture emerged after the baptism.
The Russian-Orthodox culture experienced stagnation from the 15th century due to the fall of Constantinople, after which Russia lost an important partner.
The relatively late arrival of secularization in Russian culture is considered the main difference between Western European and Russian culture, as secular culture exerted influence in Western culture since the 14th century when the Renaissance occurred, whereas secular culture did not exert influence in Russia until the 17th century.
Russian culture developed under the strong influence of Southern Slavs, and this cultural synthesis ultimately defined Russian culture.
