One of these traditions is bathing in a banya.

== National Symbols and Emblems ==

Russia has designated two types of flowers as its national flowers, which are sunflowers and chamomile, a designation inherited from the Soviet era.
The national gemstone of Russia is garnet, which has its origins in the Imperial era when rhodolite garnets were mined from the Ural Mountains and established as a national symbol.
The national colors of Russia are white, blue, and red.
The Russian flag dates from the end of the Tsardom of Russia period and was widely used during the time of the Russian Empire.
The national anthem of Russia has the same melody as the Soviet anthem but different lyrics.

== Social Customs and Etiquette ==

French kisses and hugs used as greetings are considered social etiquette similar to handshakes in Russia and are not considered problematic in Russia.
Russians have a tradition of bathing that includes washing in hot steam baths somewhat similar to saunas.

== Folk Art and Craftsmanship ==

Russian folk art is an important aspect of Russian popular culture.
Matryoshka dolls, Dymkovo toys, Khokhloma style, Gzhel ceramics, and Palekh miniatures are forms of Russian folk art.
Craftsmanship is an important aspect of Russian folk culture.

== Cultural Evolution and Ideology ==

The 19th century is widely recognized as the peak of Russian culture, during which most Russian cultural carriers were oriented towards Western Europe and ancient Russian culture was rediscovered and entered the arts.
Around 1900, Russia joined the European avant-garde [cite: 2636].
Most major artists and philosophers left Russia after the Russian Revolution, and a new generation of artists emerged to create art suitable for communist-socialist states.
During the Soviet period, traditional cultural forms were significantly abandoned, and new communist content was attempted to replace traditional cultural forms.
The disappearance of European culture in the country was a consequence, and the disappearance of folk culture in the country was a consequence.
Russia experienced a major cultural crisis in the late 20th century, at which time artists in the country had to reorient themselves, no longer needed to adhere to state regulations, and had to compete with popular culture.
Some Russian ideologs and philosophers believe Russia is not part of the West, not part of Asia, and is a mixture of both West and Asia [cite: 2973], a view that Samuel Huntington classifies as an Orthodox civilization [cite: 2973].

Since the 1980s, there has been a return to old Russian traditions.
At the same time, Soviet cultural heritage is not being rejected.

== Contemporary Figures ==

Eduard Limonov is still alive.

== Definitions and historical origins ==

Russian culture refers to the culture of the Russian ethnic group and includes the cultures of other ethnic groups living in the Russian Empire, the former Soviet Union, and modern Russia.
Russia's cultural borders have been historically variable and uncertain.
According to the United Nations, Russia belongs to countries with the richest cultural heritage.
Russian culture began as a synthesis of Byzantine and Slavic cultures for the next millennium, and this cultural fusion formed the basis of modern Russian culture.
Eastern Orthodox Christianity later had a significant role and influence on the country's art, architecture, and culture.

== Symbols and mottos ==

The imperial motto is "God is with us" and the Soviet motto is "Proletarians of all countries, unite!".
The complete Soviet hammer and sickle emblem still appears in many public places, and Soviet symbols are often found on military equipment and at war memorials.

== Traditional clothing ==

Traditional Russian clothing for men includes the kaftan, kosovorotka, and ushanka.
Traditional Russian clothing for women includes the sarafan and kokoshnik.
Traditional Russian footwear includes lapti and valenki.
Cossack clothing originates from southern Russia and includes the burka and papaha.

== Banya ==

One of these traditions is the Russian steam bath, which is also known as a banya.

== National Symbols ==

The aspect ratio of the Russian flag is 2:3.
The Russian national anthem was a patriotic song after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, and the song was composed by Mikhail Glinka.
The melody of the Soviet Union anthem was adopted as the Russian national anthem in 2000, the composer of the Soviet Union anthem melody was Alexander Alexandrov, and new lyrics were written by Sergey Mikhalkov.

Russia has eight—public, patriotic, and religious—official holidays.
The year starts with New Year's Day on 1 January, soon followed by Russian Orthodox Christmas on 7 January; the two are the country's most popular holidays.
Defender of the Fatherland Day, dedicated to men, is celebrated on 23 February.
International Women's Day on 8 March, gained momentum in Russia during the Soviet era.
The annual celebration of women has become so popular, especially among Russian men, that Moscow's flower vendors often see profits of "15 times" more than other holidays.
Spring and Labour Day, originally a Soviet era holiday dedicated to workers, is celebrated on 1 May.

Victory Day, which honours Soviet victory over Nazi Germany and the End of World War II in Europe, is celebrated on 9 May as an annual large parade in Moscow's Red Square; and marks the famous Immortal Regiment civil event.
Other patriotic holidays include Russia Day on 12 June, celebrated to commemorate Russia's declaration of sovereignty from the collapsing Soviet Union; and Unity Day on 4 November, commemorating the 1612 uprising which marked the end of the Polish occupation of Moscow.

There are many popular non-public holidays.
Old New Year is celebrated on 14 January.
Maslenitsa is an ancient and popular East Slavic folk holiday.
Cosmonautics Day on 12 April, in tribute to the first human trip into space.
Two major Christian holidays are Easter and Trinity Sunday.

== New Year and Christmas ==

New Year's Day is celebrated continuously from January 1st to January 5th, and the New Year holiday was extended in 2005.
Russian Orthodox Christians do not celebrate Christmas on December 24, while other Christian denominations celebrate Christmas on December 24.
The celebration takes place according to the Julian calendar, and the Russian Orthodox Church follows the Julian calendar in its entirety.
January 7 was declared an official holiday in Russia in 1991, and all fixed-date Christian holidays are 13 days later than Western ones.
Christmas Eve is called Sotschelnik in Russia and is celebrated on January 6 in Russia.
Russians celebrate Christmas two weeks later than Lutherans and Catholics because the church calendar is 13 days behind the Gregorian calendar.
Many people celebrate the Old New Year.
Russian New Year traditions are similar to Western Christmas traditions and include trees and gifts.
Ded Moroz (Father Frost) plays the same role as Santa Claus, and the local version of Santa Claus in Russia is called Ded Moroz.
The decorated Christmas tree is a tradition in Russia, and gift-giving is a tradition in Russia.

== Easter and Orthodox Traditions ==

Easter is the most popular religious holiday in Russia, and more than 90% of all Russian citizens celebrate it, with a large number of non-religious organizations also celebrating the holiday. [517,518]
More than three-quarters of Russians celebrate Easter by making traditional Easter cake, colored eggs, and paskha. [517,518]
Orthodox Christians celebrate the Feast of the Theophany on January 7, which is one of the oldest Orthodox holidays.
Millions of Russians participate in the event every year, and the event takes place on the night of January 18th to January 19th.
Holidays celebrated in Russia are strongly connected to the church, and Paskha (Easter) is a calendar festival in Russia.
One tradition is coloring and decorating eggs, and one tradition is baking special sweets and cakes.
Easter is the most popular religious holiday in Russia, and a large segment of the Russian population celebrates it, with many non-religious people also celebrating Easter.
More than three-quarters of the Russian population celebrate Easter, and Russians make traditional Easter cakes during Easter celebrations.

Russians dye eggs as part of their Easter celebrations.

== Victory Day ==

Victory Day holds a high status among the population and is the second most popular holiday in the country.
The holiday is held to commemorate the heroism of the sacrifices made by the Russian people.
The Soviet Army defeated the Nazi German Army on May 9, 1945, ending a bloody four-year war on this date [cite: 1494].
Many celebrations are held across the country to mark this event [cite: 1494].
War veterans gather in Russia in early May throughout the country.
The meeting often begins at a grave, a monument to the unknown soldier, or an eternal flame.
The commemoration ceremony is continued at an official reception.
People give carnations to war veterans on Victory Day.
Similar parades occur in all major Russian cities and in many cities in Russia [cite: 3109].
In 2011, military parades took place in 23 cities.
The parade is offered by the President of Russia, and Vladimir Putin attends the parade [cite: 1494].

Victory Day was established to commemorate the victory of the Soviet Union over Germany in the German-Soviet War in 1945.
May 9th has been a public holiday since 1965.
The parade is hosted by the President of Russia.
Similar parades take place in all major cities in Russia, in cities with the status of Hero City, and in Military Glory Cities.

== Maslenitsa ==

Maslenitsa is a calendar festival in Russia that welcomes spring and blossoming and celebrates the beginning of spring.
The date of Maslenitsa changes every year and depends on the date of Easter (Paskha), with the interval between the celebration of Maslenitsa and Paskha usually being about seven weeks.
Maslenitsa celebrations last for one week, beginning on Monday and ending on the following Sunday.
Each day of the Maslenitsa celebration has a specific name.
One of the famous foods of the festival is blini, which symbolizes the sun.
The last day of the Maslenitsa festival is called the Farewell Day and involves lighting a fire and burning an effigy of winter and cold.

== Ivan Kupala Day ==

Ivan Kupala Day is a calendar festival in Russia that celebrates the arrival of summer and is usually held two weeks after the start of the summer season.
Ancient Russians named the god of fertility and abundance in summer Kupala, and to honor this god, people sang songs at night and jumped over fire.
After the appearance of Christianity in Russia, the festival of Kupala merged with Christian customs, and the god Kupala was renamed Ivan after baptism.

== Women's and Men's Holidays ==

International Women's Day is one such commemorative holiday that honors women and mothers, who receive gifts on this day, and combines Mother's Day and Valentine's Day traditions.
Defender of the Fatherland Day especially honors those who serve in the army.

== Professional and Specialized Holidays ==

There are many corporate holidays in addition to public holidays, and the most important of these days are officially celebrated.
One of these holidays is Miner's Day, Teachers' Day, Doctors' Day, Diplomats' Day, Cultural Workers' Day, Nurses' Day, and Lawyers' Day.
May 28 is the day of the border guards, October 5 is Teachers' Day, November 10 is Police Day, and September 13 is recognized as Programmer's Day.
Programmer's Day was officially approved by the Russian Ministry of Information Technology and Communications on July 24, 2009.
The Day of the Special Forces is a holiday.

== City and Regional Holidays ==

Russia has holidays dedicated to specific cities, such as Moscow Day, which takes place at the beginning of September.

== Historical and Abolished Holidays ==

The Day of the October Revolution, which takes place on November 7 and is considered the most important national holiday for Communists, was abolished.
Religious holidays were not allowed during the Soviet era.
The victory of the Tsarist faction over the democratic faction is a national holiday.
The victory of the Russian Orthodox Church over Roman Catholicism is a national holiday.
This holiday is still observed in the 21st century.

== Other Religious and Cultural Observances ==

The roots and origins of calendar rituals in Russia date back to ancient times, and these calendar festivals are based on seasonal changes or religious origins.
New Year (Christian) is a calendar festival in Russia, and Kurban Bayram is celebrated by Russian Muslims.

== Holiday Scheduling ==

If a statutory holiday falls on a Thursday, it is common to establish a Friday as a day off.

== New Year and Orthodox Christmas ==

New Year's Day is a non-working day, and the period from January 1st to January 5th consists of non-working days.
January 2, January 3, January 4, January 5, and January 8 are public holidays designated as New Year's holidays.
Christmas is celebrated according to the Julian calendar, which is accepted by the Russian Orthodox Church.

== Defender of the Fatherland Day ==

February 23 honors Russian military personnel.
Defender of the Fatherland Day is the successor to Red Army Day and Soviet Army and Navy Day.
The holiday was originally established to commemorate the first combat encounters between the newly formed Red Army and German forces during World War I in 1918.

== International Women's Day ==

International Women's Day was originally established as a day to honor female workers in 1910 and as a day of international worker solidarity at the Eighth Congress of the Second International.
The holiday was established to commemorate the dispersal of a workers' demonstration in Chicago in 1886.
In the RSFSR and USSR, it became an official holiday in 1918 as the Day of International Solidarity of Workers and was celebrated starting in 1921.
In the RSFSR and USSR, March 8 became an official public holiday starting in 1965.
In Russia, March 8 combines Mother's Day traditions and Valentine's Day traditions.

== Spring and Labour Day ==

May Day has lost significance.

== Russia Day ==

Russia Day was originally known as Independence Day of Russia and was established to commemorate the adoption of the Declaration on State Sovereignty of the RSFSR in 1990.
From 1649 to 1917, it was celebrated as the day of the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God.
It was re-established in 2004, and the 2004 establishment commemorates the liberation of Moscow from Polish invaders.

== Easter and Maslenitsa ==

Maslenitsa is a pre-Christian spring holiday that occurs in February or March and takes place one week before Easter as well as the week before Lent according to the Julian calendar.
Easter is the most popular religious holiday in Russia, and more than 90% of all Russian citizens celebrate it, including people who do not believe in many religions and non-Christians, while a source states that more than three-quarters of the Russian population celebrate Easter [517,4227].
Orthodox Easter occurs in spring after Lent according to the Julian calendar.
The celebration involves making traditional Easter cakes, dyed eggs, and pasha [517,4227].
January 25 is a day off for students.

== Islamic and Buddhist Holidays ==

Uraza Bayram is celebrated by Russian Muslims.
Both Eid holidays of Islam are public holidays in the Republic of Bashkortostan, the Republic of Ingushetia, and the Kabardino-Balkarian Republic.
Buryatia and Kalmykia declared Vaisakha as a holiday.

== Other Official and Professional Holidays ==

Russia celebrates a number of professional holidays and a number of religious holidays.
The July 8 holiday is the Russian equivalent of Valentine's Day and focuses on family love and fidelity.
The Day of Slavic Alphabet and Culture is on May 24.
Naval Day falls on the last Sunday of July and includes a naval parade in St.
Petersburg and a naval parade in Vladivostok.

== Work Regulations on Holidays ==

Work is permitted on non-working holidays, including work that cannot be suspended due to production and technical conditions, operations in continuously operating organizations, work necessitated by the need to serve the public, and urgent repair and loading/unloading work.

Early Russian painting is represented in icons and vibrant frescos.
In the early 15th century, the master icon painter Andrei Rublev created some of Russia's most treasured religious art.
The Russian Academy of Arts, which was established in 1757, to train Russian artists, brought Western techniques of secular painting to Russia.
In the 18th century, academicians Ivan Argunov, Dmitry Levitzky, Vladimir Borovikovsky became influential.
The early 19th century saw many prominent paintings by Karl Briullov and Alexander Ivanov, both of whom were known for Romantic historical canvases.
Ivan Aivazovsky, another Romantic painter, is considered one of the greatest masters of marine art.

In the 1860s, a group of critical realists (Peredvizhniki), led by Ivan Kramskoy, Ilya Repin and Vasiliy Perov broke with the academy, and portrayed the many-sided aspects of social life in paintings.
The turn of the 20th century saw the rise of symbolism; represented by Mikhail Vrubel and Nicholas Roerich.
The Russian avant-garde flourished from approximately 1890 to 1930; and globally influential artists from this era were El Lissitzky, Kazimir Malevich, Natalia Goncharova, Wassily Kandinsky, and Marc Chagall.

The history of Russian architecture begins with early woodcraft buildings of ancient Slavs, and the church architecture of Kievan Rus'.
Following the Christianization of Kievan Rus', for several centuries it was influenced predominantly by Byzantine architecture.
Aristotle Fioravanti and other Italian architects brought Renaissance trends into Russia.
The 16th century saw the development of the unique tent-like churches; and the onion dome design, which is a distinctive feature of Russian architecture.
In the 17th century, the "fiery style" of ornamentation flourished in Moscow and Yaroslavl, gradually paving the way for the Naryshkin baroque of the 1680s.

After the reforms of Peter the Great, Russia's architecture became influenced by Western European styles.
The 18th-century taste for Rococo architecture led to the splendid works of Bartolomeo Rastrelli and his followers.
The most influential Russian architects of the eighteenth century; Vasily Bazhenov, Matvey Kazakov, and Ivan Starov, created lasting monuments in Moscow and Saint Petersburg and established a base for the more Russian forms that followed.
During the reign of Catherine the Great, Saint Petersburg was transformed into an outdoor museum of Neoclassical architecture.
Under Alexander I, Empire style became the de facto architectural style.
The second half of the 19th century was dominated by the Neo-Byzantine and Russian Revival style.
In the early 20th century, Russian neoclassical revival became a trend.
Prevalent styles of the late 20th century were Art Nouveau, Constructivism, and Socialist Classicism.

== Byzantine heritage and early iconography ==

Russians inherited this art form from Byzantium.
Fresco art flourished between the 14th and 16th centuries [586,587].
Grigory Vefan was a prominent painter around 1340 [586,587].
Andrei Rublev was a distinguished painter known for his poetic style and depth of work [586,587].
Dionysius was a prominent painter active between 1440 and 1503 [586,587].
Relief sculpture reached a high level in Vladimir-Suzdal churches [586,587].

== Kievan Rus and Vladimir-Suzdal architecture ==

After the fall of Kiev, Russian architectural history continued in the principalities of Vladimir-Suzdal and Novgorod.
The 11th century was an era of architectural flourishing in Kievan Rus [cite: 584].
The Golden Gate in Kiev can be taken as an example of the architecture of this era and is located in the southern part of the city [cite: 584].
Ancient Orthodox churches were decorated with numerous domes that were gilded or painted in bright colors [cite: 582,583].
The new style is called the Vladimir-Suzdal style.
Woodblock printing developed in books during the 16th century [cite: 586,587].

== Pre-Christian destruction and fortified architecture ==

Some pre-Christian architectural remains were destroyed by the passage of time, while the majority were destroyed by humans.
Christians zealously destroyed everything that reminded them of polytheism.
The Renaissance arrived in Russia from the late 15th century onwards.
Any architectural remains from this period show signs of fortified buildings, and even churches were built with the possibility of using them as fortresses in mind.

== Narishkin Baroque and 17th-century styles ==

The 17th century is known as the era of Narishkin Baroque, which predates Russian Baroque.
This architectural style was named after the Narishkin noble family, who were the first to build churches in the Russian Empire in the Baroque style.
All palaces built by the Narishkin family in the Baroque style are located in the Moscow region, and the term "Moscow Baroque" became synonymous with "Narishkin Baroque".
In the 17th century, decorative features dominated wall paintings.

== The Russian Academy of Arts and 18th-century painters ==

The purpose of the Russian Academy of Arts was to give an international role and status to Russian artists.
Ivan Argunov, Fyodor Rokotov, Vladimir Borovikovsky, and Dmitry Levitsky were among the most famous painters of the academy.
The academy sent artists abroad in the 1830s, including Aleksander Ivanov and Karl Briullov.

== Romanticism and 19th-century landscape and history painting ==

Ivan Shishkin, Arkhip Kuindzhi, Vasily Polenov, Isaac Levitan, Vasily Surikov, and Victor Vasnetsov were one of the most famous artists.

== The Peredvizhniki and critical realism ==

These artists highlighted the conditions of the poor and depicted the government as caricatures.
Some artists focused on human suffering after the abolition of slavery.

== The Russian avant-garde and modernist movements ==

The term refers to a large and influential wave of modernist art.
The Russian avant-garde included several distinct art movements, including Neo-primitivism, Suprematism, Constructivism, Rayonism, and Futurism.
Wladimir Tatlin and Aleksander Rodchenko were among the most famous artists of that time.
The Russian avant-garde reached its peak between 1917 and 1932, with the year 1932 marking the end of this peak period.

== Soviet art, socialist realism, and the Stalin era ==

The genre's ideas began to clash with socialist realism under Stalin.
Many Soviet artists combined innovation with socialist realism, including Ernst Neizvestny, Ilya Kabakov, Mikhail Shemakin, Erik Bulatov, and Vera Mukhina.

== World War II art and post-war monuments ==

Some Soviet artists painted anti-fascist subjects, and events in World War II were depicted in a particularly patriotic manner.
After the war, sculptors created numerous monuments for the fallen.

== Russian artists in Western Europe ==

Many Russian artists worked in Western Europe.
Wassily Kandinsky's works and ideas were collected worldwide.
Marc Chagall's works and ideas were collected worldwide.
Naum Gabo's works and ideas were collected worldwide.
This spread the impact of Russian art internationally.

== Folk art: Khokhloma, Gostovo, and Gzhel ==

Khokhloma is an example of such folk art crafts and produced wooden items such as spoons, cups, and furniture.
These wooden items were painted with bright gold and red colors, sometimes with light green colors, against a black background.
Gold is not used in the painting process at all, as silver-colored tin is used instead of gold and aluminum powder is also used as an alternative material.
There was a town called Gostovo in the suburbs of Moscow where the residents were famous for their art of painting on metal trays.
There were more than 20 villages located northeast of Moscow that merged together and became famous for their ceramic industries.
One of these villages is called Gzhel, and the name Gzhel ceramics comes from this village.

== Printing and decorative arts ==

Metal printing spread in the 17th century.

== The Moscow Kremlin ==

The Moscow Kremlin is located in the center of Moscow and its construction was completed in 1495.
The complex serves as the official residence of the President of Russia and was used to receive high-ranking officials during the Soviet era.
The Kremlin was declared a World Heritage Site together with Red Square in 1990.

== Peterhof Palace and park ensembles ==

Peterhof Palace is a palace-park ensemble located on the southern coast of the Gulf of Finland in the city of Peterhof.
Peterhof is a city of federal significance situated in the Petrodvorets district of Saint Petersburg, and the area was known as Petrodvorets from 1944 to 1997.
Peterhof Road was named in honor of the ensemble, and a part of that road is under the jurisdiction of the Peterhof State Museum-Reserve.
Peterhof combines several palace-park ensembles that were formed over two centuries.
The Lower Park, the Upper Garden, and the English Park are ensembles developed in the 18th century.
Sergiyevka, the Alexandria Park, the Colonist Park, and the Meadow Park are park complexes created in the 19th century.

== Constructivism and Soviet architectural policy ==

The Constructivist style emerged in the 1920s and 1930s and was a Russian response to the German Bauhaus style.
The decision was made by Khrushchev and aimed to combat extremism in architecture.
During Brezhnev's era, massive spire-like buildings dominated.

== Dacha culture ==

A dacha is a house located on the outskirts of a city, and owners typically live in their dachas during the summer period.
Russian architectural history subsequently continued in the states that followed them: the Kingdom of Moscow, the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union, and contemporary Russia.

== Early Russian Architecture and Monasteries ==

The first significant buildings began to be constructed in the 12th century and in the 13th century.
White architecture from that era is also known as the Old Russian style and was built using white limestone.
The Church of the Dormition of the Theotokos represents this architectural style and these churches are located in Vladimir.
The Solovetsky Monastery was founded in the 15th century and the Moscow Kremlin was founded in the 15th century.
The Trinity-Sergius Lavra is a significant building of the 14th century.
Aristotele Fioravanti built the Uspensky Cathedral in the Moscow Kremlin.
The most significant buildings of the 16th century were the Church of Vasily the Blessed, the Ascension Cathedral in Kolomenskoye, the New Nunnery Monastery, and the Assumption of the Theotokos Monastery in Sviyazhsk.
Kizhi Pogost is an example of wooden sacred architecture, dates from the 18th century, and is located on Lake Onega.

== Saint Basil's Cathedral ==

Saint Basil's Cathedral is an Orthodox church located in the center of Moscow on Red Square.
The church was the tallest building in Moscow until the construction of Ivan the Great Bell Tower.
The church is one of the world's most famous architectural monuments and symbolizes the Heavenly Jerusalem.
The patterns decorating the domes remain an unsolved puzzle to this day, and the meaning of the colors used here remains an unsolved puzzle to this day.
In the previous century, the writer Chayev hypothesized that the colors of the church domes could be explained by the dream of the holy hero Blessed Andrei Yurodivy (of Constantinople).
According to church legends, the feast of the covering of the Mother of God celebrated in the Orthodox world was specifically related to this person.
The cathedral is 65 meters high and consists of small churches.
The altars of these churches are dedicated to holidays coinciding with decisive battle days for Kazan.
One church is dedicated to the Holy Trinity.
One church is dedicated to Saint Nicholas by Miracle, specifically honoring his icon located in Vyatka-Vilyuoretsk.
One church is dedicated to the Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem.
One church is dedicated to Martyrs Adrian and Natalia, originally dedicated to Saints Kyrian and Iustinian and celebrated on October 2.
One church is dedicated to Merciful Saint John, until the 18th century dedicated to Saints Pavel, Alexander, and John of Constantinople and celebrated on November 6.
One church is dedicated to Alexander Svirsky, celebrated on April 17 and August 30.
One church is dedicated to Varlaam the Fool-for-Christ, celebrated on November 6 and the first Friday of the Apostles' Fast.

There are eight churches arranged in a cross shape, four of which are arranged in a cross pattern while the other four are located between the cross-shaped ones.
These eight churches have onion-shaped domes and are formed around a central ninth church dedicated to the intercession of God's Mother.
One church is dedicated to Enlightener Gregory, who is celebrated on September 30.

== Red Square and UNESCO Sites ==

The Red Square was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1990 jointly with the Kremlin.
Concerts are currently held in the square, and religious and historical holidays are commemorated there.
Some historical centers of Russian cities were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, including those of St.
Petersburg, Veliky Novgorod, and Yaroslavl.

== 17th and 18th Century Styles: Baroque, Rococo, and Classicism ==

The great era of Russian architecture began in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Monarchs of an increasingly powerful empire attempted to Europeanize the country during this period.
Europe offered baroque architecture to Russia at that time, and baroque was the primary architectural style offered by Europe.
Siberian Baroque appeared shortly after Naryshkin Baroque in Russia.
The Winter Palace served as the residence of Russian tsars from 1732 to 1917, and the Hermitage Museum is currently located in the Winter Palace.
The Peterhof Palace is often called the 'Russian Versailles' and is Baroque in style.
Russian Rococo is represented primarily by the Catherine Palace, which was a summer residence of the Russian tsars.
Classicism is represented by the Mikhailovsky Palace in St.
Petersburg, where the State Russian Museum is currently located.
The Tauride Palace is also an example of Classicism in St.
Petersburg.

== 19th Century Historicism ==

In St.
Petersburg, 19th-century Historicism is represented by the Church of the Resurrection of Christ, St.
Isaac's Cathedral, and the Kazan Cathedral.
Construction was primarily taking place in Moscow at that time, where Historicism produced the Great Kremlin Palace, the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, the building of the Bolshoi Theatre, the neoclassical building of the Pushkin Museum, and the GUM department store.

== Soviet and Modern Architecture ==

Functionalism became dominant in Soviet-era architecture, and Khrushchev criticized the limits of ancient academic architecture.
Buildings were constructed to solve the housing problem, and various types of apartment buildings were built abundantly from the 1950s.
Stalinist neoclassicism of the 20th century is part of the broader stream of socialist realism.
The Seven Sisters are Stalinist skyscrapers located in Moscow that were built between 1947 and 1957.
One of these buildings houses Lomonosov University, and another of these buildings houses the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The White House is a representative building of socialist realism that was built in 1965 and currently serves as the seat of the Russian government.
Many temples that were demolished during the Soviet era have been rebuilt, and the restoration of various historical buildings destroyed in World War II continued.

== Parks and Gardens ==

The Alexandrov Park and Daça are park complexes created in the 19th century.

== Asian and European Architectural Synthesis ==

Other Italian architects brought Renaissance styles to Russia in the late 15th century.
The Kazan Kremlin and the fortress of Bulgaria show traces of a combination of Asian and European architecture that date back to the time of the Golden Horde.

== Major Museums and Collections ==

The Hermitage is located in St.
Petersburg and manages the largest collection of paintings in the world.
The Tretyakov Gallery is located in Moscow, where Russian visual art treasures are concentrated, and its collection includes 40,000 icons.
The Pushkin Museum and the State Russian Museum are important exhibition institutions.

== Russian Painting: Icons, Academics, and Realism ==

Isaak Levitan, Ivan Shishkin, and Viktor Vasnetsov are famous Russian painters.
Realism dominated the end of the 19th century.
Most visual arts had to serve the dictatorship of the proletariat after the October Revolution.
Restrictions on what artists could paint began to be relaxed in the late 1980s.

== Monuments and Memorials ==

The monument named Motherland Calls is located on Mamayev Kurgan near Volgograd.
The monument was built to commemorate the Battle of Stalingrad, a decisive battle of World War II.
The statue is the largest female statue in the world, and the woman depicted resembles the ancient goddess of victory Nike.

== Traditional Folk Art and Craftsmanship ==

Residential houses in Russia were built using block construction for a long time, a type known as an Isba, and these blockhouses can still be found today in villages. The houses are usually painted in blue or green tones, which are colors associated with Orthodoxy and believed to drive away evil spirits, and they feature elaborate carved window frames that are mostly white. Traditional Russian craftsmanship is an important aspect of Russian folk culture.
Woodturning and wood carving developed in the forest zone of Northeast Russia, while pottery craftsmanship developed in areas where clay was available.
Lace was crocheted in the northern regions of Russia, which had extensive flax fields.
The Ural region is famous for its casting art, weapon jewelry, and jewelry articles, and it has rich deposits of iron ore and semi-precious stones.

The Ural region has rich deposits of gemstones.
Dymkowo ceramic toys, Chochloma, ceramics from Gschel, and lacquer miniatures from Palech are famous.
Matryoshka dolls are the most popular Russian souvenir.
The Matryoshka doll appeared a few years before the 1900 Paris World's Fair, was exhibited at the 1900 Paris World's Fair, and won a medal at the 1900 Paris World's Fair.

== Religious Architecture and Symbolism ==

The onion domes of Russian Orthodox churches have a special meaning, where three domes represent the Trinity and five domes represent Christ and the four Evangelists.
Columns and pillars symbolize angels and saints.
Early sacred buildings in Russia are oriented like Byzantine ones around a Greek cross, a design crowned by five domes.
A distinct Russian style likely originally developed only in the field of wooden architecture, though no buildings made of this material older than the 17th century have survived due to the building material.
The churches that emerged from this style feature a simpler central layout and a large octagonal central tower, and they became more decorative over time.

== Origins and Old Russian Literature ==

Russian literary history began in the 10th century, and until that time, literature was largely influenced by Christianity.

The emergence of Russian literature was linked to the development of feudal Rus' literacy and culture, while the foundation of Russian literature was oral folk creativity.
Old Russian literature developed between the 11th and 14th centuries.
Integral connections between Rus and Byzantium played a significant role in the development of Old Russian literature, and integral connections between Rus and South Slavic culture played a significant role in the development of Old Russian literature.

Fatty, high-energy foods are necessary in winter due to the cold.
Kasha is a porridge.
Botvina is considered a traditional Russian dish.
Russian cuisine uses many fruits.
Vodka is usually made from rye or wheat.

There are 400 news agencies in Russia, among which the largest internationally operating are TASS, RIA Novosti, Sputnik, and Interfax.
Television is the most popular medium in Russia.
Among the 3,000 licensed radio stations nationwide, notable ones include Radio Rossii, Vesti FM, Echo of Moscow, Radio Mayak, and Russkoye Radio.
Of the 16,000 registered newspapers, , Komsomolskaya Pravda, , Izvestia, and Moskovskij Komsomolets are popular.
State-run Channel One and Russia-1 are the leading news channels, while RT is the flagship of Russia's international media operations.
Russia has the largest video gaming market in Europe, with over 65 million players nationwide.

Russian and later Soviet cinema was a hotbed of invention, resulting in world-renowned films such as The Battleship Potemkin, which was named the greatest film of all time at the Brussels World's Fair in 1958.
Soviet-era filmmakers, most notably Sergei Eisenstein and Andrei Tarkovsky, would go on to become among of the world's most innovative and influential directors.
Eisenstein was a student of Lev Kuleshov, who developed the groundbreaking Soviet montage theory of film editing at the world's first film school, the All-Union Institute of Cinematography.
Dziga Vertov's "Kino-Eye" theory had a huge impact on the development of documentary filmmaking and cinema realism.
Many Soviet socialist realism films were artistically successful, including Chapaev, The Cranes Are Flying, and Ballad of a Soldier.

The 1960s and 1970s saw a greater variety of artistic styles in Soviet cinema.
The comedies of Eldar Ryazanov and Leonid Gaidai of that time were immensely popular, with many of the catchphrases still in use today.
In 1961–68 Sergey Bondarchuk directed an Oscar-winning film adaptation of Leo Tolstoy's epic War and Peace, which was the most expensive film made in the Soviet Union.
In 1969, Vladimir Motyl's White Sun of the Desert was released, a very popular film in a genre of ostern; the film is traditionally watched by cosmonauts before any trip into space.
After the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the Russian cinema industry suffered large losses—however, since the late 2000s, it has seen growth once again, and continues to expand.

== History of Russian Cinema ==

Cinema arrived in Russia with the French in 1896, and the first cinematographic devices appeared in April 1896, four months after the first Parisian cinematic sessions took place.
The first permanent cinema opened in May 1896 on Nevsky Prospect in St.
Petersburg, and the first cinemas opened in Russia in 1903.
Camillo Serf conducted the first documentary film shoots in Russia, and the footage depicted celebrations for the coronation of Emperor Nicholas II.
Movie screenings quickly became a popular form of entertainment, and Western films were initially considered a form of cheap entertainment for the working class.
The first feature film in Russia was screened in 1911, and the first feature film in Russia was 'Defense of Sevastopol' [596,597].
The first Russian feature films were adaptations of fragments from classic works of Russian literature and adaptations of folk songs.
Russian cinema had a more serious purpose after the 1917 revolution, and Stalin made socialist realism the state policy.
Socialist realism placed a damper on creativity [98,99].

The first Russian feature films illustrated episodes from Russian history, with examples of these literary adaptations including 'Song of the Merchant Kalashnikov', 'The Idiot', and 'The Fountain of Bakhchisaray'.
An example of a film adapted from a folk song is 'The Swashbuckler Merchant', while examples of films illustrating Russian history include 'The Death of Ivan the Terrible' and 'Peter the Great'.
The first full-length film in Russia was released in 1911, and the title of the film is 'Defense of Sevastopol'.

== Cinema Industry Trends and Notable Works ==

'White Sun of the Desert' introduced a new genre known as 'osterns'.
The Russian film industry experienced a crisis in the 1980s and 1990s, during which state subsidies for film production were drastically reduced and fewer films were produced.
More people started going to theaters at the beginning of the 21st century due to the country's improving economy.
Ticket sales in 2007 were 37% higher than in the previous year.
Russian films are highly rated internationally.
The feature-length film Roesskii Koftsjeg, also known as 'Russian Ark', was released in 2002 and was shot in one single continuous take.

== Media Ownership and State Control ==

Most media are controlled by the state, with large news agencies and television channels being particularly controlled by the state, though the degree of control varies significantly.
State-owned enterprises or oligarchs exercise control over media, and these entities are known as government-friendly.
Gazprom-Media is part of Gazprom, which is the world's largest gas producer and is mostly controlled by the Russian state.
Gazprom-Media holds majority shares in other newspapers, television, and radio stations.
NTW (Independent Television) is one of the media outlets owned by Gazprom-Media; it was originally founded as a private broadcaster in 1993 by oligarch Vladimir Gusinsky and was acquired by Gazprom in 2001.
Itogi is a weekly newspaper owned by Gazprom-Media that became famous for sensational reports about the war in Chechnya.
Echo Moskva (Moscow Echo) is a radio station owned by Gazprom-Media in which Gazprom holds a 66 percent stake, and it is associated with critical journalism.
The newspaper Kommersant has a circulation of 115,000.

Kommersant and the liberal internet newspaper gazeta.ru are owned by billionaire Alisher Usmanov.
WGTRK, which stands for the All-Russian State Company for Television and Radio, is a significant media owner that owns the broadcaster Rossija, the radio station Radio Majak, and the news agency Ria Novosti.
Ria Novosti has correspondents in more than forty countries, while Rossija has eighty regional TV channels.
WGTRK also owns several internet newspapers, including vesti.ru and strana.ru.
Oligarchs often owned more than one media company and support Kremlin policy.
The euphoria of the early 1990s gradually gave way to a type of government-friendly journalism, a trend that was especially evident on Russia's television channels.
These television channels may also act as a mouthpiece for influential oligarchs.

== Key Media Outlets and Circulation ==

The newspaper Rossijskaja Gazeta is directly controlled by the Russian government, functions as a type of state newspaper, and has a circulation of approximately 430,000 copies.
All laws and regulations of the Moscow government only come into force after being published in this newspaper.
The publishing house of Rossijskaja Gazeta is managed by Aleksander Gorbenko, a Moscow official who oversees the government's contact with mass media reporters.
Itar-Tass is the most important Russian news agency and is state-owned.
Izvestia is one of the oldest newspapers in the country, has a circulation of approximately 130,000, and is owned by the Moscow media company Gazprom-Media.
According to mediaatlas.ru, Perwyj Kanal currently attracts the most viewers, more than Rossija and more than NTW.
Regarding printed media, the tabloid newspaper Moskovsky Komsomolets is the most popular daily in the Russian market, is also the cheapest daily in the Russian market, and has a readership of approximately 1.3 million.

== Media Regulation and Roskomnadzor ==

A new national agency called Roskomnadsor was established in March 2007.
Roskomnadsor is responsible for overseeing mass media, communications, and Russia's cultural heritage.
The agency issues licenses and maintains a database of personal data of Russian citizens.
Roskomnadsor is able to monitor individual internet usage, and this monitoring capability is nearly complete.
The Russian Press Law allows Roskomnadzor to warn media outlets about their conduct, and the agency can shut down a media outlet after two warnings.
Roskomnadsor provides information about the media landscape in Russia.
The total number of media outlets listed by the agency was 66,032 in early 2011.
There were 5,254 television stations, 3,769 radio stations, 28,449 newspapers, and 21,572 magazines listed.
The agency Roskomnadzor may restrict access to unwanted websites.

== Press Freedom and Journalist Safety ==

Despite these prerequisites, there is no nationwide broadcaster that provides independent reporting and information on government affairs or offers critical commentary on government policy.
More than 300 journalists have been murdered since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, a statistic based on data from the Russian Journalists' Association and reported on by the Moscow Bureau for Human Rights.
In 2009, 57 journalists became victims of murder attacks.
Nowaja Gazeta is known for its critical stance towards the government and has been subjected to pressure multiple times.
The newspaper is owned by former president Mikhail Gorbachev and banker Alexander Lebedev.
In the autumn of 2010, Roskomnadsor threatened to revoke the newspaper's print license after the newspaper cited an article from a neo-Nazi organization's program and was sued for spreading extremist propaganda.
Ten journalists who worked for Nowaja Gazeta have been killed since 2001.
Several leading journalists have been murdered, including Paul Klebnikov and Anna Politkovskaya.
Reporters Without Borders published a press freedom index in 2017.

Russia ranked 148th out of 180 countries in the 2017 Press Freedom Index.

== Media Consumption and Technology ==

Newspaper vending machines are located in Moscow's metro stations.
A survey conducted by the Russian WZiom Institute found that 95 percent of the Russian population prefers television as their main source of information while only 5 percent prefers newspapers.
There is a rapidly growing market for pay television, and Tricolor is the main provider of satellite distribution.
A project aims to ensure access to digital television reception for all households.
About 30 percent of the population has access to the internet, which is considered the most liberal news medium and provides a media platform for Russian opposition groups.
The Russian government plans to facilitate access to the internet by expanding high-speed internet connections.

== News agencies and print media ==

RIA Novosti is the largest and most modern news agency in Russia and is a state information and analysis agency that has been in existence since 1993.
The daily press of the USSR was supplied with information for decades, primarily provided by the semi-official news agency TASS.
A free press developed in Russia after the collapse of the USSR.
Newspapers are the second most preferred source of information among Russians.
Komsomolskaja Prawda is the most important daily newspaper and has a circulation of 830,000 copies today.
Vladimir Potanin owns Komsomolskaya Pravda and is one of the richest people in the country.
Moskovsky Komsomolets is owned by Vladimir Potanin, is a tabloid newspaper, and is the most popular print media in the country.
Rossijskaja gaseta is a daily newspaper, an official publication of the Russian government, and has a circulation of 430,000 copies.
The Boulevard newspaper claims to reach approximately 1.3 million readers.
Moscow Times is a Russian newspaper published in English.

The most important information agencies are ITAR-TASS, RIA Novosti, and Interfax.

Ria Novosti is a state news agency of Russia operating in Russian.

Rosijskaja Gazeta is a newspaper controlled by the Russian government.
Kommersant, Nezavisimaja Gazeta, Novaja Gazeta, and Pravda are Russian newspapers.

== Radio and television landscape ==

Russia was among the first countries to introduce radio and television.
Radio and television channels were limited during the Soviet era.
In the last two decades, many private and state-owned radio and television stations have appeared.
Radio Russia is a national radio network operated by the Russian state-owned broadcasting company.

== State control and media freedom ==

Russia Today is a state-owned national satellite news channel operated by the Russian state-owned broadcasting company that launched its English-language broadcast in 2005 and its Arabic version in 2007.
In recent years, the Kremlin has strengthened its control over major television networks in Russia, including Channel One, RT (Russia Today), and NTV.
The government owns 51% of the national television network Channel One, while the remaining shares are owned by stockholders.
The Kremlin took control of the NTV channel in 2001 and ordered the closure of TV-6 station in January 2002.
Critics state that independent media suffered as a result of this increased control.
State influence in the field of television is complete, and the state has complete influence in the television sector.
All television stations broadcasting nationwide are either directly state-owned or under state control.
There are no independent media outlets.[1060,1061] The law restricts the work of the media.[1005,1006] The German Federal Foreign Office criticizes restrictions on press freedom in Russia.

There is a state-owned television channel that is entirely under control.
Media freedom in Russia involves the ability of media directors to implement independent policies, the ability of journalists to access information sources, and the ability of journalists to work without external pressure.
Russian media include internet media.
According to Russian Federation laws, media can be state-owned or privately owned.
The ranking was published by Reporters Without Borders in 2013.
Freedom House reported on Russia in 2015 and gave Russia a score of 8.93 out of 100.
New laws were introduced in Russia in 2014 that extended state control over mass media.
Multiple international organizations criticize various aspects of press freedom.
William Dunkerley is a media expert who works at the American University in Moscow.

== Early cinema and the Soviet era ==

Russian cinema experienced its first period of prosperity during World War I [596,597].
Cinema journalism developed rapidly during this period [596,597].
Eleven film magazines were published in Russia in 1916 [596,597].
Two thousand seven hundred films were produced during the Russian Empire era [596,597].
Only 300 of those films remained by 1917 [596,597].
Russian cinema experienced a strong surge after 1917.
Soviet cinema also experienced a strong surge after 1917.
This surge resulted in the creation of several world-famous films.
The Battleship Potemkin is one such famous film.
Sergei Mikhailovich Eisenstein is the director of The Battleship Potemkin.
Lev Kuleshov was a film director and theorist.
Dziga Vertov became a classic of documentary film.
Russian films began to appear after the October Revolution.
The film-eye theory was used for filming in the most realistic manner, like the human eye.
Socialist realism policy imposed some limitations on creativity.
Soviet restrictions on creativity existed.
Several world-famous films were produced despite these restrictions.
The film Wings Over the Caucasus (Leyləklər Uçarkən) is an example of a successful Soviet film under this policy.
The film Song of the Soldier (Əsgər Nəğməsi) is an example of a successful Soviet film under this policy.
The song Ballad of a Soldier was made in the Soviet Union.

During Stalin's era, state socialist realism policies somewhat limited filmmakers' creativity.
The film series War and Peace was released in 1967.
The film Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears was released in 1980 and was directed by Vladimir Menshov.
Three Soviet films and one Russian film have won an Academy Award.
The film Wings of the Wind, also known as Crane Flies South, was directed by Mikhail Kalatozov.

== Post-war renaissance and classic directors ==

A new renaissance of Soviet cinema emerged after World War II and was associated with the names Bondarchuk and Chukhrai [cite: 598,599].
Dovzhenko, Pudovkin, and Alexandrov were among these directors [cite: 598,599].
The film War and Peace was released in 1965 and won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film in 1968 [cite: 598,599].
The film Moscow Does Not Know Tears was directed by Vladimir Menshov [cite: 600,601].
The film The Ninth Company was directed by Mikhail Kalatozov and won the Golden Palm at the Cannes Film Festival in 1958 [cite: 600,601].
The film Ivan's Childhood was directed by Andrei Tarkovsky and won the Golden Lion award at the Venice Film Festival in 1962 [cite: 600,601].
Solaris is another film by Andrei Tarkovsky and won an award at the Cannes Film Festival in 1972 [cite: 600,601].
Irony of Fate is a comedy directed by Eldar Ryazanov.
Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears is an Oscar-winning film directed by Vladimir Menshov.
Andrei Konchalovsky is a famous film director [cite: 815].
Nikita Mikhalkov is a famous film director [cite: 815].

== International awards and recognition ==

The film *Return* (Vozvrashcheniye) was directed by Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev and won the Golden Lion award at the 2003 Venice International Film Festival.
Gleb Panfilov won the Golden Bear award, which is awarded at the Berlinale film festival, in 1987.
Alexandr Sokurov won the Golden Lion at the festival that took place in Venice in 2011.
Andrei Zvyagintsev won a Golden Globe award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2014.

== Animation history and iconic characters ==

Russian animation dates back to the late period of the Russian Empire and has historical roots in the era preceding the Soviet Union.
During the Soviet era, Soyuzmultfilm, an animation studio, was the largest animation producer.
Soviet animation developed a wide range of leading techniques and featured diverse aesthetic styles.
Ivan Ivanov-Vano, Fyodor Khitruk, and Alexander Tatarsky were prominent Soviet animators.
Many Soviet cartoon characters were iconic images of Russian cinema and were also iconic in many surrounding countries.
Russian Winnie-the-Pooh and The Wolf and the Rabbit (Nu, Pogodi!) are among these characters.
The most famous characters belong to Russia and surrounding countries, including Cheburashka, Misha the Bear (Russian Winnie the Pooh), and the wolf and the hare from 'Wait for the Hare!'.

== Crisis and recovery in the 1990s and 2000s ==

The late 1980s and 1990s were a period of crisis in Russian animation and Russian film. [cite: 604,605]
Government support was significantly reduced during this time, which led to a decrease in the number of films produced. [cite: 604,605]
Filmmakers were given freedom to express themselves during this period. [cite: 604,605]
The early years of the 21st century brought an increase in viewership against the backdrop of economic recovery. [cite: 604,605]
The total Russian box office revenue in 2007 was approximately $565 million, representing a 37% increase compared to the previous year. [cite: 606,607]

== Modern blockbusters and popular films ==

The drama film Island was directed by Pavel Longin and received several local awards.
Fyodor Bondarchuk is an actor who directed a film based on real events that occurred during the war in Afghanistan, which is considered one of the most popular films in Russia.
The movie Night Watch (2004) was the first true blockbuster and had a sequel.
Irony of Fate 2 (2007), Mysterious Island (2008), Stalingrad (2013), and Viy (2014) are one of the most successful Russian films.

== Actors and film awards ==

Yevgeny Leonov and Mikhail Ulyanov were popular actors.
The main Russian film award is called the Nika, which has been given annually since 1987 by the Russian Film Academy in Moscow.

== Television landscape and reach ==

Television is the primary information source for 85% of the Russian population and is often the only information source for this group, while the government carefully controls the content direction of television programs.
In most parts of Russia, three nationwide television channels and one to two regional television channels can be received.
More than a dozen television providers are available in Moscow, and the number of available providers depends on the location within Moscow.
These providers can be received via terrestrial transmission.
The First Channel (Erster Kanal) has the widest reach nationwide, with 99.8% of the Russian population able to receive it and a weekly audience reaching over 80% of the population.
A portion of Russian television channels is operated by the state media conglomerate VGTRK.
According to its own statements, the channel Rossiya 1 can be received by approximately 98.8% of the Russian population.
The name of the cultural channel is Rossija K, and a sports channel named Sport exists.
Both the Sport and Rossija K channels are operated by WGTRK.
Vesti is one of the most important news channels in Russia and is part of the Telekanal Rossija network and the RTR network.

The TV channel Russian TV International is produced specifically for Russians living abroad.
Russia uses the SECAM television standard, and the Russian variant of SECAM is the Eastern Europe version.
The channel Sport currently broadcasts on the TW-6 frequency.
Russia plans to introduce DVB-T in the 2010s.
Such devices are allegedly subsidized to enable the population to purchase the relatively expensive device.

== International broadcasting and RT ==

Golos Rossii (Voice of Russia) is an international broadcaster.
RIA Novosti was merged with Golos Rossii to form the international information agency Rossiya Segodnya (Russia Today).
Russia Today has existed since 2005, is based in Moscow, broadcasts in English among other languages, and has the stated goal of presenting the Russian perspective on international events to the audience.
Russia Today is considered a propaganda instrument directly initiated by the Kremlin.
The idea for the founding of Russia Today is attributed to Mikhail Lesin.
In 2011, the channel had more employees worldwide than Fox News.
The channel spreads conspiracy theories and succeeded in gaining a large audience in the West.

== Radio broadcasting ==

The situation in the radio sector is similar to that of television.
There are numerous private radio stations in Russia, most of which are local stations, while some Moscow stations have licenses in the regions.
Radio Rossii is a state-owned radio station.
The radio station Echo Moskwa existed until 2022, when it was forced to cease operations, and until its forced interruption, it was the only remaining representative of government-critical media.
Russian radio stations currently use FM frequencies in the range of 87.5 MHz to 108.0 MHz, whereas the OIRT band, which ranged from 65.9 MHz to 73.1 MHz, was used during Soviet times.
Many Russian apartments have a radio jack that allows receiving one to three stations.
An extensive foreign broadcasting service is operated under the name Voice of Russia, which is the national radio station.
KBS World Radio broadcasts in Russian.
There is a radio station in Sakhalin.

Russia was among the first countries in the world to introduce radio and among the first countries in the world to introduce television.
Voice of Russia is one of the oldest radio stations in the country.
Russian media includes the State Radio of Russia in Russian.
In 2006, there were approximately 3,500 radio stations in Russia.
The radio station broadcasts in Korean.
The radio station is run by Russian intelligence.
The radio station is operated by the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

== Media ownership and historical evolution ==

There have been many restructuring phases in the Russian media sector since the collapse of the Soviet system.
State reforms privatized the media market at the beginning of the 1990s.
Many newspapers, publishers, and television broadcasters formed alliances with oligarchs to ensure their survival.
The oligarchs exercised political influence over the media through manipulation.
Media empires owned by Boris Berezovsky and Vladimir Gusinsky, including the Media Most empire of Boris Berezovsky, opposed President Putin and were dismantled by court order.
Gazprom-Media and WGTRK, the All-Russian State Company for Television and Radio, are among the largest Russian media holdings.
A new media group was added to the 'List of Strategic Enterprises of Russia', which are enterprises having special significance for the defense capability and security of the country.
Several private television channels developed in Russia during the 1990s, some with nationwide reach, that included independent programming and government-critical information programs.

At the beginning of the 2000s, nationwide receivable broadcasters came under indirect state control.
Some nationwide receivable broadcasters were closed down and replaced by state-run broadcasters.

== Censorship, regulation, and press freedom ==

Censorship occurs in practice due to repression and bans of regime-critical broadcasters, ownership structures, and partial self-censorship.
According to Reporters Without Borders, Russia ranked 149th out of 180 countries in 2019, and press freedom in Russia is continuing to decline.
Guidelines with language rules and argumentation lines are written and sent to broadcasters.
Supervision, control, and censorship occur below the Kremlin administration, and the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media (Roskomnadzor) carries out this supervision.
This supervision covers both the media landscape and private communication in electronic media.
Roskomnadsor blocked almost all independent media since February 2022.
The Duma passed a censorship law in March 2022 that mandates reporting only based on official state sources, and violating this law carries the threat of high prison sentences.
Roskomnadsor is the authority responsible for media censorship and oversees mass media, communication, and the protection of cultural heritage.
Roskomnadsor listed 66,032 media outlets in Russia based on data from the year 2012, including 3,769 radio stations and 21,572 magazines.

There are 5,254 TV stations.
Andreas Umland pointed out in 2016 that state television channels are not mass media in the Western sense and utilize propaganda.
Press freedom is experiencing a general downward trend.
In 2002, the country was recorded as 'partially free'.
Only Turkey scored worse than Russia in Europe on that list, and Turkey ranked 165th in Europe on that list.

== Impact of the 2022 information war ==

After the 2022 ban on remaining domestic media and Western social networks, Russians increasingly turned to Telegram channels to access information, and the Kremlin uses channels close to it to influence public opinion through this opportunity.
Independent media, Facebook, and Instagram can only be accessed via VPN, and independent media left the country.

== Violence against journalists ==

Journalist Nikolai Andruschtschenko was killed in the spring of 2017.
A report by Reporters Without Borders states that the death of the victim is directly related to his journalistic activity.

== Internet infrastructure and domains ==

The history of the internet in Russia began in September 1990, when the top-level domain '.su' was registered for the Soviet Union.
Russian websites use the '.su' domain partially or intermittently and continue to use it up to the present day.
The official top-level domain '.ru' was registered in March 1994 and is intended for Russian internet addresses.
Websites under the '.ru' domain make up a significant portion of the Russian internet, which is often referred to as the Runet.
Russia has a Cyrillic top-level domain, which is .рф.

== Internet usage and growth ==

The Russian internet segment ranked fourth worldwide around 2012 and had more than 3.6 million domain names in total.
The number of internet users in Russia increased continuously during the 2000s.
In the year 2000, there were 3.1 million internet users in Russia, accounting for 2.1% of the population.
In 2007, there were 28 million internet users in Russia, accounting for 19.5% of the population.
Russia had more than 50 million internet users in 2011 and became the leading country in Europe for internet usage.
In 2016, 102 million Russians used the internet, representing 71.3% of the population.

== Major online platforms and portals ==

Rambler, Yandex, VKontakte, RBC Informations Systems, Lenta.ru, and Gazeta.ru are among the most significant Internet projects in the Runet.
VKontakte is an online network, while RBC Informations Systems, Lenta.ru, and Gazeta.ru are information and news portals.

== Telecommunications providers ==

CenterTelekom, MGTS, North-West Telecom, and WolgaTelekom are among the most well-known providers.
Rostelekom is the largest company in the Russian telecommunications industry and operates across Russia.
As of April 1, 2011, Rostelekom acquired regional branches including Dalny Wostok (Far East), Sibir, Ural, Wolga, Jug (South), Sewero-Sapad (North-West), and Zentr (Center).
The mobile telecommunications market in Russia is shared by three main national providers: Mobile TeleSystems, Beeline, and MegaFon.

== Social media and state support ==

The Russian government provided funding for internet expansion, and social media activities in Russia experienced a very strong surge due to this state support.
Vkontakte.ru and Odnoklassniki.ru are platforms created in Russia that are particularly popular and showed higher growth rates than international platforms.
LiveJournal eventually became Russian and was used above average in Russia compared to international usage.
The gross reach of social networks in Russia was approximately 49.2 million people in 2010.

== Internet regulation and censorship ==

Starting in 2018, all communication content had to be stored and made available to the state, though a five-year postponement of this obligation was considered due to the workload in 2017.
Censorship was effectively reintroduced in Russia following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, leading to works and authors such as Ivan Vyrypaev sometimes no longer being performed by direct order, including the cancellation of Bulgakov's 'The Master and Margarita' (Adam und Eva).
The state regulatory authority repeatedly reviewed films, while propagandist Dmitri Kiselyov called for restrictions on freedom of speech in 2018 due to critical films, resulting in some foreign productions not being shown at all and release dates for other films being set so they would not compete with patriotic Russian films.

== Early cinema and Soviet era ==

Russian film history began during the era of the Russian Empire.
Alexander Chanchonkov, Ivan Mozzukhin, and Vera Khlopnaya were silent film pioneers.
Russian fairy tales formed the basis for famous Soviet fairy tale films.
Cinema in the Soviet Union was subject to strict ideological censorship.
The Soviet era produced many popular actors and many popular films.
Many Russians still consider the Soviet era as the peak of Russian film art and the peak of acting schools.

== Modern film production and awards ==

Kirill Serebrennikow is a director.
Russian films occasionally achieved international success since the 1990s.
The film 'The Sun Also Rises' (Die Sonne, die uns täuscht) was released in 1994.
'The Return' is a youth drama released in 2003 and directed by Andrei Svjagintsev.
Andrei Svjagintsev won the Golden Lion at the Venice International Film Festival for 'The Return'.
'Night Watch' (Wächter der Nacht) is a fantasy film adaptation released in 2004 that became the most commercially successful Russian film production to date.
The Nika is the most important film award in Russia and is awarded by the Russian Academy of Cinematography.

== Film studios ==

Goskino, Sowkino, Mosfilm, Lenfilm, Gorki Film Studio (formerly Meshrabpom), and Sojusmultfilm are among the largest Russian film studios.
Sojusmultfilm is an animation studio.

== Cinema attendance and market share ==

Movie attendance in Russia increased enormously up until 2012, an increase observable in Russia but not in Europe.
Cinema attendance in Russia nearly doubled, yet Russian film production maintained its market share despite this increase.
The market share of Russian films was higher than average compared to Europe, and since 2005, the market share of Russian films in Russia has always been more than a quarter of all cinema visits.

== Digital video and online content ==

Video art is very popular in modern Russia.
Russia is one of the most important markets for YouTube.
The most popular episode is from the Russian animated series 'Masha and the Bear' and has received over 3 billion views.
The Show +100500 is particularly popular and hosts BadComedian.
BadComedian makes reviews for popular movies.
The channel '+100500' is particularly popular, hosts video reviews for funny videos, and is associated with BadComedian.
Many Russian movie trailers have been nominated for Golden Trailer Awards.
Many videos by a Russian editor, poet, and publicist were uploaded to major YouTube channels, and this person is the founder of poetic trailer creation and trailer construction.
Russia is one of the primary markets for YouTube.
The most popular episode of the Russian animated TV series Masha and the Bear has over 3 billion views.

== Newspapers and Print Media ==

Argumenty i Fakty and Rossiyskaya Gazeta are among the most popular newspapers.
Pravda, Sport-Ekspress, and Komsomolskaja Pravda are widely circulated newspapers.
Komsomolskaja Pravda is a widely circulated tabloid.

ORT, RTR, and Ren TV are among the largest state-owned television channels.
There are over 250 Russian-language channels.
The main channels in Russia are Pervyi kanal, Rossija-1, and NTV.

== Soviet broadcasting structure ==

Local television broadcasts were on the 2nd program, with the Leningrad Television Studio and the Main Editorial Office for Moscow and the Moscow Region of Central Television serving as exceptions that broadcast their own 'third' programs.[3820,3821,3822,3823,3824,3825,3826,3827,3828,3829] Local radio broadcasts were on the 1st program, which was a mixed program consisting of local broadcasts and broadcasts from the First All-Union Program, while the second program broadcast the Second All-Union Program and the third program broadcast the Third All-Union Program.[3820,3821,3822,3823,3824,3825,3826,3827,3828,3829] A wired radio broadcasting network existed.[3820,3821,3822,3823,3824,3825,3826,3827,3828,3829] Local radio and television broadcasts were conducted on the 2nd TV channel and the 3rd radio channel by local state broadcasting companies, though the Moscow and St.
Petersburg regional entities transmitted their own 'third' television channels instead.[3830,3831] The first channel remained mixed and consisted of local broadcasts and broadcasts from the third federal radio channel, while the second channel broadcast the second federal radio channel and the third channel broadcast the first federal radio channel.
Wired radio broadcasting continued to exist.

== Transition of federal media (1992–2004) ==

Between 1992 and 1995, the first federal television channel, the first federal radio channel (Radio 1), and the second federal radio channel (Mayak) were managed by Ostankino, while the second federal television channel and the third federal radio channel (Radio Russia) were managed by VGTRK.
RTRK Ostankino was abolished in 1995, and a joint-stock company with state participation named 'Public Russian Television' and the All-Russian State Radio Company 'Mayak' were created to replace it.
Radio 1 was abolished in 1997, and the broadcasting of the first radio channel and the third wired television channel was transferred to various commercial radio stations.
In 1998, the 'Mayak' radio company was transferred under the management of VGTRK, and since 2004, it has been a branch of VGTRK.
From 2004 onwards, these local state broadcasting companies became branches of VGTRK.

== Doping and Sanctions ==

Doping abuse is a major stain on the reputation of Russian sports, with many indications that doping was abused in Russia and state assistance involved in the doping abuse.
The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) excluded Russia from all major competitions in 2019, and this exclusion lasted for four years.
There are exceptions to this ban, yet Russian athletes cannot compete in international competitions.
Forty-three athletes were punished, and 13 Russian medals from the Sochi Olympics were stripped.
An appeal was successfully filed regarding these sanctions, resulting in 28 Russians being cleared of doping violations and 9 medals being returned in February 2018.

== Doping Scandals and Sanctions ==

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) accuses Russia of operating systematic, state-controlled doping for years [1363,1364].
These manipulations were directed, controlled, and supervised by the Ministry of Sport and supported by the domestic secret service FSB [1363,1364].
The manipulations affected almost all sports, and a deeply rooted culture of fraud existed in the Russian Athletics Federation [1363,1364].
Positive doping samples were swapped at the 2013 World Athletics Championships in Moscow, the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi, and the 2015 World Aquatics Championships in Kazan [1363,1364].
The affected athletes were Russian [1363,1364].
In November 2015, WADA withdrew accreditation from RUSADA, the national Russian anti-doping agency.
The World Athletics Federation (IAAF) imposed an indefinite ban on Russian athletes for all international competitions, including the Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro [1366,1367].
The international federation IWF made a decision that Russian weightlifters were not allowed to compete in Rio.

WADA issued an Olympic ban for the Russian team and banned the Russian anti-doping agency RUSADA in December 2019 for four years due to various doping scandals involving manipulated athlete data.
Proceedings regarding Russian state-sponsored doping were to be heard in autumn 2020 before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), which set a date for the hearing from November 2 to November 5, and the hearing took place in November.
RUSADA filed an objection with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
This was the first time Russia hosted the FIFA World Cup, with the tournament taking place in Moscow, St.
Petersburg, and the Kaliningrad exclave.
FIFA imposed sanctions on the Russian national team due to the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, involving suspending the team from participating in the tournament, which resulted in the Russian team being eliminated in the qualifiers without playing any matches.
The criticism is due to alleged national involvement in doping issues.

Anti-doping measures have become a major issue.
Russian athletes were accused of widespread doping in 2015.
A decision was made in December 2019 to ban Russian athletes from international competitions for four years.
The World Anti-Doping Agency made a decision in 2019 regarding Russia's doping data tampering.
The WADA decided to ban Russia from participating as a nation for four years.
The ban resulted in Russia competing under the designation ROC at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics.
Russian athletes participated individually under the designation OAR (Olympic Athlete from Russia).
The official records from the Olympics were under the designation OAR.
Even if a team wins, the national flag is not raised and the national anthem is not played.
Instead, the Olympic flag is raised and the Olympic Hymn is played.
Mixed doubles curling became an official event at the PyeongChang Games.
A Russian pair initially won a bronze medal in mixed doubles curling.
Doping was discovered in the Russian pair that won the bronze medal.
The Russian pair had to return their bronze medal due to doping.

Russia faced doping allegations for several years [cite: 4008].
The IOC decided to impose sanctions on Russia on December 5, 2017 [cite: 4008].
Russian athletes and teams were forced to compete without the Russian flag and without the national anthem of Russia at podium ceremonies [cite: 4008].
This restriction applied for several years [cite: 4008].
Some of the doping was state-organized [cite: 3939].
Russia was banned from competing in all international competitions in 2019 due to doping and attempts to interfere with investigations [cite: 3940,3941,3942].
The ban lasted for 4 years and was later reduced to 2 years [cite: 3940,3941,3942].
Russia was banned from the 2020 Summer Olympics [cite: 3940,3941,3942].
Russian athletes will be forced to compete under a neutral flag for the entire duration of their ban.
Russia is currently banned from participating in a large number of different international competitions [cite: 3943,3944].

Germany and Russia had long-standing alliance traditions that existed until the end of the 19th century.
The Kingdom of Prussia was closely allied with the Russian Empire from 1763 to 1871, a period that began after the end of the Seven Years' War in 1763 and ended with the founding of the German Empire in 1871.
Prussia was saved from near total destruction twice in its history by Russia, first in 1762 when Tsar Peter III switched sides during the Seven Years' War and again in 1807 when Tsar Alexander I intervened on behalf of Napoleon in the Treaty of Tilsit.
Russians and Germans fought together during the Wars of Liberation, during which Russian soldiers played a significant role in the liberation of Germany.
After the Congress of Vienna, the alliance continued as the Holy Alliance.

The majority of the Russian postal system is handled by a state-owned company called Pochta Rossii.

Ancient Russia had a calendar system in which the year consisted of 12 months named based on natural phenomena.
After adopting Christianity, Ancient Russia used the Roman calendar system, specifically the Julian calendar, and adopted the Roman division of months and days of the week while choosing the names of the days of the week for themselves.
Monday is considered the first day of the week.
Three calendars have been used in Russia, with the Gregorian calendar serving as the main calendar used in Russia after its adoption with the establishment of the Soviet government.
Before that period, the Julian calendar was in use in Russia, a calendar that was introduced to Russia by Tsar Peter the Great and is used almost exclusively by the Russian Orthodox Church.
Before the Julian calendar, the Slavic calendar was in use.

The basis of the calendar was not the birth of Jesus Christ but the beginning of creation.
In the Slavic calendar, the year 2018 AD is equivalent to the year 7526.
The New Year was celebrated on March 1st before the start of the New Year was moved to September 1st.

The folded regions of Russia include the northwestern part of the Pacific Folded Belt, the Uralo-Mongolian epipaleozoic folded belt, and a small section of the outer zone of the Mediterranean folded belt.
The Caucasus Mountains are located in younger folded regions.
Folded regions contain significant deposits of metal ores, and the main reserves of metallic ores are located in these regions.
The Siberian platform has an Eoarchean age.
The largest coal deposits, the largest deposits of stone and potash salts, and the largest oil and gas deposits in Russia are associated with the cover of the Siberian Platform.
Copper-nickel deposits in Norilsk are associated with trap intrusions on the Siberian Platform, and diamonds are associated with kimberlite pipes on the Siberian Platform.
The Ural-Mongolian epipaleozoic fold belt consists of several structural domains and separates two ancient platforms.
The domains of this fold belt include the Rifean domain, the Baikal domain, the Salair domain, the Caledonian domain, and the Hercynian domain.
The Yenisei-Sayan-Baikal region is an area of Rifean and Baikal folding.

The Yenisei-Sayan-Baikal region surrounds the Siberian Platform.
The Preduralian marginal trough is located along the boundary with the East European Platform and is filled with Permian strata.
Coal deposits are found in the northern part of the Preduralian marginal trough, while potassium salt deposits are found in its central part.
The Pacific Folded Belt is present in the territory of Russia, where the Russian part represents its extreme northwestern section.
Ancient Dorsiferan massifs, areas of Mesozoic and Cenozoic folding, and modern tectonically active zones are located within this northwestern section.
Gold, tin, tungsten, and mercury deposits are known in the Verkhoyano-Chukotka region.
The gold deposits are associated with Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous granitic intrusions.
Coal deposits are located in molasses within the Predverkhoyansk sag and the Zyryan depression.
The West Kamchatka Folded System is a terrigenous geosynclinal complex that dates from the Upper Cretaceous period.
